definition.name: Keep the change reviewable
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the meaningful portion of this change is batched at a size and spread a reviewer can read end-to-end with confidence.

## The standard
Judge whether this change is packaged so a reviewer can actually read it end-to-end and approve it responsibly. This is a workflow practice about how work is batched for review — never a code-defect claim about the code itself. A focused change does one coherent thing across a handful of related files; a sprawling one forces the reviewer to skim, and bugs slip through the gaps. Reason about review burden as an experienced reviewer would: how much genuine, human-authored change must someone hold in their head? Use judgment, not a fixed line or file count. Size and spread are evidence of review burden, not automatic failures: account for cohesion, complexity and how the change is presented. Separate repetitive generated or vendored churn from material changes a reviewer must inspect. A migration, snapshot or generated contract can carry consequential behavior and is not discounted merely because of its file type. Judge the meaningful review work, not raw totals.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, state the fact that rules it out, and stop when there is no reviewable content to size at all, or when the change contains only reproducible generated or vendored churn with no material change requiring review.

## Sources
1. The provider counts (`context/metadata.json`): additions, deletions, total and changed-file count as synced. They establish the headline size. They never override the diff: when they materially disagree with the actual diff (a known mirror or staleness limitation), trust the diff and say so.
2. The file index (`work/change/files.json`): the per-file spread and which files carry repetitive generated, vendored or lock churn and which carry meaningful changes. It establishes breadth and lets you distinguish repetitive churn from consequential changes. It never establishes a per-commit file mapping.
3. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): ground truth for what was actually changed and how much of it is meaningful. It establishes the counts you report. It never establishes whether the code is correct.
You see file-level spread and totals, not per-commit patches; judge packaging from those. If the required size fields and the diff needed to derive them were not captured, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Read the counts, the file index and the diff, and separate the meaningful portion from churn. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: the meaningful change is small and cohesive enough that a teammate could plausibly read every meaningful line and feel confident — a tight batch. Never grade an empty or unmeasurable change as a well-sized strength.
- NOT_MET: the change is large or scattered enough that careful line-by-line review becomes impractical, so smaller or stacked changes would serve the reviewer better. Name the size and the spread you measured.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the change plainly has meaningful content, but after reading the complete diff the generated bulk cannot be separated from the meaningful portion, so you cannot size it. The work was batched; you could not measure it. Name what would let you separate them. Having measured a sprawling change is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, over the whole change.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; formative, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a light nudge toward smaller batches. MAJOR: a recommendation to split or stack, reserved for sprawl across many files that almost certainly bundles unrelated concerns. Size or spread alone never exceeds MAJOR, and raw line count by itself never reaches it.

## Grounding
State the exact additions, deletions, total and changed-file count you used and where you read them; never invent a count. For NOT_MET, describe the observable packaging — "touches N files / ~M changed lines, spread across unrelated areas" — citing the file index lines and diff hunks that show the spread, and state the captured reason any repetitive churn was discounted. For MET, cite the counts and the file index that bound the batch. Never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot see. Never impute intent, haste or character.

## Defer
Whether the touched files form one logical concern is a cohesion judgment owned by the area framing and by `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; do not re-litigate single-concern semantics that a file index cannot decide. Whether generated files belong in the change at all belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`. Here only: is the meaningful batch a size and spread one reviewer can read with confidence?

guidance.whyItMatters: A reviewer can only hold so much in their head at once. A focused change gets read carefully. A sprawling one gets skimmed, and its bugs slip through.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: One goal across a handful of related files, small enough that a teammate can read every line that matters and approve it with confidence.
guidance.goingWell: Each change is packaged for careful review

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, split the change where your reviewer would start to skim.
- Open each part that a teammate can review and merge without the rest as its own change. For example, instead of one change that adds CSV export, its settings page and its emails, open the export first. Then open the settings page and the emails as smaller changes on top of it.
- Say in the description which files are lockfile, generated or vendored updates, or put them in their own change. Then the reviewer can see what needs a careful read.
- Do the groundwork first. Move or rename code in its own change, so the next change shows only the new behavior.
- If the new code replaces old code, remove the old code in its own change, after nothing uses it.

![Three changes follow in order. The first only moves or renames code, the second adds only the new behavior, and the third removes old code after nothing uses it.](figures/split-order.svg)

## When it does not apply

- The change has nothing to review.
- The change holds only generated or vendored files that a tool can produce again, with nothing in them to review.

It still applies when a migration, a snapshot or a generated contract changes what the software does.

## Common mistakes

- Looking for a line or file limit. There is none. Instead, look at the work your reviewer must read with care. A long change that does one simple thing can be easy to read. A short change spread across unrelated areas can be hard to read.
- Splitting work into changes that cannot be read alone. Instead, make each change self-contained, so it makes sense by itself and keeps the build working.

## Sources

- [Small CLs](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html), Google Engineering Practices. Google advises small, self-contained changes, with refactorings in their own change and no hard size limit.
- [Modern code review: a case study at Google](https://doi.org/10.1145/3183519.3183525), Sadowski and others, 2018. Most changes at Google are small and get reviewed quickly. Google sells developer tools.
- [Characteristics of useful code reviews: an empirical study at Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/characteristics-of-useful-code-reviews-an-empirical-study-at-microsoft/), Bosu, Greiler and Bird, 2015. The more files a change touched, the smaller the share of its review comments that helped its author. Microsoft sells code review tools.
- [Parallel change](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ParallelChange.html), Danilo Sato, 2014. Replace code in steps, and remove the old version only after every caller uses the new one.

definition.name: Describe what changed and why
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the title and description state what this change does and a concrete reason why it exists, so a reviewer is oriented before opening the diff.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: can a reviewer understand WHAT this pull request changes and WHY from the title and description alone? Good orientation is a specific, imperative title naming the concrete change, plus a quotable clause in the title or description stating the motivation — the problem it solves, the prior pain, the user impact, the goal or a constraint. A story-id or tag prefix such as "[Feat] US5.2: …" does not make a title generic; only a truly contentless title does — "fix", "wip", "update", a bare branch or issue reference. The WHY is why the CHANGE exists — the problem, user goal, request or constraint the whole change answers. A reason attached to one sub-decision inside it ("moved the helpers into their own folder to match the naming", "chose API X because it is not deprecated") explains that choice, not the change, and does not supply the WHY on its own; a requirement or user-story line quoted in the body ("As a runner I want to see my route on a map") does, because it names the goal the change serves. Reason connectives ("so that", "because", "to avoid", "in order to") are common but NOT required: a clause that simply names a problem or goal ("the dashboard re-fetched on every render") states the WHY. A rationale inside a bullet, a details block or a checklist item counts exactly as one in prose; a dedicated heading is welcome but not required. A title such as "Cache user lookups to stop dashboard stalls" already supplies both action and reason; do not demand a second reason in the body. Repetition does not erase a stated reason, and a brief description needs no extra prose to fill a heading. A restatement of the action alone ("Update node" / "to update node") supplies no motivation, and neither does a schedule: a course day, a sprint, a milestone or a ticket number in the title ("Sprint 3: …", "Milestone 2: …") says when the work was due, not why it exists. Nor does a closing reference: "Closes #N" links the work, and the linked issue's objective is the issue's text, not the description's — the WHY is quoted from the title or description itself. A sentence that restates the title in the first person ("I added the export screen as planned"), or that only names the feature, mechanism or components built ("the report can now be exported as CSV"), is the WHAT again, not a reason. A natural statement of the user goal, the effect for users or the task the change serves is a WHY, even in the same clause as the WHAT ("Let organisers export results so they can share them with their team"); it needs no separate sentence and no account of prior pain. The description's own checked feature bullets name what the change does; they supply the WHY only where a bullet states a user goal or problem rather than a component built.

## Applicability
DOES_NOT_APPLY has no ordinary case: every pull request calls for this description. Never record DOES_NOT_APPLY, and never claim a missing explanation from text you could not read.

## Sources
1. The title (`context/metadata.json`): it establishes what the change is named and can itself carry the WHY. It never establishes a motivation that is not written in it.
2. The description as written (`context/description.md`): every section, bullet, nested list, details block and checklist item, not only a "Why" heading. It establishes the WHAT and the WHY the change states. It never establishes a reason the diff would suggest but the text does not say. `work/change/description.authored.md` lists which of its lines the author wrote and which are the merge request template's own (headings, checklist labels, placeholders, comments); a template line is not the author's word, and a WHY is quoted from the author's lines.
Judge from these two and nothing else. Never read the diff to supply a rationale the description did not write. A missing body is not an empty one: if the title or body were never captured, report a collection gap and record no result. A bare reference or a clause that delegates rationale elsewhere does not state the reason on these two surfaces. Judge the authored title and description, not the unavailable linked content. Breadth of the change, when severity needs it, comes from the file and line counts in `context/metadata.json`.

## Judge
Scan the WHOLE description before deciding anything is absent. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: a title that names the actual feature, area or fix, AND a quotable clause in the title or body stating WHY. Read title and body together: a concrete problem, impact, goal or constraint in either supplies the motivation.
- NOT_MET: an explanation is supplied but misleads — it orients the reviewer toward a different change than the one described. Quote the misleading clause.
- NOT_MET: the WHY is required and missing — the body is empty or template, or the only candidate clauses restate the action. Name which is missing: a title that names nothing, a body that names no reason, or both. An empty body and a restatement require different evidence and different feedback; say which you found.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: you genuinely cannot tell a restatement from a motivation AND that clause is the only candidate WHY. Quote it and do not resolve the doubt in either direction. Having read the whole title and body and found no reason is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. Calibrate by review cost, not by counters. MINOR, the usual band: a small, single-file change with a thin description; a generic-but-harmless title atop an otherwise informative body, the lightest case; a body that enumerates what changed but omits the why — it still orients. Toward MAJOR: a contentless body on a broad, multi-file change, the heaviest cost. Do not inflate a small change with a thin description.

## Grounding
To claim the WHY is observed, quote the exact rationale clause verbatim from the title or body. To call it absent, cite the boundary: the title, and the body quoted or stated to be empty or template, with every bullet, nested list and checklist item read. Never fabricate a verdict on a field you cannot see. Never claim what the diff does; the description is the subject. Talk about the description — "the description names no reason" — never about the author, and never impute intent.

## Defer
Code quality belongs to the craft practices; how the commits are partitioned belongs to `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; conduct in review threads belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; whether a reviewer can verify the change belongs to `states-how-to-verify-the-change`. Here only: does the description orient a reviewer on what and why?

guidance.whyItMatters: Your reviewer was not in your head when you wrote the code. A sentence on why you made the change spares them from reverse-engineering your intent from the diff, and missing that rationale is one of the most common things that leaves a reviewer confused.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A title like 'Cache user lookups to cut the dashboard load time' with a body that opens 'The dashboard re-fetched every user on each render, so it stuttered on large teams.'
guidance.goingWell: Every description says what changed and why

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Write a title that names the concrete change, as an instruction. A prefix such as a story ID or a tag, like “[Feat] US5.2:”, is fine.
- Say why the change exists, in the title or the description. Name the problem it solves, the effect for users, the goal, or a constraint. For example, instead of listing files, write “Let organizers export results as CSV, so they can share them”.
- Give the reason for the whole change, not only for one choice inside it. “Moved the helpers to match the naming” explains a choice. It does not say why the change exists.
- If the change answers an issue, also write its main point in the description. A link tells the reviewer where to look, but it does not say why.
- Before you ask for a review, replace every template placeholder with your own words.

## When it does not apply

- There is no usual case where it does not apply. Every pull or merge request needs a title and a description that say what changed and why.

It still applies when the change is small.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking you need a “Why” heading or words such as “because” or “so that”. Instead, name the problem or the goal anywhere in the title or the description. A bullet or a checklist item works too.
- Repeating the change as its reason. “I added the export screen as planned” says what, and “Sprint 3” says when. Instead, name the problem or the user goal that the change serves.
- Listing only the parts you built. The reviewer then knows what changed, but not why. Instead, name the problem or the goal that those parts serve. It can be part of the same sentence.
- Leaving an old reason in place after the change grew or changed direction. A reason for a different change sends the reviewer the wrong way. Instead, update the description when the work changes.

## Sources

- [Writing good CL descriptions](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/cl-descriptions.html), Google Engineering Practices. The first line says what the change does. The description also says why, because code can show what it does but not why it exists.
- [Describe your changes](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/process/submitting-patches.html#describe-your-changes), Linux kernel documentation. Describe the problem and its effect on users, and make the description clear without links.
- [Confusion in code reviews: reasons, impacts, and coping strategies](https://doi.org/10.1109/SANER.2019.8668024), Ebert, Castor, Novielli and Serebrenik, 2019. Missing rationale was the reason for confusion that reviewers reported most often, and confusion delays the merge decision.

definition.name: State how to verify the change
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: for the material effect of this change, a reviewer who knows the repository's documented setup can find where to start, what to do and what to expect — from what the author supplied or explicitly adopted.

## The standard
Judge ONE check, for the main material effect in the patch: the one the title, description or adopted issue says the change is for, else the bulk of it. It is communicated when three elements are available, each from any permitted source: an ENTRY (a command, a screen, a named test, an authored preview, a documented setup step), an ACTION (run, tap, enter, configure, restart, or — for an appearance-only change — render and inspect) and an EXPECTED RESULT (a stated requirement, an assertion, a visible state, a persisted value). A sentence that names where to look and what is now there — "the settings screen now shows a dark-mode switch", "the chart now shows a weekly total", "verify the list updates" — is an entry and an expected result; do not demand a literal value or a numbered step list on top of it. A list of the types added ("a service, a DTO and a view model") is neither, and so is "fixed the login flow" without the failure it removes or what now happens. The lapse is a material effect with nothing anywhere saying what success looks like. "Testing: N/A" or an empty heading is evidence of nothing; read every source below.

## Applicability
This is a gate. When the change is one of these kinds and nothing else, record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the kind, and stop: these have no runtime result to check. The kinds: an empty diff; whitespace, formatting or unchanged file moves; planning prose; a conceptual diagram and its explanatory README; README prose that explains architecture or tool usage without an operational procedure; scaffolding — a template "Hello World" view nothing references, a control still holding Xcode's placeholder tokens, the deletion of template files the project does not reference. Scaffolding beside a material effect is never the main effect. Judge the patch, not the title; a documentation change that adds setup or run instructions IS material. Material effects: behaviour, appearance, navigation, persistence, configuration or project settings (build manifests, dependencies, ignore patterns, editor settings that run commands), tests, build scripts, and operational documentation (setup, run, deploy).

## Sources
Read all of these before judging; an element found anywhere here counts as author-supplied.
1. The title and the WHOLE description (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist and step list, not only a "Testing" heading. A captured image that can be inspected may communicate a visual expected result; its caption or surrounding text can independently state one. An image reference or heading alone does not establish what the image shows. If the image is the only candidate evidence and required acquisition failed, report a collection gap; if it was acquired but cannot be interpreted, state the unresolved question.
2. A linked issue the author adopted (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`): named with a closing keyword (Closes, Resolves, Fixes #N) in the author's own prose, the title or branch was created from it, or the description says the change implements it. Its acceptance criteria are expected results; its steps and title are the author's instructions. A "#N" inside a template's example or comment, a number without "#", or an issue only found by number search is NOT adopted.
3. The patch (`work/change/diff.patch`): an authored preview, story, runnable sample or executable test is an ENTRY for the view or items it exercises. A preview is live: rendering it and using the view's own controls (a toggle, a field) is an ACTION; it does not establish navigation from other screens, callbacks or persistence.
4. The repository's documented setup (README, CONTRIBUTING, a documented generate/build/run route in `<repositoryRoot>`): prerequisites and generic run/build steps; do not demand them repeated. For a project-configuration change (a renamed target, a build manifest, package additions) that route IS the check, and a project that generates and builds with the new configuration is its expected result.
5. The author's own words in the discussion (`context/general_comments.json`, `context/review_threads.json`) where they state a check or a prerequisite. A reviewer's report of testing is NOT the author's instructions.
The implementation can confirm reachability or contradict an instruction; it never supplies instructions by itself: a view's own literal text is not a stated expected result.

## Judge
After the applicability gate, assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: the main material effect has an entry, an action and an expected result across the sources, and following them would let a reviewer see the effect. This holds when the description says "N/A", when the elements are split between a title, a preview, an issue and a screenshot, and when secondary effects have no check. Looks like a lapse but is not: "put your own OpenAI key in Secrets.xcconfig" — a declared prerequisite belongs in a good check.
- NOT_MET: followed as written, the check for the main effect cannot be performed as communicated or checks the wrong thing: it describes a different change than the patch makes (a button said to do nothing navigates), names a control or screen the code lacks, needs a secret, input or device no source says how to obtain (a key the code reads from an untracked file), or declares "no UI change" when the UI changes. An adopted issue's criterion the change does not implement, or a slip the title and code correct ("player" for "team"), is not misleading while the rest of the check reaches the effect. Quote the instruction and the contradicting code or fact.
- NOT_MET: no source supplies a usable check for the main material effect AND it needs running, interacting, configuring or observing to confirm. Name the missing element(s). A preview alone for an interactive change, with no stated or shown result, is absent.
- MET also applies when the author explicitly removed or refused a harmful or plainly unnecessary procedure and the remaining verification is adequate. Removal alone and an empty heading do not establish conformance.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE when successfully captured sources leave a deciding fact genuinely unresolved; state the question that would settle it. Failed acquisition of an adopted issue needed to settle the check is a collection gap, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE. Having read every source and found no usable check for a material effect is NOT_MET.
One result per practice per review; keep the same check in the summary, the evidence and the rationale.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; almost always MINOR: a bounded addition or correction fixes it — one missing element, one misleading detail, one undocumented prerequisite. MAJOR: a significant effect is unverifiable as communicated, or the instruction sends the reviewer to a materially wrong check. CRITICAL only for a communicated procedure that demonstrably risks production data loss or live-credential disclosure; never hypothetical.

## Grounding
Cite the exact lines that supply each element: description or issue lines, the diff lines of a preview or test, the screenshot reference, README lines. For a claim based on absence, evidence.search records the boundary you searched and the citations show the diff lines of the effect that needs the check. Never claim a build, test or app run was executed. Judge the instructions, not correctness: a clear check that would expose a defect is still a useful check.

## Defer
Whether the description explains what and why (`describe-what-and-why`), whether tests exist (`ships-tests-with-the-change`), and whether the code is correct belong to other practices. Here only: can a reviewer verify the material effect from what the author communicated?

guidance.whyItMatters: A reviewer who knows where to start, what to do and what to expect can check the change in minutes and trusts what they see. Without that, they either guess at a procedure, skip the check, or ask — and the change waits.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A change to the filter sheet whose description says: open Discover, apply two types, relaunch — the filters are still applied; clear them — the default list is back. The steps name the screen, the action and what success looks like, and the linked issue's acceptance criteria say the same.
guidance.goingWell: Every change says how to check that it works

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Write the check for the main effect of your change, the one that your title or issue names.
- Say where to start, such as a screen, a command, a named test or a preview that you wrote. You do not need to repeat the setup steps that your README gives.
- Say what to do there, such as run, select, enter or restart.
- Say what the reviewer will see when it works. For example, instead of “Fixed the login flow”, write “Sign in with a wrong password. The form says that the password is wrong”.
- If the check needs a key, a device or test data, say how to get it.

## When it does not apply

- The change is empty.
- The change only fixes whitespace or formatting, or moves files without changing them.
- The change only adds planning notes.
- The change only adds a diagram and the README text that explains it.
- The change only explains the design or a tool in the README, with no setup, run or deploy steps.
- The change only adds or removes starter code, such as an unused “Hello World” view or Xcode’s placeholder text.

It still applies when the change adds setup, run or deploy steps, or changes settings, dependencies, tests or build scripts.
It also applies when starter code sits beside a real change.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that you need a long, numbered test plan. One sentence that names where to look and what is there now can be enough. An example is “The settings screen now shows a dark mode switch”.
- Writing “Testing: N/A” or leaving the heading empty. That tells the reviewer nothing. Instead, write the check, or name the issue whose acceptance criteria give it, such as with “Closes #12”.
- Listing the parts that you added, such as “a service, a model and a view”. Instead, say what the reviewer will now see.
- Leaving a check that names a button or a screen that the change does not have. Instead, update the check to match the button or screen that the change has.

## Sources

- [Merge request workflow](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/contributing/merge_request_workflow/), GitLab. Its definition of done asks for the steps or setup that reviewers need to see the change.
- [Differential user guide: test plans](https://we.phorge.it/book/phorge/article/differential_test_plans/), Phorge, the maintained fork of the Phabricator code review tool. A test plan lists repeatable steps, with enough detail that someone new to the change can check how it behaves.
- [Commit message style guide](https://fuchsia.dev/fuchsia-src/contribute/commit-message-style-guide), Fuchsia project at Google. A `Test:` line tells reviewers which tests ran, and complex test steps go in a linked issue.

definition.name: Make the change’s status clear and link its issue
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: how the change is handed off — presented as genuinely ready for others' time, and traceable back to the issue it answers.

## The standard
Judge two things about the handoff, combined into one result. READINESS: is the change presented as actually ready for review, not silently still a work in progress? TRACEABILITY: can a reader follow it back to the motivating issue? Good: an out-of-draft pull request with no authored unfinished-work or review-hold statements and a quotable closing reference — "Closes #482", or an issue id embedded in the branch slug. Bad: a contradictory handoff — a title that declares the work unfinished or asks reviewers to hold off while the pull request is openly non-draft — or a substantive feature or fix change with no traceable reference anywhere a reader would look. Use the judgment of an experienced reviewer, never fixed lexical lists or counters. Title text is a readiness statement only when it says the work is unfinished or that review should wait; a word that names something the product handles or the feature being built is not. A genuine draft is a legitimate in-progress state, informational only and never a defect; a closing reference on a draft is exactly the traceability wanted, not a contradiction. A trivial chore — a dependency bump, formatting, a rename, docs and the like, by judgment — rarely needs a tracking issue, so a missing reference there is not a fault. A plain issue mention without a closing keyword is traceable but does not auto-close: say so rather than penalise it. Readiness is read from what the author says, not from the form, against the slice the handoff says it delivers: ready for review means the author asks for review now, not that review, checks or approval already happened. An authored statement that implementation within that slice is unfinished — "still need to add the error state", "not done yet", an open to-do item the author wrote — or that reviewers should wait before reviewing, contradicts readiness on a non-draft pull request. A checklist the form supplies, left as supplied, is boilerplate: it states nothing about the work, ticked or not. When the author adopted a checklist — wrote it, edited its items or ticked some — read its open items, together with any prose that accounts for them, as the author's account of who owes each item and when: an open item whose substance is the author's unfinished work within the slice, and that nothing the author wrote settles, says the work is not finished. Verification the author asks reviewers to do during the review, a condition before merge such as passing checks or an approval, and follow-on work the author places outside this slice do not by themselves say the slice is unready; "do not merge until approved" states a merge condition, not a hold on review, unless the surrounding prose says review should wait. Never infer that something was or was not built, tested or run from a tick, a missing tick or a missing file.

## Applicability
DOES_NOT_APPLY has no ordinary case: a pull request IS a handoff, so the applicability for readiness and traceability always arises. A trivial chore needing no tracking issue is an observed handoff judged on its readiness, not an inapplicable one.

## Sources
Reason only from metadata that is actually present.
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): the draft flag, the title, the branch name, and `head_checks` when the provider's checks or pipeline reported on the reviewed head (SUCCESS, FAILURE, PENDING, CANCELLED, NONE; absent when never observed). It establishes the declared state, any title marker, an issue id in the branch slug, and the checks reported for the reviewed head. A failing check does not independently establish a readiness or traceability failure; do not add a separate CI criterion. Never assert a build, CI or merge state the record does not carry. The linked items (`context/linked_work_items.json`) say for each issue whether the provider records it as a closing candidate for this change (`how: closesOnMerge`) or the text merely mentions it (`how: mentions`); quote that field rather than inferring a link from a number.
2. The description (`context/description.md`) and its authored view (`work/change/description.authored.md`, which separates the author's lines from the form's and lists the form's items the author ticked): the closing reference or plain mention, any authored statement of what is finished or not, and any checklist with its ticks. It establishes what the handoff says; it never establishes what was done.
3. The change (`work/change/files.json`, `work/change/diff.patch`): which files changed and what their changed lines do — enough to tell a trivial chore from a substantive feature or fix. It never establishes that the change builds, runs or was tested: manual verification, external test suites and existing unchanged tests need no test file in this diff. Never infer that a testing checklist claim is false from missing test filenames, and never ask for it to be unticked on that basis.
When the deciding fact is not observable — the draft flag was never populated, or the context is un-enriched — the handoff still happened and you could not read it: report a collection gap, name the fact you could not read, and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the pull request is out of draft with no title or authored statement that the work is unfinished or that review should wait, and a reference is quotable in the title, the description or the branch — or the change is a trivial chore that needs none. A genuine draft with a closing reference is also MET.
- NOT_MET: a contradiction of readiness on a non-draft pull request — a title that declares the work unfinished or holds review, or an authored statement that the work within its slice is unfinished or that review should wait, including an open item of an adopted checklist as described above. A form's checklist left as supplied, reviewer verification, a merge condition or follow-on work outside the slice is never this cell on its own. Quote the offending token or the author's lines.
- NOT_MET: a substantive feature or fix change with no traceable reference on any of the three surfaces — title, description, branch — after scanning all of them.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE only when the changed lines themselves leave open whether a change is a trivial chore or substantive; name what would settle it. A missing draft flag is a collection gap, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE. Having scanned the three surfaces and found no reference on a substantive change is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, combining the sub-checks by taking the most severe. A genuine draft never makes a NOT_MET on readiness; note it as context, and it never lifts the severity.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on handoff alone — non-blocking and formative, a workflow practice to grow. MINOR, the usual band: a mixed marker alone, a missing reference alone, or an authored statement of unfinished work. MAJOR: a substantive handoff that is both mis-signalled and untraceable.

## Grounding
Quote the exact token relied on: the issue reference, the offending title marker, the draft flag value, the author's lines that say the work is unfinished. For NOT_MET, name the surfaces scanned — title, description, branch — and the changed files or lines that make the change substantive. Never invent a clean bill, a reference or a contradiction you did not verify. Describe the observable statements; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Test-suite adequacy and automated-test presence belong to `ships-tests-with-the-change`; scope cohesion belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; commit-message quality belongs to `commit-subjects-explain-each-change`. Here only: is the handoff ready and traceable?

guidance.whyItMatters: A clear handoff helps reviewers decide when to give work their attention and follow it back to the need it answers.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A feature change kept in Draft while unfinished, with an issue reference such as '#482'. When the work is ready for review, its status and description agree. A small formatting chore can stand on its own without a tracking issue.
guidance.goingWell: The change's status is clear, and substantive work names the issue it answers.

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- While the work is unfinished, open the pull or merge request as a draft.
- When your work is finished, remove title or description words that say work is left or that review should wait.
- Finish each open to-do item, or say that it moves to follow-on work outside this change.
- Name the issue that the change answers in the title, the description or the branch name. For example, instead of the title “Fix login timeout” and nothing else, write “Fixes #482” in the description.
- Use a closing keyword, such as “Closes” or “Fixes”, when the merge should close the issue. A plain mention links the change to the issue, but the issue stays open.

![If the work is unfinished, three steps follow in order. First, open a draft. Next, finish the work and settle your own to-dos. Last, mark it ready to ask for review now.](figures/draft-to-ready.svg)

## When it does not apply

- There is no usual case where it does not apply. Every pull or merge request hands work to a reviewer.

It still applies when the change is a small chore with no tracking issue. Then only its readiness for review counts.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a draft as a fault. A draft is a normal state for unfinished work. Instead, keep unfinished work in draft with its issue reference.
- Marking a change ready while your own words say work is left. An example is “still need to add the error state”. Instead, finish that work first, or keep the change in draft.
- Holding back a small chore because it has no issue. A dependency bump, a formatting fix, a rename or a docs fix can stand on its own. Instead, mark it ready when the work is done.
- Reading a merge condition as a hold. “Do not merge until approved” asks for a review. It does not ask reviewers to wait.

## Sources

- [About pull requests: draft pull requests](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests#draft-pull-requests), GitHub Docs. A draft shares work in progress without a formal review request. Marking it ready requests reviews from code owners.
- [Linking a pull request to an issue](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue), GitHub Docs. A closing keyword such as “Fixes” closes the issue when the change merges into the default branch.
- [Crosslinking issues](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/issues/crosslinking_issues/), GitLab Docs. A mention in a description, a commit or a branch name links the issue. Closing it on merge is a separate choice.
- [Writing good CL descriptions](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/cl-descriptions.html), Google Engineering Practices. Relevant bug numbers and other background help reviewers and later readers understand the change.

definition.name: Write commit subjects a reviewer can follow
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: each authored commit subject names a specific action and object, so a reviewer can follow the history without opening the diff.

## The standard
Judge whether the pull request's commit SUBJECTS let a reviewer follow the change step by step. A legible subject names a specific action and object, so someone reading the history understands the described step without opening the diff. Judge clarity, not format: a `type:` prefix (feat, fix, refactor, chore) is acceptable but never required, and terse is fine when the object of the change is clear ("wire up depth buffer", "cache detection results", "split parser into lexer + reader" are all legible). Uninformative: a subject that carries no specific information about the change — a bare "wip", "fix", "update", "lint" or "stuff" with no object, a lone punctuation mark, placeholder junk, a bare issue reference or branch slug with no description, "address comments" with no specifics, a subject cut off mid-phrase, or the same subject repeated verbatim across commits. The test is the object: "update changelog", "rename settings tab" and "ignore build output" name what was touched and are legible however terse; "small changes", "fix" and "cleanup" name nothing. These are open examples, not a closed list; reason as an experienced reviewer would about whether each subject carries real information. A subject pairing a reference WITH a real summary ("#39: switch logging to the shared Logger") is legible, not noise. This is a workflow practice about how history is written, never a claim about the code itself.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Automatic merge commits ("Merge branch ...", "Merge pull request ...", or two or more `parents`) are git plumbing, not authored summaries; exclude them from the judgment. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, say so, and stop when only merge commits remain after that exclusion: no authored subject was written here.

## Sources
1. The commits (`context/commits.json`), staged from the pinned range of the change: each subject, its body and its `parents`. They establish what each authored subject says. Judge each subject on its own. The subject describes the step; the record does not establish what the code does or whether it matches that description.
The leads from the practice script below these criteria, when present, show authored subjects and their shapes: bare, repeated or cut off. They are places to look, never verdicts. If `context/commits.json` is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no result; uncollected subjects are never authored silence and never COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every authored subject names a specific action and object; a reviewer can read top to bottom and follow the work.
- NOT_MET: some authored subjects carry no specific information about the change. Quote the noisy subjects and explain what information their words leave unclear.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: no ordinary case. A subject you have read is either informative or not; never invent a subject or a clean bill you did not read.
One result per practice per review, over every authored subject. State how many subjects you saw.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on subject quality alone — a formative practice to grow, never a merge gate. Scale to how much the noise degrades a reviewer's ability to follow the history, and weigh review burden proportionally: a single-commit change is inherently low-burden. TRIVIAL: a lone straggler in an otherwise clear history, the gentlest nudge. MINOR, the usual band: several uninformative subjects that make the history hard to follow. MAJOR: a history that is mostly noise, where a reviewer genuinely cannot follow the change commit by commit.

## Grounding
Every claim rests on the subject text you quote: the deciding subjects — the noisy ones for NOT_MET, and the subjects you accepted for MET. Quote the deciding subjects verbatim with their short SHA and cite the corresponding lines in the captured `context/commits.json` files. Never cite a diff line or a repository file for this result — its evidence is subject text — and never record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE because the subjects have no line of their own to cite. Describe observable behaviour only; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Legibility of the pull request title and description belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; the scope and cohesion of what a commit touches belongs to `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; code correctness belongs to other practices. Here only: does each authored subject describe a specific step to the reader?

guidance.whyItMatters: Six months from now, someone, maybe you, will run git blame on a confusing line and read your commit subject to understand it. 'wip' and 'fix stuff' tell them nothing, while a clear subject tells the whole story.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A history you can read top to bottom, where each subject names exactly what that step did, such as 'Extract the retry logic into a helper' then 'Add a timeout to the upload call'.
guidance.goingWell: Commit subjects say what each step changed

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- In each commit subject, name what that commit changed, for a reader who will not open the diff.
- Name the thing that you changed. For example, instead of “fix”, write “Stop the export from dropping the last row”.
- Before you ask for a review, read your subjects from top to bottom.
- Reword each subject that a teammate cannot follow without the diff.

## When it does not apply

- Merge commits, which have two or more parents, such as “Merge branch …” or “Merge pull request …”. Git or your provider writes these subjects, so they do not count.
- A pull or merge request that has only merge commits. There is no subject that you wrote.

It still applies when the pull or merge request has only one commit.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that a subject needs a prefix such as “feat:” or a set length. It needs neither. “Update the changelog” is short and still names what changed. Instead, check that each subject names the thing that you changed.
- Writing a word with no object, such as “wip”, “cleanup” or “small changes”. Instead, add the thing you changed, such as “Remove unused imports from the parser”.
- Giving several commits the same subject, such as “fix” three times. Instead, name what each step did, so a reviewer can follow each step.
- Writing only an issue number, a branch name or “address comments”. Instead, add a short summary beside the reference, such as “#39: switch logging to the shared logger”.

## Sources

- [The canonical patch format](https://docs.kernel.org/process/submitting-patches.html#the-canonical-patch-format), Linux kernel documentation. The summary phrase should describe its patch, and a series should not use the same phrase for every patch. People who scan history with `git log --oneline` may see only that phrase.
- [git-commit](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit#_discussion), Git documentation. Git recommends a first line that summarizes the change. Git uses the text up to the first blank line as the commit title.
- [How to write a Git commit message](https://cbea.ms/git-commit/), Chris Beams, 2014. A clear log lets you review other people’s commits on your own. It also helps you learn later why a change happened.
- [What makes a good commit message?](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2202.02974), Tian, Zhang, Stol, Jiang and Liu, 2022. A commit message is an audit trail of how code changed and why. Many messages in active open source projects lack information.

definition.name: Say which acceptance criteria are done
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a pull request that closes a tracked work item with checkable acceptance criteria says which of those criteria it satisfies and which it defers.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: when a change CLOSES a tracked work item that carries checkable acceptance criteria — a Definition-of-Done or acceptance-criteria heading, a task list, a Given-When-Then block, an enumerated must/should list — can a reviewer tell from the pull request itself which criteria this change satisfies and which are deferred? A good handoff maps the change to those criteria: "Closes #57: login and reset done here; rate-limit deferred to #61", or a checked task list mirroring the item's entries, so the change can be confirmed against its own done-list without reverse-engineering. This is a delivery and traceability practice about how the change is handed off — never a code-defect claim and never an assertion that a criterion is unmet.

## Applicability
This is a gate. The applicability exists only when the authored handoff claims to close a tracked item that carries a quotable, checkable criterion. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name what ruled it out, and stop when the linked item you could read carries no closing entry with a checkable criterion: no closing reference at all, or an item that states no checkable criterion — a title alone, a user story ("As a …, I want …"), or prose with no list, checklist or acceptance section is not a checkable criterion. A candidate item alone does not open the applicability, and neither does a body that references an item without a checkable criterion. How an item is referenced — a closing keyword, a bare mention, a branch number — is a syntax fact, not adoption: inspect the exact mention in context, since examples, templates and code may name unrelated work.

## Sources
1. The description (`context/description.md`) and the title (`context/metadata.json`): the closing reference and any done/deferred mapping — a checked task list, a Given-When-Then or DoD block, a sentence naming what is done and what moves elsewhere. They establish what the handoff says. They never establish whether a criterion is met.
2. The source branch (`context/metadata.json`) and the commits (`context/commits.json`): further places a work-item number may appear. They establish how the item is referenced, nothing more.
3. Each linked item (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`: number, title, url, state, labels, body; `how` in `linked_work_items.json`): the criteria block to map against. It establishes whether a checkable criterion exists and its exact wording. It never establishes that the pull request adopted it; the closing reference in the text or the provider's own link (`how: closesOnMerge`) does that.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the touched-file set, read only to ground a heavier severity. It never establishes that a criterion is met or unmet.
5. The inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): open it and state either the linked or closing issue you found, quoting its `#number "title" (state)`, or that you scanned the inventory and found none.
If the linked items were not captured, you cannot tell whether there was a done-list to map to: when the body carries a closing reference but no mapping and the item's criteria are unreadable, report a collection gap and record no result. The MET path does not depend on that file: a body that carries a closing reference together with an explicit checked task list, Given-When-Then or DoD block mapping the change to enumerated criteria is judged from the body alone.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the closing pull request maps the change to the item's criteria — stating what is done here and what is deferred. The mapping may be implicit: a body whose statements name the substance of each criterion as done (or deferred) honours it, and a checklist that copies the criteria is a mapping; a checklist format is never required. A template's own Definition of Done — items about the merge request's form (title format, lint, a local build, screenshots) rather than the item's criteria — maps nothing, however many of its boxes are ticked. Quote the closing reference and the criteria span.
- NOT_MET: a quotable closing reference to an item with a checkable criteria block, and the body neither names the substance of the criteria as done nor defers them — a restatement of the title, an empty template, or a body that speaks of something else. Frame it as a forward-looking handoff request — "state which of #N's criteria this satisfies and which are deferred" — never as a failure.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the captured text leaves genuinely open whether the mention closes the item; name the question that would settle it. Having read the body and the item and found no mapping is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review. Use your judgment as an experienced reviewer for cases not enumerated here.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a single nudge to state coverage. MAJOR only when, having actually scanned the touched-file set in the diff, you can ground a plausible gap: a concrete quoted criterion has no corresponding surface in the touched files — the item requires an error state and the diff adds only the happy path — and the body does not mark it deferred. Phrase even this as "state whether <criterion> is in scope here or deferred". When you cannot ground a gap, stay MINOR. Identical inputs yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Every result quotes the work-item number, its closing reference, and the exact criterion span from the linked item's body, citing the item's url. For NOT_MET, the citations show the closing reference, the criteria block, and the body read through without a mapping. You have the diff and an excerpt, not the running system: never claim to have run, compiled or verified the change, and never assert a specific criterion is unmet, missing or broken — you point at a handoff gap, not at correctness. Never invent or demand a criterion the item never stated. Describe what the body says against what the item states; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue itself is well written belongs to the issue-authoring practices (`issue-has-checkable-outcome`); the pull request description in general belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; marking the change ready and linking its issue at all belongs to `ready-and-traceable-handoff`. Here only: does the closing change say which stated criteria it covers?

guidance.whyItMatters: When you close an issue, everyone assumes its whole checklist is done. A quick note on what you finished and what you left for later spares your reviewer from re-checking each item, and keeps the unfinished work from quietly disappearing.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A line in the description such as 'Closes #57: login and reset are done here, the rate-limit item moves to #61', so the change can be checked against its own definition of done.
guidance.goingWell: Each change says which acceptance criteria it met

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, find the acceptance criteria in the issue that your change closes. They can be a checklist, a list of musts, or “Given …, when …, then …” steps.
- In the description, after the closing reference, name each criterion that this change finishes. For example, write “Fixes #212. Done here: CSV export and the download button. Deferred to #215: PDF export.” instead of “Fixes #212”.
- Say that each criterion you leave for later is deferred. Add its follow-up issue if it has one.

## When it does not apply

- Your change does not say that it closes an issue.
- The issue that it closes has no criteria that you can check. It has only a title or a user story such as “As a …, I want …”. Or its text is prose with no list, checklist or acceptance section.
- An issue looks related, but your change does not name it.
- The issue number shows up only in an example, a template or code, and it names other work.

It still applies when the provider links the issue to close on merge, even if the description does not say so.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that you must copy the issue’s checklist. A checklist is one way. Plain sentences that say which criteria are done and which are deferred work just as well.
- Ticking the boxes of the description template, such as a passing lint or added screenshots, and stopping there. Those boxes are about the form of the change. Instead, match the change to the criteria in the issue.
- Writing only the closing reference, or repeating the issue title. The issue then closes as if every item were done. Instead, state which criteria are done here and which are deferred.
- Leaving an open item out of the description. It disappears when the issue closes. Instead, say that it is deferred. Add its follow-up issue if it has one.

## Sources

- [Linking a pull request to an issue](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue), GitHub Docs. A closing keyword such as “Closes” closes the issue when the pull request merges into the default branch. A link from the side panel does too.
- [Managing issues](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/issues/managing_issues/), GitLab Docs. A closing pattern in a merge request closes the issue on merge.
- [The Scrum Guide](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html), Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, 2020. An item that does not meet the Definition of Done returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

definition.name: Respond to each review comment

appliesWhen.otherwise: nobody left a review comment on this pull request

definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the author visibly engages with each substantive reviewer request within the captured review record.

## The standard
Judge one practice: when a reviewer left a substantive inline or conversation comment — a question or a change request on this work — did the author visibly engage with it rather than leave it sitting silent? The standard is ENGAGEMENT, not agreement and not completeness. A loop is closed by any visible response: a reply that fixes it; a reply that declines with a stated reason; a clarifying question back; a pointer to a commit or SHA that addresses it; a thread the reviewer or the author marked resolved; a global "Done" or "Addressed" posted after the review batch, even unanchored and unresolved; a request about the pull request itself that the record shows carried out — the description, title or link edited as asked, or a draft marked ready, which a merge also shows since a draft cannot be merged; or the reviewer's own later note saying the point was taken up ("Thanks, all addressed"). A bare later approval or "Looks good" says the reviewer accepted the work, not that the author engaged. Looks like a lapse but is not: resolved nitpicks followed by the reviewer's "Thanks, all addressed", despite a leftover template header. Bad: a question or change request on this work with no reply, no resolution and no commit that plausibly addresses it — "What does this attribute mean?" still unanswered when the work merged.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Reviewer input is a note whose author login differs from the pull request author character-for-character; a note by the pull request author is never reviewer input, and the author gets no credit for replying to themselves. Treat a human's login as a real reviewer whatever its shape (a numeric or token-like login is still a person on a provider that anonymises accounts). A comment the record flags `bot` (an access token, an app, a review service; this tool's own notes are never in the record) is reviewer input when it asks something of the change: silence toward an automated problems is the same open loop. A note is substantive only when it asks something of this change. It asks nothing when it is praise, thanks, an acknowledgement ("LGTM", "+1", "Looks good"), an explanation, or help addressed to someone else; nor when it is advice the reviewer attached to their own approval — the same reviewer approved after it with no commit or author note between them — that defers itself to later work ("for next iteration", "next time", "in general", "be mindful") or explicitly leaves the choice to the author ("optional", "non-blocking nitpick"). Polite wording such as "consider" or "if possible" alone does not make a substantive request optional. Such a note asks something again when it makes the approval conditional ("approving once X is fixed") or asks a question. An author who wrote no note at all is not an identity problem: the author's side is then the commits, the resolutions and the description. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when no note asks something of this change: a freshly opened pull request, or a reviewer's "Approved. Two ideas for next time: …" posted with their approval. One exception: when the same login is recorded on a comment and on the reply that answers it (a known mirror limitation that collapses identities), you cannot tell whether a reviewer spoke at all — that is COULD_NOT_DETERMINE, never DOES_NOT_APPLY. A reviewer login that differs from the author's is never that case.

## Sources
1. The inline comments (`context/comments.json`: `path`, `line`, `body`, `author`, `created_at`, and `thread` and `in_reply_to` where the provider records them) and the threads (`context/review_threads.json`: each thread's resolution state and who resolved it, and `reviewDecisions`: who approved and when). Scan the ENTIRE record for a later author note that answers a comment. The leads from the practice script below these criteria list every note by someone other than the author, inline and conversation, one row each, with the author's replies, the resolution, the reviewer's later note, the reviewer's approval after it and what came between, whether it came after the hand-off, and the commits after it: decide every row.
2. The general comments (`context/general_comments.json`): conversation-level questions and change requests, and author replies posted outside a thread. Same partition, same scan.
3. The pull request author and state (`context/metadata.json`): the login to partition by, the description as captured, and whether and when the work merged or closed.
4. The commits (`context/commits.json`: each with its message, `committedAt` and the `files` it touched): a follow-up commit counts as uptake when it comes after the comment and touches the commented file, or when its message observably ties to the comment — a shared path or a shared concrete term. Uptake is judged on the request's substance, not its letter. When a commit is the only candidate response, read its changed lines before crediting it: a later commit on the file says the file moved, not that the ask was taken up.
A visible reply, resolution or fulfilled workflow request can settle engagement without commit history. When no such response is captured, unavailable commits cannot establish that no change addressed the request: report that collection gap and record no result.
An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When a substantive reviewer comment is visible but the facts that would settle its uptake are not, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every substantive reviewer comment has a visible response of one of the kinds above; a resolution or the reviewer's settling note counts whatever the head still shows. Quote the reply, the resolution marker, or the matching commit-message phrase.
- NOT_MET: at least one substantive reviewer comment drew no response of any kind in the complete captured record while the work remains open, or was posted before the work merged or closed and remained unanswered. Name the single most consequential open thread, quote it, and point forward to replying in-thread or pushing a fix; a missing same-line reply, RESOLVED mark or commit reference alone is never the deciding clause.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the collapsed-identity case above, or when the only substantive notes were posted after the work merged or closed and drew no reply here — their uptake would sit in later work this record does not carry. Name the question. A note posted before the hand-off with no response found anywhere is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, over all reviewer comments; an unanswered note posted after the hand-off is set aside when earlier notes decide.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: an open question on still-open work. MAJOR: an ignored change request, or an open loop on work already handed off — merged or closed.

## Grounding
Quote the reviewer comment in every cell. When you assert uptake, quote the reply, the resolution marker, the reviewer's settling note or the commit-message phrase that ties to it; never infer uptake from a commit's mere presence or timing. Never invent a reply, a resolution, or a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the state of the work — "this thread is still open" — never the person, and never impute intent or a causal outcome.

## Defer
Whether the resulting code is correct or the fix complete belongs to other practices. Merge timing and merging past unresolved threads belong to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: was each substantive reviewer comment engaged with?

guidance.whyItMatters: A reviewer spent real attention pointing at a specific line. When the thread just sits there, they cannot tell whether you agreed, fixed it, or missed it, and they will hesitate before putting in that effort again.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Every reviewer comment gets a visible response, either a follow-up commit that addresses it or a short reply like 'Good catch, switched to the shared client in a2b1c3', so no thread sits unanswered.
guidance.goingWell: Every reviewer comment gets a visible answer
