guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Address each question or change request from a reviewer in a way that they can see. For example, instead of leaving “What does this attribute mean?” unanswered, reply with what it means.
- Choose a response that fits: a fix, a link to an issue for later work, or a question back.
- If you reply after a fix, name the commit, such as “Done, renamed it to `retryLimit` in 4f2e9a1”.
- After many small fixes in one push, post one note such as “Addressed all comments in 4f2e9a1”.
- When you do not agree, reply with your reason.

## When it does not apply

- Nobody else has left a comment yet, such as on a pull or merge request that you just opened.
- The comment is your own. Only comments from other people ask something of you.
- The comment asks nothing of the change. Examples are praise, thanks, “LGTM”, “+1”, an explanation, or help for someone else.
- The reviewer approved with advice for later work, such as “next time”. The same goes for a choice they left to you, such as “optional”.

It still applies when a request uses polite words, such as “consider” or “if possible”, or when an approval waits on a fix. It also applies when advice asks a question, or when a review bot asks for a change.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that you must agree with every comment. You only need to respond, and a reason to decline is a response.
- Taking the reviewer’s approval as your answer. An approval shows that they accept the work, not that you answered them. Answer each open question.
- Counting any later commit on the file as your answer. A commit can touch the file and still miss the point. Instead, make the change that was asked, or reply with what changed.
- Leaving a comment from a review bot without a response. Fix the point, or say why it does not apply.

## Sources

- [Handling reviewer comments](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/handling-comments.html), Google Engineering Practices. Ask the reviewer when you do not understand a comment, and explain your reasons when you disagree.
- [Respectful changes](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/HEAD/docs/cl_respect.md), Chromium project. Answer each question, and adopt, defer, or push back on each suggestion with more information.
- [Jetpack code review etiquette](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/frameworks/support/+/refs/heads/androidx-main/code-review.md), AndroidX project. Follow up on every comment, with the fix or with your reason for not making it.
- [An empirical study of overlooked code review comments in OSS projects](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.2026.3681776), Li and others, 2026. In 80 Java projects, about 7.5% of pull requests had a comment with no reply and no fix. They took longer to review and were accepted less often.

definition.name: Resolve open threads before merging
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: dated evidence establishes that standing reviewer requests and open threads were resolved or superseded before merge.

## The standard
At the moment the change MERGED, was the review loop closed first — every reviewer's gate either resolved or superseded — or did the change land while a reviewer's request or an open thread still stood? This is a process practice about closing the loop before merge, never a claim that the merged code is wrong: the code may be perfectly correct and still have skipped the re-review a reviewer asked for. A later approval supersedes a change-request only if it occurred before the merge; a resolution after merge does not establish that the loop was closed beforehand. A gate is a formal request for changes (`CHANGES_REQUESTED`), a review thread not resolved, or a reviewer's explicit request that the work not merge until something is done ("do not merge until the crash is fixed"), wherever it is written, until the same reviewer lifts it. Read what the reviewer asked of this merge, not the politeness of its wording. Advice for later work and a suggestion the reviewer plainly leaves to the author's choice are no gate: whether such a comment was answered or taken up belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`. A thread resolved before the merge is closed, whatever it asked for.

## Applicability
This is a gate. If the change did not merge, record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name that fact, and stop: there is no merged loop to assess. DOES_NOT_APPLY has no other ordinary case.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): `state`, and `merged_at` when the provider recorded it. It establishes that the change merged and when. It never establishes the review state.
2. The review-decision and thread-resolution records (`context/review_threads.json`): each reviewer's decision, each thread's path, line, resolution and `resolvedAt` when the provider dated it, and their dates. They establish the review state at the merge timestamp when read as dated events: a thread whose `resolvedAt` is after `merged_at` was open at the merge, and the leads from the practice script list it beside the never-resolved ones. A current decision or resolution field is a current-state fact, not automatically a historical one; a latest-state snapshot, a filename or a record count never by itself proves the historical record is complete.
3. The discussion (`context/general_comments.json`, and the inline comments in `context/comments.json`, each carrying the `thread` it belongs to): dated comments that ask for the merge to wait, or explain a supersession or a resolution. They establish a blocking request a reviewer wrote, and why a gate was lifted, when dated. They never turn advice into a gate. The leads from the practice script below these criteria list the merge — who, when — and one row per thread the record does not mark RESOLVED, with its `id`, anchor, opening time and whether it is outdated; it says whether the threads file was captured at all.
The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) establishes nothing here: never use the code to infer a reviewer's decision. If the change merged but `context/review_threads.json` is absent or truncated, the loop had some state at merge and you could not read it: report a collection gap and record no result. Never treat a missing file as an empty loop.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context. Judge the captured gates reviewer by reviewer: each reviewer's own requests and threads, settled or standing at `merged_at`. A reviewer's standing approval dated before the merge supersedes that same reviewer's earlier formal change-request decisions (`CHANGES_REQUESTED`), never another reviewer's. Approval does not lift an explicit hold the reviewer retains or qualifies in the approval or accompanying discussion. A thread resolution dated before the merge closes that thread. `decisionHistoryComplete: false` warns that withdrawn or replaced decisions may be missing from the capture; it is not itself a gate, and it does not undo a dated closure.
- NOT_MET: dated evidence shows a gate still standing at merge — a thread whose `resolvedAt` follows `merged_at`, a thread that nobody resolved (quote its path:line), or a reviewer's change-request or explicit request to hold the merge that the record shows still stood then (name the reviewer, quote the decision or the request). Another reviewer's approval never lifts it.
- MET: every captured gate was settled before the merge, and the required sources were captured without truncation. State the evidence relied on: "merged; reviewer X's change-requests superseded by their approval dated before the merge; every thread resolved before the merge". Record MET without claiming that the review history is exhaustive.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE when a captured fact that decides the result is unknown — a change-request with no date that could precede or follow the merge; a latest approval or resolution with no date, so it cannot be placed before the merge; or one reviewer's request beside another reviewer's approval when the captured record cannot settle whether the requester's gate was lifted or replaced before the merge. Name the missing fact. Never record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for a gate the capture does not show. An approval's time decides only whether it lifted a standing gate: with none, no approval time is needed. A thread whose `resolvedAt` precedes `merged_at` needs no further date, such as when a requested edit took effect.
A missing or truncated required source is a collection gap, not a result.
One result per practice per review, on the single at-merge question.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on loop closure alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a merely open thread with no standing request, the lighter lapse. MAJOR: landing over a reviewer's still-standing request-changes gate, the heavier miss. Equivalent observed states get equivalent treatment.

## Grounding
For NOT_MET, quote the deciding review evidence and the dated facts that show it still stood at the merge timestamp. For MET, cite the captured bounded review record — the merge timestamp, each captured decision and each thread's resolution with dates — that shows none remained. Describe only the observable state: "merged with N request-changes still standing; thread at <path:line> unresolved at merge". Never "you ignored the reviewer" or "you merged broken code"; never a claim about the code's correctness; never a current open or resolved state offered as proof of the state at merge.

## Defer
Whether threads on an OPEN pull request are being taken up belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`. Here only: was the loop closed at the moment of merge? Do not double-flag.

guidance.whyItMatters: Merging while a reviewer still has changes requested skips the very check they asked for, and tells them their review did not count. It is also evidence of review quality, not just a courtesy: changes that land with little reviewer discussion tend to carry more defects that surface after release. Resolving the threads first keeps review worth doing.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: By the time you merge, every open thread is resolved and anyone who requested changes has come back with an approval, so nothing lands over an objection.
guidance.goingWell: Nothing merges over an open thread or objection

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you merge, look at the pull or merge request for open threads and for reviewers who requested changes.
- When a comment says “do not merge until the crash is fixed”, wait until its reviewer lifts it.
- Resolve each thread before you merge.
- When a reviewer requests changes, ask that reviewer to look again after your fix. For example, instead of merging right after you push the fix, wait for that reviewer to approve it.

## When it does not apply

- The pull or merge request did not merge.

It still applies when the merged code is correct.

## Common mistakes

- Merging because the code works. This practice is about the review, not about the code. Correct code can still skip the second look that a reviewer asked for. Instead, wait for their approval.
- Resolving threads after you merge. A thread you resolve after the merge was still open when the work landed. Instead, resolve it first, then merge.
- Treating every comment as a request to wait. A suggestion the reviewer leaves to you, or advice for later work, is not a request to hold the merge. Instead, look for what the reviewer asked of this merge, not how politely they wrote it. Still resolve its thread before you merge.

## Sources

- [About protected branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches), GitHub Docs. A repository can block a merge until every conversation is resolved. With required reviews, an admin who requests changes must approve before the merge.
- [Comments and threads](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/discussions/), GitLab Docs. A project can block a merge until every thread is resolved.
- [How to write code review comments](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/comments.html), Google Engineering Practices. Reviewers can label a comment as a nit, optional, or for later. Then the author can tell required changes from suggestions.
- [The impact of code review coverage and code review participation on software quality](https://rebels.cs.uwaterloo.ca/confpaper/2014/05/30/the-impact-of-code-review-coverage-and-code-review-participation-on-software-quality.html), McIntosh and others, 2014. In Qt, VTK and ITK, components with low reviewer participation had more defects after release.

definition.name: State a problem a maintainer can act on
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no applicability for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.

For a practice about requested work, establish the current request from the complete issue body and the discussion the practice names. Brief, vague or title-only requests still pass this premise.

When genuinely conflicting current statements leave that request unresolved, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for the request-dependent judgment, cite the conflict, and judge neither statement under the standard. Position or date alone does not resolve it. If an explicit authored withdrawal leaves no work requested, record DOES_NOT_APPLY for that judgment and treat earlier requirements as history. Judge a remaining request under the practice's standard. Historical and closure practices retain their own subjects, including accounting for dropped or deferred work.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the issue, read on its own, lets a maintainer picture the work at the scope it states and begin.

## The standard
Judge whether the issue states enough for a maintainer to begin the kind of work it requests. A specific title must locate the work. Its body, comments or a materialized document it delegates to must state the following core:

- Defect, including an untyped issue asserting a malfunction: actual behaviour, expected behaviour and a concrete reproduction path. Steps, a stack trace, an exact error or a failing test can provide that path.
- Capability request: a concrete requested behaviour a maintainer can begin building. Who benefits, why, an acceptance block, a design and a specification are not additional prerequisites.
- Epic, umbrella or requirement card: substantive scope at that level; implementation detail can live in child work.

A concrete, quotable acceptance-criteria, Definition-of-Done or Given-When-Then block can supply the core on its own. Assess other forms by the kind of work they actually request.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when there is no work-kind to judge: a pure question or open discussion that asserts no defect and requests no capability. Do not demand reproduction steps of a discussion. A title that names a task or a capability ("Add a dark-mode toggle", "Update the setup guide") is engineering work even when the body is empty: the gate passes and the empty body is the lapse, never DOES_NOT_APPLY.

## Sources
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, template field, step list and criteria block. It establishes the kind of work and the substance stated inline. An image: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The title and labels (`context/metadata.json`): a deliverable-type label names the kind of work. It never establishes substance by itself; an empty template echoing the title under such a label is still empty.
3. The comments (`context/comments.json`): evidence from the captured issue; substance stated there counts. They never establish substance you cannot quote from them.
4. Linked design, decision or spec documents (`context/docs/`): when the issue delegates its substance to a document materialized here, read it. A concrete capability or interface the document actually specifies is substance an implementer can start from; count it as observed rather than demanding the issue restate it inline. A generic document or a placeholder marker that does not concretely pin THIS work supplies nothing.
When the issue delegates its substance to a specific named document that was NOT materialized, you cannot tell whether that substance exists: report a collection gap and record no result, never a claim against prose you were never shown. If the issue text was not captured completely, the same.

## Judge
These conformance cases apply after the shared issue premise establishes a current request.
- MET: a specific title locates the work and its kind's core is genuinely present and quotable — inline, in a comment, or in a materialized document the issue delegates to.
- NOT_MET: the title does not locate the work, or a required element of its kind's core is missing because the issue delegates to nothing and states none itself, or the materialized document is generic or a placeholder. Name the missing element.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the standard itself has no ordinary undecidable case. A complete but empty or vague body is an assessed gap — NOT_MET — not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE; an incomplete capture is a collection gap, not a result.
One result per practice per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — a non-blocking authoring-practice nudge, not a merge gate. Identify the missing required elements of this standard before assigning severity.

Severity depends on the kind of work.

- Defect: MINOR when the issue states a concrete observable malfunction or a reproduction path. A stated concrete malfunction establishes a defect's core even without reproduction steps. MAJOR when the issue states neither a concrete observable malfunction nor a reproduction path.
- Capability request, epic or card: MINOR when the requested work is concrete and startable but its title does not locate it. MAJOR when the work is unstartable because no concrete capability or scope is stated.

An empty body, a placeholder or repetition of a vague title supplies no core.

## Grounding
Every element you call present must be quotable from the captured issue — the title, the body, a comment, or the materialized document; an element you cannot quote is absent. For NOT_MET, evidence.search records the boundary you searched, and the citations quote from it: the whole body, the labels, the comments, and the `context/docs/` documents or their absence. Never invent content and never grant a clean bill you did not verify. Describe the observable gap — "the body names a symptom but no reproduction path" — never the reporter's intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue has a checkable or measurable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: can a maintainer picture the work and start?

guidance.whyItMatters: Clear descriptions help the next maintainer understand the requested change or problem. They reduce guesswork and give planning and discussion a useful starting point.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A bug report that reads 'uploading a 0-byte file returns 500, I expected a clear validation error' and lists the exact steps to reproduce, so a maintainer can start straight away. Or a request that names one concrete capability with who it helps and why, such as 'reviewers lose track of which files changed in large diffs, so add a per-file changed-lines summary to the review view'.
guidance.goingWell: Issues state a problem a maintainer can act on

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Write a title that says which work the issue is about. For example, instead of “Search broken”, write “Search with a quote mark shows an error page”.
- For a bug, say what happened and what you expected to happen.
- For a bug, give a way to see it fail. Steps, a stack trace, the exact error or a failing test all work.
- For a request, describe the behavior you want, so that someone can start to build it. You can leave out who it helps, why, and a design.
- For an epic, an issue that groups related work, state the scope of the whole. The detail can go in the smaller issues under it.

## When it does not apply

- The issue only asks a question or opens a discussion. It reports no bug and asks for no new behavior.

It still applies when the title names a task, such as “Add a dark-mode toggle”, and the body is empty.

## Common mistakes

- Filling in a template that only repeats the title, even under a bug or feature label. A label names the kind of work, not the work. Instead, write the problem or the behavior in your own words.
- Writing “It does not work”. Instead, say what you saw and what you expected, so a maintainer knows what is wrong.
- Writing only your guess at the cause. Instead, report what you saw. Add your guess only as an extra.
- Pointing to a general document or a placeholder. Instead, link a document that describes this work, or write the work in the issue.

## Sources

- [Bug writing guidelines](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/page.cgi?id=bug-writing.html), Mozilla. A good bug report has a summary that names the problem. It also gives steps to reproduce, the actual result and the expected result.
- [What makes a good bug report?](https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.2010.63), Zimmermann and others, 2010. Developers at Apache, Eclipse and Mozilla found steps to reproduce, stack traces and test cases most helpful. Reporters found them hardest to give.
- [How to report bugs effectively](https://www.chiark.greenend.org.uk/~sgtatham/bugs.html), Simon Tatham, 1999. Let the programmer see the failure, and say exactly what you expected. Report the symptoms along with any guess.

definition.name: Keep the issue to one concern
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no applicability for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.

For a practice about requested work, establish the current request from the complete issue body and the discussion the practice names. Brief, vague or title-only requests still pass this premise.

When genuinely conflicting current statements leave that request unresolved, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for the request-dependent judgment, cite the conflict, and judge neither statement under the standard. Position or date alone does not resolve it. If an explicit authored withdrawal leaves no work requested, record DOES_NOT_APPLY for that judgment and treat earlier requirements as history. Judge a remaining request under the practice's standard. Historical and closure practices retain their own subjects, including accounting for dropped or deferred work.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: how the issue is scoped — one cohesive deliverable at the issue's intended level, rather than unrelated asks stapled into one ticket.

## The standard
A good issue tracks ONE cohesive deliverable: something that can be picked up, worked and closed as a single items. Judge cohesion as an experienced reviewer would: is there a single thread of intent, or have unrelated asks been stapled together so that some deliverables can land while the rest lingers? The test is whether a maintainer would naturally assign, estimate and close it as one thing, or would be fighting to. One feature, one bug, one question is one concern. Internal decomposition is still ONE concern: implementation sub-steps, a checklist that builds up one capability, a sub-issue rollup that breaks one feature into trackable children. An epic that bundles several RELATED facets of the same feature area (create, rename, delete plus search for one entity) is ONE concern at its altitude; that breadth is what makes it an epic. The tell of bundling is separable threads of intent targeting different concerns, never the mere presence of "and" or a long checklist.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when there is no concrete deliverable to scope at all: a pure question, a support request, an open discussion, an empty or title-only body, or an untouched template. Do not manufacture a MET from that absence.

## Sources
Judge only from the issue body, its discussion, its labels and its sub-issue rollup as captured.
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist and step list, and the sub-issue rollup when the capture carries it. It establishes the deliverable(s) named and how they relate. It never establishes what the author meant beyond the written spans.
2. The labels and title (`context/metadata.json`): the issue's intended level — epic, feature, bug, task. They establish the altitude at which to judge cohesion. They never establish cohesion by themselves.
3. The WHOLE discussion (`context/comments.json`): an authored decision or an accepted clarification can establish the current request. A proposed change is not an adopted request merely because it is later. Read it together with the body under the shared issue premise.
An image in the body: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. If the body or discussion was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
These conformance cases apply after the shared issue premise establishes a current request.
- MET: one cohesive deliverable, including any internal decomposition or related-facet epic described above.
- NOT_MET: genuinely unrelated deliverables fused into one ticket — "add CSV export, fix the date picker, and bump the chart library". Feed forward the single most consequential split: name the concerns to break into linked issues. Never enumerate every clause.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE when the complete text genuinely leaves one journey versus separate deliverables unresolved; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. A partly captured issue is a collection gap, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on scoping alone — a formative practice, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: separable asks that a maintainer could still split without stranding work. MAJOR: clearly unrelated bundling that will genuinely strand work, with some deliverables landing and the rest lingering open.

## Grounding
Quote the actual span(s) that name the deliverable(s) you are judging; for NOT_MET, the spans that name each separable concern. Describe the observable bundling — "the body names three deliverables with no shared thread" — never carelessness or intent. Never invent a deliverable, a clean bill, or a bundling you did not read.

## Defer
Whether an epic should itself be split into tracked child stories belongs to `breaks-large-work-into-trackable-subtasks`; do not double-count it. Here only: is this issue one concern at its level?

guidance.whyItMatters: An issue that quietly bundles three unrelated asks cannot be assigned, estimated, or closed cleanly. One deliverable lands, the rest linger, and the whole thing stays open forever, tracking nothing.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: One issue, one deliverable, such as 'add CSV export to the reports page', rather than 'add CSV export, fix the date picker, and bump the chart library' crammed into one ticket.
guidance.goingWell: Each issue asks for one deliverable, not a bundle

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you file the issue, name the one result that closes it. If closing it also needs a result with a different goal, that result is a second concern.
- Open one issue for each concern. For example, instead of one issue for dark mode and the login timeout, open two issues.
- Before you open a new issue, search the open issues for each ask. If an open issue already covers an ask, link to that issue in place of the ask.
- Keep all the steps of one result in its issue. A checklist that builds one feature belongs together, so a maintainer can assign, estimate and close it as one thing.
- For an epic, a large issue for one feature area, keep the related parts of that area together. Create, rename and delete for one item are one concern at that level.

## When it does not apply

- The issue asks a question and asks for no work.
- The issue is a support request.
- The issue opens a discussion and names nothing to build or fix yet.
- The body is empty, or the issue has only a title.
- The body is the issue template, with nothing changed.

## Common mistakes

- Splitting an issue because its title has “and” or its checklist is long. Neither one makes it a bundle. Instead, look for asks with different goals that could each land and close on their own.
- Adding an unrelated ask to an open issue to save time. Different people often handle different asks, and an ask that hides in another issue can stay undone. Instead, open a new issue for it.
- Splitting the asks into issues that do not point to each other. Instead, link each new issue to the others, so the context stays easy to find.

## Sources

- [Bug Writing Guidelines](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/page.cgi?id=bug-writing.html), Mozilla. Open a new report for each issue, so the fix workflow can finish for each one.
- [How to pre-screen Browser-General bugs](https://www-archive.mozilla.org/quality/browser/prescreening), Mozilla, 2004, archived page. A report that lists several unrelated problems goes to different engineers, and some of its problems may never get fixed.
- [INVEST in good stories, and SMART tasks](https://xp123.com/invest-in-good-stories-and-smart-tasks/), Bill Wake, 2003. Stories are easiest to work with when they do not overlap and can be built in any order. A good story can be estimated.

definition.name: Define a checkable outcome
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no applicability for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.

For a practice about requested work, establish the current request from the complete issue body and the discussion the practice names. Brief, vague or title-only requests still pass this premise.

When genuinely conflicting current statements leave that request unresolved, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for the request-dependent judgment, cite the conflict, and judge neither statement under the standard. Position or date alone does not resolve it. If an explicit authored withdrawal leaves no work requested, record DOES_NOT_APPLY for that judgment and treat earlier requirements as history. Judge a remaining request under the practice's standard. Historical and closure practices retain their own subjects, including accounting for dropped or deferred work.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a quotable finish line — an outcome a maintainer could later verify as DONE from the issue alone.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does this issue define an outcome a maintainer could later verify as done? A good issue draws a clear finish line: a reader can tell, from the issue alone, what state of the world means the work is complete. The line can take many shapes — an acceptance checklist, a Given-When-Then block, a story's who/what/why phrased so the result is testable, or, for a bug, a stated expected behaviour a fix must restore. The form does not matter; the testability does. Use judgment as an experienced reviewer would; do not hunt for a keyword or label. Good: "export downloads a valid CSV; an empty result shows a friendly message". Bad: "improve performance" with nothing that could ever read as done, or a body that only echoes its title. For an umbrella, epic or requirement card, the right checkable outcome is a definition of done that decomposes into child work, not an inline checklist: bundling many capabilities is expected of it.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when there is nothing whose "done" this practice could define: a question, a support request, an open discussion, or a bare board or ceremony placeholder with no asserted problem and no requested capability. A missing checklist on something that was never engineering work is not a defect. A title that names a task or a capability ("Add a dark-mode toggle", "Add package") with an empty body is engineering work whose done was never defined: the gate passes and NOT_MET is the answer, never DOES_NOT_APPLY.

## Sources
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist, criteria block and expected-behaviour statement. It establishes a finish line you can quote. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The labels and title (`context/metadata.json`): the kind of issue, including whether it is an umbrella, epic or requirement card. They never establish a finish line by themselves.
3. The comments (`context/comments.json`): a finish line stated there counts. They never establish one you cannot quote.
4. A linked design or spec document the issue delegates to, materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`: when it states a concrete, testable contract THIS work must satisfy — specific behaviours, status codes, API or state conditions — that contract IS a quotable finish line. Read and quote it before concluding none exists. A generic guideline, or a placeholder document that does not pin this deliverable's done-state, supplies nothing. A document never materialised is not evidence in either direction: when the issue delegates its finish line to a specific document you were not shown, report a collection gap and record no result, never a claim against prose you were not shown.
5. Child work: sub-issues or a task list referenced in the body or comments, or child entries in `context/project_inventory.json` when captured. For an umbrella, they establish the decomposition that makes its outcome checkable.

## Judge
These conformance cases apply after the shared issue premise establishes a current request.
- MET: the finish line is quotable from the body, a comment, or a materialised document; or, for an umbrella, children or tracked sub-issues already carry the decomposition — MET with no severity.
- NOT_MET: a real deliverable to build, and no quotable outcome in the issue or any materialised document it delegates to. For an umbrella with substantive prose but no child-mapped done, this is a gentle decomposition nudge, not a hard failure; do not double-alarm.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the standard itself has no ordinary undecidable case. A body read in full that states no finish line is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE; a document you were not shown is a collection gap.
One result per practice per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — a formative authoring practice, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: everything softer is a single nudge, including the umbrella decomposition nudge. MAJOR: a maintainer genuinely cannot tell when ANY of the work is done — a real deliverable with neither a verifiable outcome nor a decomposition.

## Grounding
Quote the span you relied on: the checklist, criteria block, expected behaviour, the document sentence with its `context/docs/...` file path, or the child references. For NOT_MET, evidence.search records the boundary searched, and the citations quote from it: the whole body, the labels, the comments, and the `context/docs/` documents or their absence. Never invent a checklist, a clean bill or an exoneration you did not read. Never assert technical feasibility, design correctness or the author's competence. Describe the observable gap in the issue, never the author's character or motive.

## Defer
Whether the problem itself is well stated — observed versus expected, who/what/why as a narrative — belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`; do not write that relationship into the feedback. Here only: is there a verifiable finish line?

guidance.whyItMatters: Without a clear line for 'done', nobody can tell when the work is finished, including the person doing it. A checkable outcome turns 'improve performance' from an open-ended wish into a task someone can actually complete.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A short acceptance checklist a maintainer can tick off when the work is truly finished, such as 'export downloads a valid CSV' and 'an empty result shows a friendly message', rather than a vague hope of improvement.
guidance.goingWell: Every issue says what done looks like

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Write each point of done so that someone who reads the issue can answer yes or no. For example, instead of “make search better”, write “a search for an exact title shows that issue first”.
- Pick the form that suits the work, such as a short checklist or a Given, When, Then block. The block gives the start state, the action, and the result you expect.
- For a bug, state the behavior that the fix must bring back.
- If a linked design document holds the finish line, check that it states what this work must do. A general guideline does not tell anyone when this issue is done.
- For an epic or another umbrella issue, define done as its child issues. Each child issue then carries its own finish line.

## When it does not apply

- The issue asks a question.
- The issue is a support request.
- The issue opens a discussion.
- The issue is a placeholder on a board or for a team meeting, with no problem and no requested change.

It still applies when the title names a task, such as “Add a dark-mode toggle”, and the body is empty.

## Common mistakes

- Adding a heading such as “Acceptance criteria” with vague points under it. The form does not matter. Instead, write each point so that someone can test it.
- Repeating the title in the body. Instead, add what will be true when the work is finished.
- Writing a goal that never ends, such as “improve performance”. Instead, name a result that someone can test.
- Agreeing on the finish line only in a call or a chat. Instead, write it in the issue or in a comment, so that someone can quote it later.

## Sources

- [INVEST in good stories, and SMART tasks](https://xp123.com/invest-in-good-stories-and-smart-tasks/), Bill Wake, 2003. A good story is testable. If nobody knows how to test it, the story may not be clear enough.
- [Given When Then](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/GivenWhenThen.html), Martin Fowler, 2013. A scenario states the starting state, the action, and the change that you expect.
- [Acceptance testing](https://agilealliance.org/glossary/acceptance/), Agile Alliance glossary. Acceptance tests describe behavior as examples or scenarios, and each one passes or fails.

definition.name: Point the issue to the context it depends on
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no applicability for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.

For a practice about requested work, establish the current request from the complete issue body and the discussion the practice names. Brief, vague or title-only requests still pass this premise.

When genuinely conflicting current statements leave that request unresolved, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for the request-dependent judgment, cite the conflict, and judge neither statement under the standard. Position or date alone does not resolve it. If an explicit authored withdrawal leaves no work requested, record DOES_NOT_APPLY for that judgment and treat earlier requirements as history. Judge a remaining request under the practice's standard. Historical and closure practices retain their own subjects, including accounting for dropped or deferred work.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: an issue that depends on a design, decision, spec, runbook or data model recorded elsewhere points the implementer to the document that holds it.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when an issue clearly depends on prior context an implementer would need to act on it correctly — an existing design, a decision record, a spec, a runbook, a data model — does the issue point them to that context with a link to the relevant document, instead of assuming the reader already carries it? The need is judged from the issue's own text: it leans on decisions or designs made elsewhere — "per our architecture", "following the agreed rollout plan", "as decided for the billing redesign", "must match the data model" — such that someone picking it up cold could not proceed correctly without reading that source. A link count never establishes that need, and a link to an unrelated document is not credit. Do not infer a hidden dependency the text does not express.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the issue is self-contained: a clear bug report, a small well-described change, a question. Most issues are; prefer DOES_NOT_APPLY whenever the issue reads as self-contained, and never penalize a self-contained issue for lacking links.

## Sources
1. The title and the whole body (`context/description.md`, `context/metadata.json`): every phrase that appeals to context made elsewhere, and every link. It establishes whether the issue leans on external context and whether it points anywhere. It never establishes that a linked document is relevant; a bare link is not evidence on its own. An image: read its caption and the sentence around it. A link outside the wiki counts on the same terms as a wiki link. The source location does not decide relevance.
2. The captured linked documents, including wiki documents under `context/docs/`: read each to judge whether it is actually the context the issue leans on. A document establishes relevance when a passage in it carries the design, decision or spec the issue depends on. It never establishes relevance by its title alone.
3. The whole discussion (`context/comments.json`): establish the current request under the shared issue premise before judging the dependency and its pointer.
If the body or discussion was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no result.
When the issue links a specific document that was NOT materialized for you, you cannot tell whether it carries the context: report a collection gap and record no result — neither credit nor criticism.

## Judge
These conformance cases apply after the shared issue premise establishes a current request.
- MET: the issue genuinely rests on prior design, decision or spec context and links the specific materialized document that carries it, so an implementer can proceed without hunting or guessing.
- NOT_MET: the issue plainly leans on context made elsewhere but leaves the reader no pointer to it — nothing, or only a materialized document that does not carry that context — so they must reconstruct or reverse-engineer the intent.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the standard itself has no ordinary undecidable case. Having read the whole issue and the materialized documents and found no pointer to the context it leans on is NOT_MET; a linked document that was not materialized is a collection gap, not a result.
One result per practice per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — a non-blocking authoring nudge, not a gate. MINOR, the usual band: a mild lean on unstated context — a nudge to link the source. MAJOR only when the missing context is load-bearing enough that an implementer would likely build the wrong thing without it. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding
For NOT_MET quote the exact phrase in the issue that appeals to external context ("as decided…", "per the design", "must match…") and state what context an implementer would need but is not pointed to. For MET cite the captured document's file path and quote or closely paraphrase the passage that shows it is the relevant context. Never invent a document, a decision or a dependency; talk about the issue's text, never the reporter's intent or character.

## Defer
Whether the issue is actionable on its own terms belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`; the two are disjoint. Here only: does an issue that depends on external design or decision context actually point to it?

guidance.whyItMatters: An issue that silently depends on decisions made elsewhere forces every implementer to re-discover the context — or, worse, to guess it and build the wrong thing.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: When work depends on an existing design or decision, the issue links the document that holds it, so whoever picks it up starts with the rationale already in hand.
guidance.goingWell: Issues link the design or decision they rest on

visual.alt: An issue that says “Per the agreed plan” with no link to the plan leaves the context guessed. An issue that says “Per the rollout plan” and links the plan document gives the context known.

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- When the issue says “as decided” or “per the design”, find the document that holds that design or decision.
- Link that document. For example, instead of “follow the agreed rollout plan”, write “follow the billing rollout plan” and link it.
- Say in your own words what the linked document decides. Some readers cannot open the link.
- If nobody wrote the decision down, record it before you link to it.

## When it does not apply

- The issue is a clear bug report that stands on its own.
- The issue asks for a small change and describes it fully.
- The issue asks a question.

It still applies when an issue says “as decided” or “per the design” and does not say where to find it.

## Common mistakes

- Adding links to look thorough. More links do not help. A link to a document without the decision does not help either. Instead, link the document that holds the decision the issue leans on.
- Linking a whole wiki space or a folder. The reader must still search for the decision. Instead, link the document that holds it.
- Writing “as we discussed” and trusting that the reader was there. The person who picks up the issue may not have been. Instead, link the record of what was decided.

## Sources

- [Writing good CL descriptions](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/cl-descriptions.html), Google Engineering Practices. Google advises linking design documents in a change description. It also advises enough context in the text, because some readers cannot open a link.
- [Documenting architecture decisions](https://www.cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions), Michael Nygard, 2011. Without the recorded reason for a decision, a new teammate can only accept it blindly or change it blindly.
- [Information needs in collocated software development teams](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICSE.2007.45), Ko, DeLine and Venolia, 2007. Developers often put off design questions, such as why code was written a certain way. The only source was a coworker who was away. Two of the authors work at Microsoft, which sells developer tools.

definition.name: Leave specific, actionable review comments
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the substantive comments a reviewer wrote on this pull request each point at something concrete and tell the author what to do about it.

## The standard
Judge the craft of the comments a reviewer wrote — never whether the reviewer's claim about the code is correct, and never the author's code. A useful comment names a specific construct or anchors to a real line AND states an actionable substance: what is wrong, what to change, a concrete alternative, or a pointed question a maintainer can actually answer. A vague comment is a content-free gesture that leaves the author guessing: "this is messy", "fix this", "cleanup", a bare "?". Inline (diff-anchored) notes and conversation-tab notes meet the same standard. A blunt but specific comment is useful here; a polite but vague one is not. A reviewer comment is one whose author differs from the pull request author in the metadata.

## Applicability
This is a gate. The practice judges reviewer activity, not the changed code: "a big pull request got little review" is not a result, and an unreviewed or draft pull request is never a substandard review. Build one list of every review note in your context, wherever it is carried — inline arrays, general or conversation notes, any discussion thread rendered in the captured review text. Set aside the notes that carry no reviewer-craft evidence: the author's own self-notes; automation output (a comment the record flags `bot`: an access token, an app, a review service — the reviewer craft judged here is a person's); bare approvals or acknowledgements ("LGTM", "+1"); author-uptake or status replies that report what was done rather than ask for a change; off-topic chatter unconnected to anything this diff touches. When no substantive reviewer comment survives, the applicability never arose, whether or not `context/review_threads.json` records a bare approval — the common case for a freshly opened pull request: record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop — never absent. Do not abstain merely because a field name or flag is missing while a real reviewer comment is plainly visible: read it and judge it.

## Sources
1. The inline review comments (`context/comments.json`): each comment's author, body and path:line anchor. The review decisions (`context/review_threads.json`) add the body a reviewer wrote with an approval or a request for changes. They establish the diff-anchored comments and their positions.
2. The conversation notes (`context/general_comments.json`): each note's author and body. A conversation note has no position; it establishes only author and body.
3. The pull request metadata (`context/metadata.json`): the pull request author, which separates reviewer comments from author notes.
4. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the hunk a comment anchors to. Read it to confirm the comment points at something real. It never establishes whether the comment's claim is correct; assess the comment, not the code.
If the captured record shows a review happened but the comment bodies were not materialized for you, reviewer craft exists that you could not read: report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
assess the standard against all relevant evidence over the substantive reviewer comments that remain.
- MET: every substantive comment is specific and actionable — the author can tell what to change.
- NOT_MET: vague comments leave the author guessing — from a stray straggler among useful notes to a review that is predominantly empty gestures. Quote each one.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: no ordinary case. A comment you can read is judged; one you cannot read is a collection gap.
One result per practice per review, over all the substantive reviewer comments together.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on comment quality alone — a workflow practice, not a merge gate. Scale to how much of the review is content-free. MINOR, the usual band: a stray vague straggler; a lone unhelpful comment is a light cost, never a serious one. MAJOR: a review that is predominantly empty gestures, leaving the author unable to act. Equivalent situations yield equivalent severity.

## Grounding
Quote verbatim every comment you call vague — with its path:line for an inline comment; by author and body for a conversation note, which has no position, so never invent a file:line for it. Quote at least one useful comment when one exists. Never call a comment vague without quoting it; never fabricate a comment to avoid looking idle. Talk about the comments; never grade the reviewer as a person or impute intent.

## Defer
Whether the author took the comments up or left threads open belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; tone and politeness belong to `reviews-respectfully-asks-rather-than-demands`. Here only: could the author act on what the reviewer wrote?

guidance.whyItMatters: 'This looks off' leaves the author guessing what to change and why. A comment that points at the exact line and names the concern gets fixed, while a vague one just slows the change down.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A note anchored to the line that says 'this throws when items is empty, so guard the loop or return early on a null list', so the author knows exactly what to do next.
guidance.goingWell: Review comments name the line and the fix

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Point at the exact place. Comment on the line, or name the file, function or value.
- Say what is wrong and what to change. Instead of “Fix this”, write “`retries` never resets, so reset it after a successful call”.
- If you are not sure of the fix, name the problem or ask a question that the author can answer.
- Give a note on the conversation the same detail as a note on a line. Name the file or function in it.
- Mark an optional suggestion with “Optional:”. Then the author knows which changes you need.

## When it does not apply

- The practice looks at your comments, not at the code. A large pull or merge request with little review is not a lapse.
- The pull or merge request has no substantive review comment yet.
- The note is the author’s own note.
- The note comes from a bot, an app or an automated review service.
- The note is only an approval, such as “LGTM” or “+1”.
- The note reports what someone did and asks for no change.
- The note is off-topic and is not about the change.

It still applies when you write the note on the conversation and not on a line.

## Common mistakes

- Softening a point until it says nothing, such as “Maybe look at this again”. Instead, name the problem and the change.
- Leaving a bare “?” on a line. Instead, write the question you want answered, such as which input reaches this branch.
- Writing “Needs cleanup” on the conversation. Instead, name the file or function and say what to clean up.

## Sources

- [How to write code review comments](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/comments.html), Google Engineering Practices. Google advises a balance between pointing out problems and giving direct guidance. It also suggests labels that tell required changes from optional suggestions.
- [Characteristics of useful code reviews: an empirical study at Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/characteristics-of-useful-code-reviews-an-empirical-study-at-microsoft/), Bosu, Greiler and Bird, 2015. Comments that authors found useful often led to a change near the lines that they pointed at. Microsoft sells code review tools.
- [Predicting usefulness of code review comments using textual features and developer experience](https://doi.org/10.1109/MSR.2017.17), Rahman, Roy and Kula, 2017. Useful comments named relevant code elements and shared more words with the changed code.

definition.name: Comment on the code, not the person
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: how the REVIEWER's substantive comments are voiced — as questions, suggestions and reasoned disagreement aimed at the code, or as orders, sarcasm or contempt aimed at the person.

## The standard
Judge whether the reviewer's comments stay civil and collaborative: concerns raised as questions or suggestions, disagreement carrying a reason ("I'd prefer X because Y"), rather than bare orders, belittling, sarcasm, contempt, name-calling or hostility aimed at the author. This is about HOW feedback is voiced, never whether the technical point is correct. Directness, brevity and strong technical disagreement are not incivility: "This will NPE when items is empty" is blunt and civil. A command paired with a reason is fine. Do not flag a word like "just" or "obviously" when it reads neutrally; judge the whole phrasing in context as an experienced reviewer would. The subject is the reviewer, never the changed code: "a big pull request got little review" is not a result.

## Applicability
This is a gate. A reviewer is anyone whose author differs from the pull request author; never grade the author's own words. Skip comments the record flags `bot` and bare approvals ("LGTM", "+1") — they carry no human reviewer tone. The flag is the provider's classification; never guess from the shape of a login: a numeric or token-like login without the flag is a real human reviewer, not automation. When no substantive reviewer comment survives this filter, whether or not a bare approval was recorded — the common case for a freshly opened, unreviewed pull request — the applicability never arose: record DOES_NOT_APPLY, say so, and stop. Never absent; an unreviewed pull request is never a substandard review. This is the only DOES_NOT_APPLY case.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): the author, to apply the filter, and the state. It establishes who is a reviewer. It never establishes tone.
2. Inline review comments (`context/comments.json`): each carries path, line, body and author. The review decisions (`context/review_threads.json`) add the body a reviewer wrote with an approval or a request for changes. They establish what a reviewer said at a position in the code.
3. Conversation-tab comments (`context/general_comments.json`): author and body, no path or line. They establish what a reviewer said about the change as a whole.
Judge tone across both comment sources. An image in a comment: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. If the record shows a review happened but the comment bodies are not in your context, there was reviewer speech you could not read: report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: at least one substantive reviewer comment survives the filter and every one is civil and collaborative — a concern posed so the author can respond, disagreement kept on the code.
- NOT_MET: one or more comments carry a quotable incivility marker: a bare order with no reason and no softening ("Change this."), belittling that implies the author should not have needed telling, sarcasm or contempt, name-calling, hostility aimed at the person.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE when the complete captured context leaves the tone of a quoted comment genuinely ambiguous; name what would settle it. Comment bodies you could not acquire are a collection gap, not a result.
One result per practice per review, over every surviving reviewer comment.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on tone alone — a formative communication practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a single sharp-but-impersonal edge. MAJOR: a pattern across several comments, or contempt, name-calling or hostility aimed at the person. Identical comments yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote every marker you count verbatim, with its author; never fabricate a comment, a clean bill or an exoneration. Cite an inline comment only by the path and line it actually carries; cite a conversation-tab comment by author and quoted text and leave the location empty. Frame everything about the COMMENT — "this phrasing reads as a demand" — never about the reviewer as a person; no hunches, no psychoanalysing, no intent inferred beyond the words. For MET, cite the surviving comments you read.

## Defer
Whether a comment is specific, actionable or technically right belongs to `leaves-useful-specific-review-comments` and `reviews-substantively-with-understanding`; a vague-but-civil comment is still MET here. Here only: does the phrasing land on the code and not on the author?

guidance.whyItMatters: The same point can be made as a question or as a put-down, and people remember which one you chose. A curious question gets acted on, while sarcasm and bare orders breed defensiveness and make the next review harder.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: 'What happens if this runs twice, could we hit a race here?' rather than 'this is obviously broken, did you even test it?', so disagreement lands on the code and never on the author.
guidance.goingWell: Comments land on the code, never on the author

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Write about the code, never about the person who wrote it. Say what the code does, not what the author failed to do.
- When you have a concern, ask a real question or make a suggestion that the author can answer.
- When you ask for a change, give your reason. For example, instead of “Change this”, write “Could we use a map here? The list lookup scans the whole list for each item”.
- When you disagree, say what you prefer and why: “I’d prefer X because Y”.
- Before you post, remove sarcasm and any words that say the author should have known better.

## When it does not apply

- You wrote the pull or merge request. Your own comments on it do not count.
- A bot wrote the comment.
- The only comment is a bare approval, such as “LGTM” or “+1”.
- No reviewer has left a real comment yet, such as on a new pull or merge request.

It still applies when an account name looks automated but the account is not marked as a bot.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that being direct is rude. A short, blunt comment about the code is fine, such as “This fails when the list is empty”. Strong technical disagreement is fine too. Keep the point clear, and keep it on the code.
- Checking only for single words such as “just” or “obviously”. Such a word is fine when it reads neutrally. Read the whole comment, and check where it points: at the code or at the author.
- Asking a question only to belittle, such as “Did you even run this?”. The author cannot answer it. Instead, say what you think is wrong and why.
- Letting frustration show when a change comes back again. Frustration, name-calling and impatience are common in uncivil reviews. Instead, restate the open concern and give your reason.

## Sources

- [How to write code review comments](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/comments.html), Google Engineering Practices. Comment on the code and never on the developer, and often explain why you ask for a change.
- [Destructive criticism in software code review impacts inclusion](https://research.google/pubs/destructive-criticism-in-software-code-review-impacts-inclusion/), Gunawardena and others, 2022. The study surveyed 93 software practitioners. Women saw destructive criticism as less appropriate. They were also less motivated to keep working with the developer who gave it.
- [Characterizing incivility in open source code review discussions](https://doi.org/10.1145/3479497), Ferreira, Cheng and Adams, 2021. In Linux kernel reviews, the most frequent features of uncivil emails were frustration, name calling and impatience. The study also found civil ways to disagree.

definition.name: Explain consequential review judgments
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a review whose captured context called for written reasoning carries a substantive comment grounded in the change.

## The standard
Judge the written explanation accompanying a review, not whether the reviewer read or understood the change. A substantive comment makes the reviewer's reasoning inspectable: it names or quotes a concrete diff element — a path, a symbol or a term that actually appears in the diff or summary you can see — or asks a real clarifying question about the change. One such comment is enough; polish, tone and specificity are not graded here. A bare approval or acknowledgement ("LGTM", "+1", a lone thumbs-up) supplies no written reasoning, but it does not establish that the review was careless or superficial. Written reasoning is owed only when the captured context establishes a need for it: a request to explain a consequential trade-off, or a documented review requirement. Change size or risk alone does not make commentary mandatory. A reviewer is anyone whose login differs from the pull request author. Discount machine noise and empty ceremony: a comment or decision the record flags `bot` is not human review, and a content-free approval is not engagement. The flag is the provider's classification of the account; a login's shape decides nothing.

## Applicability
This is a gate. This practice judges REVIEWER activity, never the changed code; "a big PR got little review" is not a result. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when no review has happened yet (no reviewer comment and no approval), when `context/review_threads.json` has no review decision and no substantive reviewer comment survives the author-exclusion filter, or when the context demonstrates no need for an explanation and none was supplied. An unreviewed or draft pull request is never a substandard review; do not manufacture praise or criticism from a bare approval.

## Sources
1. The review decisions (`context/review_threads.json`) and the inline diff comments (`context/comments.json`), with their authors. They establish who reviewed, what was approved, and any inline reasoning. An empty inline thread never establishes missing reasoning across the other sources, nor an unperformed review.
2. The general comments (`context/general_comments.json`): the conversation and discussion notes. The substance of a review may live here rather than inline; read whatever review notes are materialized, under whatever heading, before concluding nothing substantive exists. They also establish a request for an explanation, when one was made.
3. The description and metadata (`context/description.md`, `context/metadata.json`): the author's login for the reviewer filter, and any documented review requirement or trade-off the change raises. They never establish that reasoning was written.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) and the checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether a comment's named path, symbol or term actually appears in the change, and the real size of the change once obviously generated or vendored bulk (lockfiles, generated clients, migrations, snapshots) is discounted — a "big" diff that is mostly generated is smaller than its line count. They never make commentary mandatory on their own.
Judge from the review notes and the change-size evidence present in your context; do not claim per-comment or per-line facts you cannot see. Missing or incomplete required sources are a collection gap with no result; never read a missing count as zero.

## Judge
assess the standard against all relevant evidence, after inspecting every declared source of review comments.
- MET: an applicable review includes a substantive comment grounded in the change, inline or in the discussion.
- NOT_MET: the captured context establishes that written reasoning was demonstrably required or requested, the review was approved without it, and every declared review-comment source holds nothing but bare approvals or acknowledgements.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE only when the captured requirement or explanation remains genuinely ambiguous after every available source is inspected; name the unresolved question. Having read every source and found no reasoning where none was demonstrably required is DOES_NOT_APPLY, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review. Equivalent inputs yield equivalent calls.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — a non-blocking practice. Severity reflects the concrete coordination or decision-recording consequence of the missing explanation, never an assumption about how carefully the reviewer read. MINOR, the usual band: the missing reasoning costs the team little to recover. MAJOR: the missing reasoning leaves a consequential decision with no inspectable basis for the author or other reviewers.

## Grounding
Cite the written comment for MET, and the diff element it names when it names one. For NOT_MET, cite the context that establishes why an explanation was needed, the approval that supplied none, and the boundary: every declared review-comment source inspected. Never invent a comment, a file, a size or a clean bill you did not verify. Neither a not-yet-reviewed change nor an approval without commentary establishes a superficial review; describe what was written, never how the reviewer read.

## Defer
Whether the comments were specific and well-worded belongs to `leaves-useful-specific-review-comments`; whether the author acted on them belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`. Do not double-flag them here. Here only: does the written explanation meet its demonstrated purpose?

guidance.whyItMatters: A short explanation makes the basis of an important approval or concern available to the author and other reviewers. A bare approval alone does not show what was checked; it also does not prove that the reviewer failed to read the change.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: For a consequential authorization change, a reviewer names the permission check they considered and explains why it addresses the concern, or asks a specific unresolved question. A routine change with no material concern may need only a brief approval.
guidance.goingWell: Reviews that call for reasoning get it in writing

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- When the author or another reviewer asks you to explain a choice, write your answer with your approval.
- If your project’s review rules ask reviewers to record what they checked, write it down with your approval.
- Name something that is in the change: a file, a function or a term that you checked. For example, a change sets who can edit a project. Instead of “LGTM” (looks good to me), write “`canEdit()` now checks the project role, so viewers cannot save”.
- If you’re still unsure, ask one real question about the change, such as which code calls the new check. A real question also shows your reasoning.
- Write it where your team reads it. An inline comment and a note in the discussion both work. One short comment is enough.

## When it does not apply

- Nobody has reviewed the change yet. It has no approval and no reviewer comment. This includes a draft.
- There is no review decision, and no reviewer has written a comment with substance.
- Nobody asked for a reason, no review rule needs one, and you approved without one.

## Common mistakes

- Treating size or risk alone as a reason you must explain. Instead, write your reason when someone asks for it or when your review rules need it.
- Answering a request for your reasoning with only “LGTM” or a thumbs-up. Instead, write one sentence that says what you checked and why it answers the concern.
- Giving a reason that fits any change, such as “Looks safe to me”. Instead, name the file, function or term that you checked, so others can check it too.
- Reading a teammate’s bare approval as proof that they skipped the change. Instead, ask for their reason if you need it.

## Sources

- [How to write code review comments](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/comments.html), Google Engineering Practices. Saying why helps the author understand a comment. Google also says that you do not always need to.
- [Information needs in contemporary code review](https://research.tudelft.nl/en/publications/information-needs-in-contemporary-code-review), Pascarella and others, 2018. In open-source code review, reviewers most often asked about alternatives, their own understanding of the change, and its reason.
- [Expectations, outcomes, and challenges of modern code review](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICSE.2013.6606617), Bacchelli and Bird, 2013. At Microsoft, understanding the change was the key part of code review, and reviews spread knowledge and team awareness. Microsoft sells code review tools.

definition.name: Include tests with the change
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a test for the changed production behaviour arriving in the same change.

## The standard
Judge one workflow practice: when the change introduces non-trivial production behaviour, does a test for THAT behaviour arrive in the same diff? You are not hunting for missing edge cases, doing a lint sweep or re-judging the change's size; you are asking whether the new logic ships locked in by a test that could observe it. Production behaviour: a new function or endpoint, a new branch or computation, a changed validation or state transition. A covering test plausibly exercises that behaviour: it touches the same symbol, endpoint or path, or asserts the corrected result. A bug fix is strongest when it ships a test that would fail on the old code and pass on the new. Judge the PRESENCE and plausible linkage of a covering test, never its naming, readability or assertion style.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when there is no production surface to judge: the diff is empty, or — after setting aside generated, vendored, lock and migration files, which are neither production logic nor a test of it — it is test-only, docs-only, config-only, or a pure rename, format or type-only change with no quotable added behaviour. Layout is not behaviour: a view, control or style change with no branch, computation or state transition — a button whose action is empty, a title, a colour, a spacing — leaves nothing a test could observe, and is DOES_NOT_APPLY. A test-only change does not establish the applicability.

## Sources
This is decided from the diff alone.
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): classify each changed file as production or test by its path and name, using judgment about test conventions across languages. The production hunks establish the behaviour added or changed; the test hunks establish whether a test names the same symbol, endpoint or path, or asserts the corrected result. Neither establishes that any test ran.
2. The commits (`context/commits.json`): subjects that say what the change does, such as naming a fix. They establish the shape of the change; they never establish a per-commit mapping, since per-commit patches are not in your context.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): existing tests near the changed code, for context on where a covering test would live. The absence of a repository-wide test inventory is never a reason to abstain: load-bearing, testable logic shipped into a repository with no test target at all is the lesson, and is judged, not abstained from.
If a required portion of the production or test diff is truncated or unavailable, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the diff adds or changes real production behaviour and the same diff adds or updates a test that plausibly exercises it. Quote the production line and the test span that names the shared symbol or asserts the corrected result.
- NOT_MET: the diff adds testable production behaviour, and no test in the same diff exercises it — after scanning every test file in the diff. Never manufacture untested logic to force this cell.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE only when the complete captured evidence leaves the relationship between a test and the changed behaviour genuinely ambiguous; name what would settle it. Having scanned every test file in the diff and found none that covers a quotable behaviour is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE. A truncated diff is a collection gap, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, on the single most consequential untested behaviour when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. Reason about consequence, never a line count. MINOR, the usual band: a single small, focused piece of untested logic that one test would pin. MAJOR: a defect fix shipping with nothing to lock the corrected behaviour in, or substantial or branching untested logic. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the exact added span relied on: the `[L<n>]` production line embodying the behaviour, and for MET the `[L<n>]` test span naming the shared symbol. NOT_MET requires the quoted untested production line AND a stated scan of the diff's test files confirming that none covers it — that scan is the boundary. Never invent a test, a file or a clean bill you did not read. Never claim a test ran or passed, and never claim a per-commit mapping you did not observe. Describe the observable delivery; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Change size belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; weakening an EXISTING suite belongs to `keeps-the-test-suite-honest`. Here only: did a test for the new behaviour ship with it?

guidance.whyItMatters: Automated tests preserve checked behavior as the code changes and catch regressions without repeating every manual check. Shipping a focused test with a behavior change or defect fix gives later contributors a repeatable check of the behavior the change is meant to keep.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: New logic arrives with a test beside it, and a bug fix comes with a test that fails on the old code and passes on the new, proving the behaviour is what you say it is.
guidance.goingWell: New logic and fixes arrive with a test beside them
