guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, list the behavior that your change adds or changes. Look for a new function or endpoint, a new branch or calculation, and a changed validation or state change.
- For each item, add or update a test in the same pull request or merge request. For example, you add a check for expired accounts to sign-in. Instead of leaving it untested, add a test that signs in with an expired account and expects a refusal.
- Make the test call the function, endpoint or path that you changed, or check the corrected result.
- Put the new test where the repository keeps the tests for the code near it.
- When you fix a bug, write the test first. Run it on the old code to see it fail. Fix the code in the same change. Run the test again to see it pass.

![Three steps for a bug fix follow in order. First you write the test, and it shows the bug. Then you fix the code in the same change. Last, you run the test again, and it confirms the fix.](figures/fix-order.svg)

## When it does not apply

- The change is empty.
- The change holds only tests, only docs, or only configuration. Generated files, copied third-party code, lockfiles and database migrations do not count.
- The change only renames, formats, or changes type declarations, and adds no behavior. Those files do not count.
- The change only touches layout, such as a title, a color, the spacing, or a button that does nothing yet.

It still applies when your repository has no tests yet.

## Common mistakes

- Chasing every edge case or polishing test names before the new behavior has any test. Instead, first add one test that exercises the new behavior.
- Adding any test to the change and calling it done. A test counts only when it exercises the new behavior. Instead, make it call the code you changed, or check the corrected result.
- Fixing a bug with nothing that holds the fix in place. Instead, add a test that shows the bug, and fix the bug in the same change.
- Promising the tests in a later change. Instead, ship them with the code, so later changes cannot break the behavior unnoticed.

## Sources

- [What to look for in a code review](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html), Google Engineering Practices. Google advises adding tests in the same change as the production code.
- [Testing overview](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch11.html), Adam Bender, in Software Engineering at Google, 2020. Automated tests catch mistakes early, so a team can change code with confidence and keep found bugs from coming back.
- [Self-testing code](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/SelfTestingCode.html), Martin Fowler, 2014. Work is complete only with the tests that keep it working. A bug fix starts with a test that exposes the bug.

definition.name: Keep the test suite honest
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: changed existing checks retain their regression coverage, or their removal is justified by the captured change.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: does the change preserve the existing checks, or does it weaken them without a justified reason? An honest suite keeps telling the truth: when a test starts failing, the fix addresses the underlying cause, and when a test genuinely must go, it goes with a stated, quotable reason. Unjustified weakening deletes, disables, skips, comments out or hollows out a test or its assertions without explaining why the check is gone. Do not infer the author's motive or whether the build passed. The test is one of judgment, not keywords: can the check still fail on the regression it guarded? A faithful migration that preserves assertion strength — a rename, a move, an API upgrade, splitting one test into several, or deleting a test whose subject under test is itself removed in this same diff — is not a suppression. This is a craft practice about how the change treats its safety net, not a line-by-line lint sweep and never a merge gate.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when there is no existing test the change could be lowering: the diff changes no existing hand-written test or assertion, or the patch is empty. Exclude generated or vendored test code, then inspect every remaining changed check regardless of how much generated output surrounds it. A feature with no test changes is DOES_NOT_APPLY here, not an assessed result. New tests alone create no existing check to compare. A changed existing check creates the applicability whether it is preserved or weakened.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, read exhaustively, with `work/change/files.json` to find the test files): every test hunk — an added skip or disable, a removed assertion or test block, commented-out executable test code, an assertion made trivially true, and any adjacent comment naming a tracker or a `reason=` / `@Disabled("…")` argument. It establishes what happened to each check and any reason written beside it. It never establishes that the suite ran.
2. The commits (`context/commits.json`) and the description (`context/description.md`): a line explaining a removal or skip. They establish a quotable reason tied to the change; they never establish a reason they do not state.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the unchanged surroundings of a touched test, to tell a hollowed assertion from a faithful move or split, and whether a deleted test's subject is gone. It never supplies a justification nobody wrote.
When the change touches a test surface but the patch is truncated so those hunks cannot be read, report a collection gap and record no result; unread required evidence is not a judgment.

## Judge
The undesirable behaviour is unjustified weakening. Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: a real assertion becomes trivially true, an entire test block is dropped, executable test code is commented out, or a test is skipped or disabled — and no quotable reason is tied to it anywhere in the sources above. Quote the deciding line(s).
- MET: the change touches real test code and, after a complete bounded search of every test hunk, every check is at least as strong as before, or each removal or skip has a quotable reason supported by the captured change. An arbitrary explanation does not justify discarding a still-relevant check. A faithful migration is MET, not a suppression. Name the test file(s) you inspected.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE only when a read hunk genuinely cannot settle whether a check can still fail on what it guarded; name what would settle it. A missing or truncated patch is a collection gap, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review. Name the single most consequential suppressed test and show the shape of the fix: restore the check, or record a reason that explains why it is no longer appropriate.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on test suppression alone — formative, non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a single unexplained skip. MAJOR: a deleted test, a hollowed assertion, or several unexplained suppressions, since more of the suite's honesty is lost.

## Grounding
Every result quotes the deciding test line(s) from the diff: the added skip or weakened assertion, or the removed line for a deletion. For MET, cite the test hunks inspected and any quoted reason; never record it for a diff that touches no test surface. Never claim to have run, compiled or executed the suite; you see only the patch. Never assert a suppression, or a justification, you cannot point to in the captured files — if you cannot quote it, it does not exist. Describe the observable behaviour of the diff; never impute intent or character, and never grade the author.

## Defer
Whether NEW tests were added for new logic belongs to `ships-tests-with-the-change`. Here only: does the change WEAKEN the existing safety net without saying why?

guidance.whyItMatters: Deleting or skipping a failing test to get a passing build hides the breakage instead of fixing it, and removes the alarm that would have caught it next time. The suite only protects you while it tells the truth.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Existing checks retain their regression coverage. A check that no longer applies is removed with a reason tied to the changed behavior; a still-relevant failing check is fixed at the cause rather than disabled.
guidance.goingWell: Existing checks stay effective or their removal is justified

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- When an existing test fails after your change, fix the cause. Do not weaken the test to make it pass.
- When you update a test for new behavior, keep its check as strong as before.
- When you move, rename or split a test, carry every assertion with it.
- If a test must go, say in the description or a commit message how your change made it obsolete. For example, instead of deleting a rounding test with no reason, write that your change removes rounding.
- If your change means a test should no longer run, write why in the skip itself. Tie the reason to your change, such as the text of `@Disabled("…")` in JUnit or `reason=` in pytest.

## When it does not apply

- Your change edits no existing test or assertion. For example, it adds a feature and changes no tests.
- Your change is empty.
- The only tests that you changed are generated by a tool or copied in from another project.
- Your change only adds new tests.

It still applies when you change an existing test and keep it just as strong. It also applies when a few hand-written test lines sit among many generated files.

## Common mistakes

- Treating every edit to a test as weakening the suite. A move, a rename or a split is fine. So is deleting a test together with the code it tests. Instead, ask one question: can the test still fail on the bug it guarded?
- Hollowing out a test instead of removing it. An always-true assertion or commented-out test code leaves a test that passes but checks nothing. Instead, restore the check, or remove the test and say why.
- Giving a reason that explains nothing. “Fix later” does not say why a test that still matters can go. Instead, fix the cause, or explain how your change made the test obsolete.
- Skipping a test and moving on. Many skipped tests stay skipped for years. Instead, fix the cause in this change when you can.

## Sources

- [Unit testing](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch12.html), Erik Kuefler, Software Engineering at Google, 2020. A refactoring, a new feature or a bug fix should not need changes to existing tests. Only a change in behavior should.
- [How disabled tests manifest in test maintainability challenges?](https://doi.org/10.1145/3468264.3468609), Kim, Yang, Yang and Chen, 2021. In 15 open-source Java projects, about 41% of disabled tests never came back, and most stayed disabled for years.
- [Disabling tests](https://docs.junit.org/current/writing-tests/disabling-tests.html), JUnit User Guide, the JUnit team. A reason is optional, but the JUnit team recommends a short reason for each disabled test.

definition.name: Factor out duplication instead of copy-pasting
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added hand-written code expresses each maintained rule in one appropriate place, without unjustified copy-paste.

## The standard
Judge one closed corpus: the lines this pull request adds. Flag a maintained rule or computation expressed independently in two or more added blocks, where a change to that rule would need the same correction in each copy (Fowler; Hunt & Thomas, DRY). Similar syntax is a lead to inspect, not the standard. Separate concepts may use the same framework idiom without sharing a rule; combining them merely to shorten the code creates an unnecessary coupling. A coherent multi-line computation, validation, mapping or transform, or constant or config block can be a flaggable copy. A one-liner, a guard clause, a field assignment or a forced-similar idiom (equals/hashCode, builder chains, switch arms, DI or route registrations) is not — an idiom is a few lines the platform dictates; a repeated multi-line block can carry duplicated knowledge, including a view body or a fetch-decode-assign sequence. Length alone never establishes that two blocks express the same rule. Legitimately parallel repetition is not a defect: test cases, fixtures — including preview, story and demo setups that show the same sample in another state, appearance or environment — and table-driven or parametrized bodies are meant to look alike. The exception covers the sample setup, not a production rule copied into it. Duplication can live within one function: sibling `if`, `case` or branch bodies that each repeat the same multi-line computation differing only in a constant are as flaggable as cross-function copies. Use judgment on whether two blocks are a genuine copy-paste or a coincidental shared idiom.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop only when the change offers no surface to judge: a documentation, diagram, image diff, or one whose added lines are entirely generated, vendored or test fixtures. Hand-written configuration that repeats a maintained rule is a surface to judge. A diff you read and found clean is not one of these; DOES_NOT_APPLY says the work had no subject here, which is false of it.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the `[L<n>]` new-side spans of the added hunks. It establishes every candidate pair — a flaggable pair must sit inside these lines. It never establishes duplication against unchanged repository code, which is out of scope either way; pre-existing duplication you cannot see being introduced here is not judged.
2. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`): which paths are generated or vendored (`*.gen.*`, lockfiles, OpenAPI specs, route trees, migrations and the like) or test fixtures. It establishes the hand-authored remainder you assess. It never establishes a pair.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the surrounding lines of a hunk cut off mid-block. It establishes the full shape of an added block. It never establishes a pair against code the change did not add.
The leads from the practice script below these criteria list every pair of added blocks whose lines share a shape once names and literals are set aside, with both spans, the run length and the names that differ: decide every pair, and quote both spans. If the diff was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Before choosing, scan every added hand-written block for structural sameness, including branch bodies, not just whole functions. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- NOT_MET: two or more added blocks express the same maintained rule or computation. Quote both occurrences, identify that shared knowledge and explain which change to it would need to be repeated. Names or types that differ are not enough to establish shared knowledge.
- MET: you read every added hand-written hunk and no pair repeats maintained knowledge under the standard, including when similar blocks serve independent concepts, follow the same framework idiom or are legitimately parallel repetition. This is a proof over a closed corpus, not a failure to find: the copy-paste that could have arrived with this change did not.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for a candidate pair you read and genuinely cannot call; quote it and name what would settle it. Do not resolve the doubt into MET, NOT_MET or DOES_NOT_APPLY. Having read every added hunk and found no pair is MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, covering every flagged pair.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. Calibrate to consequence and spread. MINOR, the usual band: a duplicated presentation rule whose copies would need the same correction. Similar markup without a shared maintained rule is not a lapse. Duplicated logic where a divergent copy is a real bug risk weighs more. MAJOR: a copy already spreading to several places, or several distinct duplicated blocks. Identical added code yields identical severity.

## Grounding
For NOT_MET quote both occurrences by path and `[L<n>]` span, name the shared rule and explain its repeated maintenance; a duplication claim you cannot ground in two quoted added spans is not made. For MET record `evidence.search` over the diff, cite the repeated-looking blocks you actually checked, and state in the boundary that duplication against code outside the diff is out of scope either way. Describe only the observable copy-paste practice: never assert the code is buggy, will diverge or will break, and never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether one block is too long or does too many things belongs to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`; never flag a single block here. Here only: repetition across added blocks.

guidance.whyItMatters: Copy-pasted logic means every future fix has to land in every copy, and the copy you forget keeps the old behaviour, which is exactly the bug. Pull the shared logic into one place and you fix it once.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: By the time the same validation logic shows up a third time, you stop copying it and lift the shared concept into one named helper every caller uses, leaving a single source of truth instead of copies that drift apart. You hold off when blocks only look alike by coincidence, since forcing a shared abstraction on them is worse than the duplication.
guidance.goingWell: Repeated logic gets lifted into one named helper

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Move logic that you would paste again into one named function, constant, loop or lookup table.
- Pass in what differs between the copies, such as a value, a name or a type.
- For example, instead of copying a tax calculation into two places, write one `addTax(sum)` and call it twice.
- When `if` or `case` branches repeat the same steps, set the one constant that differs in each branch. Then run the steps once after them.
- Name the shared part after the rule that it holds.

## When it does not apply

- The change only updates documentation, diagrams or images.
- Every added line is generated code, copied-in third-party (vendored) code or a test fixture.

It still applies when hand-written configuration repeats a rule that your team maintains.

## Common mistakes

- Judging by length or by looks. Length alone does not make two blocks copies, and neither does a similar shape. Instead, ask if both blocks express the same rule. If they would change for different reasons, keep them apart.
- Merging short idioms that only look alike. Some idioms repeat a few lines that the language or framework asks for. Examples are guard clauses (early `return` checks), field assignments, equality and hash methods, one-line `switch` arms and route registrations. Test cases and fixtures look alike on purpose too. Leave them as they are.
- Growing a shared helper with flags. If each new caller adds a parameter and an `if` to the helper, the callers no longer share one rule. Instead, put the code back into each caller, and then extract only the part that they truly share.

## Sources

- [Avoiding repetition](https://martinfowler.com/ieeeSoftware/repetition.pdf), Martin Fowler, IEEE Software, 2001 (DOI 10.1109/52.903160). Find what is the same and what varies, move the same part into one place, and pass in the difference. Some duplication is only a coincidence.
- [Do code clones matter?](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.05472), Juergens, Deissenboeck, Hummel and Wagner, ICSE 2009 (DOI 10.1109/ICSE.2009.5070547). In five industrial and open-source systems, copies of code were often changed in only some places. Nearly every second unplanned change of this kind was a fault.
- [The wrong abstraction](https://sandimetz.com/blog/2016/1/20/the-wrong-abstraction), Sandi Metz, 2016. A shared helper that gains a parameter and a condition for each caller is the wrong abstraction. Put the code back into the callers and extract it again.

definition.name: Keep functions small and single-purpose
definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: selected or substantially rewritten functions keep a coherent, scannable purpose without tangled concerns or obscuring nesting.

## The standard
Ask of the largest function the change introduces or substantially rewrites what a senior reviewer asks: can I hold its purpose in my head, name it in a phrase, and follow it at a glance? A focused function does one nameable job. The defect is a single body that visibly interleaves several SUBSTANTIAL, separable concerns — each a real multi-step block, genuinely interwoven, not a short serialize/encode/respond tail on a coherent pipeline — OR nests control flow so deep the core action is lost in indentation, OR runs so long its purpose stops being scannable. Not a defect: a linear pipeline of single-purpose stages (guard → build → encode → return; validate → operate → respond) is ONE purpose even when it ends by serializing a result; a thin body that delegates each step to a named helper in one call each (parse → fetch → render) is ONE orchestration, because the responsibilities live in the helpers — counting one-line delegated calls as separate concerns is the false positive to avoid. A defect: one body that parses input AND performs I/O AND applies business rules AND formats output, each written out and tangled together; a handler whose real action sits four conditionals deep. Reason like an expert about THIS code's shape. Apply no line count and no fixed concern count, and never quote a threshold to the developer. Use your judgment for cases these examples do not cover.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every hand-written function body in this file. A file with no applicable body does not apply. Use no line-count threshold. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the selected bodies on ITEM reviews with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers — the ITEM change boundary. It establishes each body's length, nesting and the concerns written out in it. It never establishes that a function is correct, or how it is factored against collaborators you cannot see.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the pinned source of every assigned body in a SCAN, and of changed bodies in an ITEM. Read it to finish reading that body. The review scope selects the occurrences; context does not expand the assigned item.
If a required body cannot be captured from either, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Read every selected body through. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- NOT_MET: a quotable selected body that carries the defect. Grade each affected function independently; never sum across files, and never escalate because many separate small functions exist — many small focused items IS the baseline.
- MET: the selected code contains bodies, you read every one, and none sprawls, nests deeply or interleaves separable concerns. The sprawl that could have arrived with the selected code did not. Record it with `evidence.search` over the selected pinned source, cite the largest body you read, and say in the boundary that you judged shape, not whether the functions are correct or well factored against collaborators you cannot see.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: no ordinary case. A body you can see is judged on its visible shape; a body you cannot see is a collection gap.
One result per practice and assigned item. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on function shape alone — a craft practice about how work is shaped, never a correctness claim, non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a reader can still follow the body and a single extraction would help. MAJOR: a body that clearly does it all, or whose core action is genuinely obscured by nesting.

## Grounding
Every NOT_MET quotes the specific `[L<n>]` selected span and names the responsibilities to split out or the nesting to flatten; a sprawl you cannot anchor to a quoted extent is not emittable. Judge only function bodies selected by the review scope in the pinned source; never reason about code outside the selected occurrences or context you did not read. Never claim to compile or run anything. Describe the observable shape; never impute intent or character.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Repeated or near-identical blocks belong to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; dead, commented-out or leftover scaffolding belongs to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Do not repeat another practice's complaint. Duplication or dead code alone does not establish tangled responsibilities, but neither removes the function-body applicability: assess the shape on its own evidence, with MET only after the full read. Here only: does each introduced body hold one nameable job a reader can follow?

guidance.whyItMatters: A function that does five things is hard to name, hard to test, and hard to change without breaking behavior you forgot it touched. Small, focused functions are the ones you can actually hold in your head.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Instead of one long method that parses, validates, saves, and notifies, you have a few short functions, each doing one clearly named step you can read and test on its own.
guidance.goingWell: Functions stay short and do one named step each

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, name the job of each new or rewritten function in a short phrase. If its job is unclear, look for mixed jobs, deep nesting, or a body that is hard to scan.
- When one body writes out several jobs and mixes them, move each job into its own function. For example, instead of one function that reads, totals and renders a report, write `readRows`, `totalRows` and `renderReport`.
- When the main action sits deep inside nested conditions, handle each special case first and return early.

![With nested checks, the main action sits deep inside the conditions and is buried. With early returns, each special case returns first, so the main action is no longer nested and is easy to find.](figures/early-returns.svg)

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds or rewrites no function body.
- Your change only touches docs, diagrams, images or configuration.
- Your change only deletes or renames code.
- Your change is mostly generated files or copied third-party code, with almost no function body that you wrote.

It still applies when every function that you added or rewrote is already small and focused. It also applies when your change copies code or leaves dead code.

## Common mistakes

- Counting lines or jobs. There is no line limit and no fixed number of jobs. Instead, ask if a reader can name the function’s job in a phrase and follow it at a glance.
- Splitting a function that already does one job. A function that checks its input, does the work and returns the result does one job. So does a function that only calls named helpers one after another. Instead, split only where several full jobs are mixed in one body.
- Splitting a long function into parts with vague names, such as `step2` or `handleData`. A vague name hides the purpose of the function. Instead, name each part after its job.

## Sources

- [Function length](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/FunctionLength.html), Martin Fowler, 2016. When you must study code to see what it does, move it into a function named after what it does. Then the purpose of the function is clear, and a reader rarely needs the body.
- [Replace nested conditional with guard clauses](https://refactoring.com/catalog/replaceNestedConditionalWithGuardClauses.html), Martin Fowler, Refactoring catalog. Check each special case first and return early, so the normal path is no longer nested.
- [Write short functions](https://google.github.io/styleguide/cppguide.html#Write_Short_Functions), Google C++ Style Guide. Google prefers small, focused functions because they are easier to read, change and test. It sets no hard length limit.
- [An empirical validation of cognitive complexity as a measure of source code understandability](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2007.12520), Muñoz Barón, Wyrich and Wagner, ESEM 2020. The study pooled about 24,000 measurements of how well people understood 427 code snippets. Code took longer to understand when it scored high on a measure that adds weight for deeper nesting. Results for correct answers were mixed.

definition.name: Leave the code clean and comment the why
definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: selected hand-written code has no established writing residue, and comments explain intent or constraints rather than restating code.

## The standard
Judge the added implementation lines, every one, for code that ships clean and comments that earn their place. Implementation is hand-written source, and markup or templates that implement application behavior. Decide each added surface by its purpose, never by its file extension or by what else the change contains: drawing data, documentation prose and configuration text are not implementation, even as editable text with comments and even beside selected code, so a comment that labels the shapes of a vector drawing is not residue. A senior reviewer scanning the implementation lines should find no residue: no commented-out code, no leftover debug or trace output, no throwaway scaffolding shipped as if final. Any comment that IS present should explain the WHY — intent, a non-obvious constraint, a items, a caveat, a reference — rather than restate the WHAT the next line already says. An interface comment may instead tell callers the contract they rely on — behavior, inputs, results, failures — even though the body below implements it; whether it adds that context, rather than repeating the declaration, decides it. Blemishes, open and illustrative: an added line that is itself plausible source behind a comment marker (a commented-out assignment, call or control statement); a leftover breakpoint; a "TEMP" or "remove before merge" stub; "// increment i" above `i++`; a comment that narrates the editing session rather than the code ("// FIX 2: added the date field", "// changed this to use X", "// moved from Foo"); a comment with no code under it, left where code was meant to follow. Print-style diagnostics belong to `logs-through-the-platform-logger`, even when they are temporary traces. Do not report the same print here as residue. Clean, open and illustrative: a comment that gives a reason ("retry once: upstream drops the first call after idle"); output that is the file's deliberate purpose (a CLI's own stdout, a test's expected output); a logger call through a real logging facility; a sanctioned TODO referencing a tracked issue. Code-shaped text inside a comment is not sufficient evidence of debris: documentation examples, API usage, commands and explanations may legitimately quote executable syntax. Assess the surrounding purpose, and flag an inactive implementation only when the captured context establishes it is leftover rather than an intentional example.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every implementation line and comment in this file. Documentation, drawing data, and configuration are not implementation. Apply the same exceptions for tracked notes and deliberate examples. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): only the lines marked ADDED (`[L<n>] +` in the annotated diff). Residue is visible in the line itself. Removed and unchanged lines are not graded; code the author commented out and DELETED is a cleanup, never a blemish.
2. The file list (`work/change/files.json`): which files are generated or vendored and so excluded.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the surrounding purpose of a file — whether its output is deliberate, whether a quoted snippet is an example. It never turns an unquotable line into a blemish.
An image or an external link: nothing.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: a quotable blemish on an added hand-written implementation line. Do not count a print-style diagnostic as a blemish here; `logs-through-the-platform-logger` owns it. One blemish is enough: a single restating comment, marker or leftover you can quote is this cell at its lightest severity, never rounded down to MET because it is alone.
- MET: you read all the added hand-written implementation lines through and none carries a blemish. This is a covered search, not a lucky miss: the residue that could have shipped did not. Record it.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE only for a single candidate line you read and genuinely cannot call — a prose comment that may be restatement or explanation, or an inactive implementation that may be leftover or an example. Quote it and do not resolve the doubt in either direction.
One result per practice per review, over all selected lines; a scatter of leftovers is one result.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a proportionate, non-blocking nudge about clarity and maintenance burden. MINOR, the usual band: a lone stray comment or marker is the lightest touch; a scatter of leftovers is a modest cleanup. MAJOR only for a demonstrated, consequential source of confusion about the maintained implementation. Line count never raises severity: a long commented-out block is still one cleanliness nudge. Do not borrow error-handling or security consequences from other practices. Identical added lines yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the exact `[L<n>]` span and file path for every blemish; a blemish you cannot quote is not counted. For an inactive implementation, also quote the context that shows it is leftover. Never infer that a line is dead or debug-only unless its quoted text shows it. For MET, cite the search over the selected pinned source and state the boundary you did not cover: unchanged lines, files this diff does not touch, generated and vendored surface, added surface that is not implementation. Never claim a build or test ran. Describe what was left in the code; never impute intent or character.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Naming, function and file size belong to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`; scope to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; duplication to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; swallowed errors to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`. Dead branches in live code and runtime defects belong to other practices. Here only: residue on added lines, and WHAT-versus-WHY comments.

guidance.whyItMatters: Stray debug output, blocks of commented-out code, and comments that just echo the line all add noise the next reader has to wade through. Clean code with a comment that explains the why reads like someone meant it.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: No leftover print statements or commented-out branches, and where a line looks surprising, a short comment gives the reason, such as 'retry once: the upstream API drops the first call after an idle period', rather than restating what the line does.
guidance.goingWell: Code lands clean, with comments that explain why

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, delete the code that you commented out while you worked. Version control keeps the old version for you.
- Remove what you used only while you worked. Examples are a breakpoint, a “TEMP” stub, or an empty comment where code was meant to go.
- If your project allows a TODO, link it to a tracked issue.
- Delete a comment that only repeats its line. You must keep every comment up to date when the code changes, so each one must earn its place.
- Where a line looks surprising, add a comment that gives the reason. Name the intent, a constraint, a unit, a caveat or a reference. For example, instead of `// sleep for 250 ms` above `sleep(250)`, write `// stay under the rate limit`.

## When it does not apply

- The change is empty.
- The change holds only generated or vendored files, such as lockfiles, build output, specs or migrations.
- The change adds no code. It changes only documentation, diagrams, images or configuration.

It still applies when the change adds markup or templates that make the app work.

## Common mistakes

- Deleting comments that help. A comment on a function can tell its callers what it takes, what it returns, and how it fails. A code example in that comment shows how to call it. Keep both when they say more than the declaration does.
- Keeping old code in a comment in case you need it again. Nobody updates it, so it soon stops matching the code around it. Instead, delete it and find it in version control when you need it.
- Writing about your edits instead of the code, such as “FIX 2: added the date field” or “moved from Foo”. The next reader sees only the code as it is now. Instead, delete the note, or say why the code is this way.

## Sources

- [What to look for in a code review](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html), Google Engineering Practices. Google recommends comments for reasons that the code cannot show, and function documentation for callers.
- [Google Python Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html), Google. Google recommends comments for tricky code, and TODO links that give context, preferably through a tracked bug.
- [The secret life of commented-out source code](https://doi.org/10.1145/3387904.3389259), Pham and Yang, 2020. Commented-out code is often not maintained, and the authors point to version control for keeping old code.
- [A large-scale empirical study on code-comment inconsistencies](https://www.inf.usi.ch/faculty/lanza/PUBS/P/Wen2019a.pdf), Wen, Nagy, Bavota and Lanza, 2019. Keeping comments up to date as the code changes takes a lot of time and care.

definition.name: Log through the platform logger, not print
definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: diagnostic messages selected go through the platform's logger, not through print-style output, in application code.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the selected application code: when it reports a diagnostic — a state, an error, a step reached — does it use the platform's logger or print-style output? Print-style output is the closed list `print(`, `debugPrint(`, `dump(` (Swift), `printf(` (Objective-C), `println(`/`print(` (Kotlin), `System.out.println`/`System.err.println`/`printStackTrace()` (JVM), `console.log/debug/info/warn/error` (TypeScript and JavaScript in application code), `print(` (Python). A logger is `Logger(subsystem:category:)`, the `os_log` functions or `NSLog`/`NSLogv`, which write to the Apple system log (Swift and Objective-C), Android's `android.util.Log` (`Log.v/d/i/w/e/wtf`, whatever its tag) or Timber, SLF4J/Log4j/`java.util.logging`, a `winston`/`pino`/framework logger, Python `logging`. Print-style output is not a lapse where it is the program's output: a command-line tool, a script, a build step, a test, a playground, a `#Preview`, or a `DEBUG`-only block (`#if DEBUG`) that removes itself from release. Exclude credential-bearing diagnostics that `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions` owns. The scope paragraphs select which diagnostic calls to judge.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every diagnostic call in this file. Preserve deliberate program output and platform logger calls. A file with no diagnostic call does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers and the file list (`work/change/files.json`): each added print-style or logger call, the file it lands in, and whether a `#if DEBUG` or a test target encloses it. It establishes what was added where. It never establishes what an unchanged file does.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether the project already has a logger (`Logger(` definitions, a logging dependency in the manifest) and whether the file is an application target or a tool. Read it to classify the file and to say whether the print was written beside an existing logger.
3. The leads from the practice script below these criteria: the print-style and logger calls it found per file, and whether the checkout defines a logger, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where the calls are added, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Enumerate the added diagnostic lines first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added diagnostic in application code goes through the platform logger, and any print-style call is the program's output or `DEBUG`-only. Quote a representative logger call.
- NOT_MET: an added print-style call reports a diagnostic in application code that ships — outside a CLI, script, test, preview or `DEBUG` block. Quote the line and the file.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: whether a file is an application target or a tool cannot be told from the diff or the checkout; name the file.
One result per practice per review, on each distinct proved problem. count the rest in the summary.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one or two prints in application code. MAJOR: an error path reported only by print, or a print that emits personal data. Credential exposure belongs to the security practice named below. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` call and its file; for NOT_MET say why the file is application code (its target, its `import SwiftUI`/`UIKit`, its path). Never claim a print is debugging output without the line; never claim a file is a tool without the fact that makes it one.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
An error swallowed rather than reported belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a secret in a message to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`; a leftover debugging line of another kind to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Do not report the same credential-bearing diagnostic here when `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions` owns its exposure. Here only: does the diagnostic go through the logger?

guidance.whyItMatters: Print-style diagnostics bypass the platform's logging facilities. The platform logger — `Logger` on Apple platforms, `Log`/Timber on Android, SLF4J on the JVM, `logging` in Python, a logger module in Node — lets application diagnostics be collected and filtered where the app runs.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Diagnostics in application code go through the platform's logger. `print`, `console.log`, `println` and `System.out` are left to output a program means to print — a command-line tool, a script, a build step, a test, a playground or a `#Preview` — or to a `DEBUG`-only block.
guidance.goingWell: Application code logs through the logger, never print

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Use the logger that your project already uses for the code around your change.
- If the project has no logger yet, add the standard logger for your platform or framework.
- Send each state, error or step through the logger, at the level that fits it. For example, instead of `print("Sync failed")`, write `logger.error("Sync failed")`.
- If you print only while you debug, log the message at the debug level instead. On Apple platforms, you can also put the print in an `#if DEBUG` block.

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds no diagnostic line to application code: no print call, such as `print` or `console.log`, and no logger call.
- The only prints you add are the program’s own output, as in a command-line tool or a script.
- The only diagnostic lines you add show a secret, such as a password or a token. A security practice covers those.

It still applies when your change adds only logger calls.

## Common mistakes

- Replacing every print with a logger call. A print that is the program’s own output is correct, as in a command-line tool or a test. Instead, keep those prints and move only the diagnostics to the logger.
- Reporting an error path only with a print. Instead, log the error at the error level. Then it reaches the platform logs at the error level, where you can filter for it.
- Printing personal data, such as an email address. Instead, leave it out of the message, or log it through a logger that can hide private values.

## Sources

- [Generating log messages from your code](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/os/generating-log-messages-from-your-code), Apple. Log messages carry a subsystem, a category and a level, so you can filter them. Errors are kept on disk, and private values can be hidden.
- [Logging HOWTO](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/logging.html), Python Software Foundation. Use `print()` for the console output of a command-line program. Use a logger to report events, warnings and handled errors while a program runs.
- [Logging Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP. Keep logging consistent across an application, and build on the logging that your framework gives you. Keep sensitive personal data out of logs, and take care with other personal data, such as email addresses.

definition.name: Handle errors instead of swallowing them
definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: selected failure paths keep their meaningful failure information visible or are safely absorbed under the Standard.

## The standard
When the selected code contains an error, rejection, invalid-input or required-result path, establish the operation and what its failure means from its captured contract, caller or owned state. Optional syntax, a defensive branch or an ordinary no-selection result alone does not establish failure.

The failure should stay visible: surfaced to a caller who can react, or recorded with enough context to diagnose it. It is handled when rethrown, returned, forwarded, wrapped with context, meaningfully recorded, or safely absorbed under the conditions below. A record may be a noticeable log, failure metric or error state the UI reads. Returning the operation's own failure result through a declared result interface propagates it: a failable parse's nil returned unchanged has not discarded an Error the operation never supplied. A captured caller is not needed to establish that return; downstream reaction is not proved. Reducing errors to one recognizable failure or unavailable result preserves their failure information when no required work remains unfinished; distinct details are needed only when the captured contract or caller requires a different response to them. That coded failure indicator needs no intent comment. A success-looking default needs failure surfaced or recorded unless the captured source establishes why absorbing it is safe. The try? syntax alone settles neither safety nor failure.

Expected cancellation is not a failure: work the program itself cancels, because a newer request superseded it or its owner went away, ends early by design, and ending it quietly is control flow that needs no comment, log or error state. The source must establish that cause — what cancels the work, and that its successor or owner then governs the state — and an error's type or name alone does not. If the captured source genuinely leaves the cause or state ownership unknown, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE and name what would settle it. A cancellation that the source shows leaves a caller waiting or a state showing unfinished work that nothing replaces is judged as a failure.

A failure is swallowed when its meaningful failure information is discarded and neither surfaced, recorded nor safely absorbed. Examples are an empty catch, unused error, ignored failure result, dropped rejection or bare return leaving required work unfinished. An empty-value check does not swallow a failure already recorded by its handler. A valid fixed URL adds no runtime-dependent parse failure. A runtime parse or network request may fail, but how that failure is handled is a separate judgment. Judge the selected code's handling as a craft practice, not a syntax sweep.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every applicable failure path in this file. Establish whether each operation can fail and whether its failure stays visible. A file with no applicable failure path does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers and the visible in-diff context. It establishes every failure path the change adds — the ITEM change boundary from the added lines — and where each error goes. It never establishes that the handling is CORRECT, that the recovery works, or that paths outside the diff behave.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when where a caught error goes, or what downstream does with the missing value, sits just outside the hunk. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
Per-commit patches are not in your context; reason from what the diff shows. If the change adds a failure path but the relevant diff is truncated or unavailable, report a collection gap and record no result: unread required evidence establishes neither absence nor uncertainty in the work.

## Judge
Enumerate the added operations and their error, invalid-input and required-result paths. Catches, try shortcuts, guards, optional bindings, early returns, failure results and fallbacks are leads to inspect, not proof of failure. Establish what fails and where it goes from the value origin, captured contract, caller or state, then apply the Standard to all actual paths. Do not assume a clean surface from a glance.
- NOT_MET: quote the added hunk that discards failure information or leaves required work unfinished. Without a quotable discard or unfinished state, you do not have a result.
- MET: failure paths are added and each is handled under the Standard. Record evidence.search over the selected pinned source and the boundary of what is visibly returned, recorded or safely absorbed, not that downstream handling or recovery works.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: an actual failure path whose relevant handling the captured source genuinely does not show; name that path and what would settle it. Optional syntax or missing external knowledge alone is not this result.
One result per practice and assigned item. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. Name each distinct proved problem.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a formative practice to grow, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a swallow on a best-effort or clearly secondary path — cleanup, teardown, optional telemetry, or a failure merely logged a touch too quietly. MAJOR: a swallow that hides a real fault from the caller or user, on a path that persists, communicates, authenticates, parses or otherwise carries consequence. Several distinct swallows, together hiding more of the change's failures, lean MAJOR. Apply these bands to the path's source-established role and consequence, not its syntax. The examples of consequential operations do not by themselves make an optional or best-effort path MAJOR.

## Grounding
Judge only added or modified constructs (new-side [L<n>] markers); never grade pre-existing context or assume unseen code. Cite the added failure and discard or unfinished state for NOT_MET; for MET, cite its returned result, recorded error or evidenced safe absorption, with the source scan and its boundary. Do not claim a caller reacted, a UI displayed it or recovery worked without evidence.

Known language and API semantics can explain the captured operation, type, value origin or state; cite that captured anchor. A specific guarantee or possible failure of an exact API is a factual premise, not a conclusion from a guard or name. Use only semantics you can establish for that operation; do not invent a documented contract or claim to have read documentation you did not read. If those semantics are uncertain, distinguish that uncertainty from what the source shows and apply the Standard. Missing knowledge is not a fault in the work. Types and fixed values visible in source can establish a case without execution. Never claim to run, compile or test, invent an exoneration or give an unverified clean bill. Describe observable behavior, not intent or character.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Whether inputs and edge cases are validated belongs to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`; a deliberate fail-fast crash on an unrecoverable state belongs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`. A printed failure with diagnostic context is recorded, not swallowed. Logger choice belongs to `logs-through-the-platform-logger`. Here only: does an added failure stay visible, or is it dropped?

guidance.whyItMatters: An empty catch block turns a failure into a silent one: the code carries on as if nothing went wrong, and you find out only when something downstream breaks with no clue why. Surfacing the error saves the 2am debugging session.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A failed call reaches someone who can act. The code passes the error to a caller who can react, records it where a person will notice, or ignores it only for a reason that the code shows.
guidance.goingWell: Failures surface or recover, never get swallowed

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- When a call fails and this code cannot fix it, pass the error to the caller with context. For example, instead of an empty `catch` on `saveOrder`, throw an error that names the order and wraps the original.
- When no caller can react, record the failure where a person will see it. Use a log that someone reads, a failure metric, or an error state on the screen.
- When the code does not show why a failure is safe to ignore, explain the reason in the handler.
- Handle each error that a call returns and each promise that rejects.
- When a lookup or a parse can fail, handle its failure branch too. A bare early return tells nobody what went wrong.

## When it does not apply

- Your hand-written code adds no call that can throw, reject or return an error. Generated or vendored files do not count.
- Your change adds no source code, such as docs, diagrams, images, or configuration only.
- Your change only ends work that a newer request replaces, or whose owner went away.
- The source proves that the guarded bad case cannot occur, such as parsing a fixed valid URL.

It still applies when your new code already handles each failure well.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that every handler must rethrow. A log that a person will see keeps the failure visible. So does an error state on the screen. A normal empty state counts only when the failure is also logged with enough context to diagnose it.
- Catching an error and never using it, or dropping it with a shortcut such as Swift’s `try?` or Go’s `_`. Instead, pass it on, log it, or write why it is safe to ignore.
- Writing “ignore” over an empty handler. Say why silence is safe, such as “the file can already be gone”.
- Leaving a TODO in place of a handler. Handle the failure before review.

## Sources

- [Simple testing can prevent most critical failures](https://www.eecg.utoronto.ca/~stumm/Yuan-OSDI-14.html), Yuan and others, 2014. The study looked at 198 failures of five distributed systems. Wrong handling of signaled errors caused 92% of the catastrophic failures. About a third came from simple mistakes, such as an empty handler or a TODO.
- [Caught exceptions: not ignored](https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html#s6.2-caught-exceptions), Google Java Style Guide. It is rarely correct to do nothing with a caught exception. When it is, a comment explains why.
- [Handle errors](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments#handle-errors), Go Code Review Comments, the Go project. Do not throw away an error with `_`. Handle it or return it.
- [CWE-390: Detection of error condition without action](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/390.html), MITRE. An attacker can use an ignored error to put the system in an unexpected state.

definition.name: Validate inputs and edge cases at the boundary
definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: selected consuming sites handle the obvious bad case of values they do not control.

## The standard
Judge whether added or modified code that consumes a value it does not control handles the obvious failure case on purpose, instead of assuming a happy path. A boundary value enters from outside the local logic: a request param, body or header; text a user typed, once it is parsed or used as a number; a decoded network or file payload, including a bundled data file; a collection filled at runtime, such as a response array or a stored list the user populates; an env, config or defaults read; the result of a third-party or RPC call. Not a boundary value: a parameter of the app's own function or view, a framework callback's arguments, view state the code owns, an author literal or constant, and a value a control already bounds (a Slider or Stepper range, a Picker over an enum). A site is in scope only when the same change also USES that value — indexes or slices it, divides by it, converts it to an integer, aggregates it, or passes it into logic that assumes a shape. A value merely forwarded, stored or displayed as the type it already has is not a consuming site: an empty string saved or shown breaks nothing.
A guard is anything on the value's path that rules out the case the site itself needs, in the hunk or in code you can trace to: a count, bounds or empty check (`isEmpty` guards `[0]`, not `[1]` or `[0..<2]`); a zero check before integer division or before a ratio that is shown or converted to an integer; a clamp; do/catch, `try?`, or a `try` that propagates out of a throwing function; a default for an absent value; an early return; a button disabled on the bad case. An operation already total on the bad case needs no guard: a Swift optional the type forces the author to unwrap (`Int(text)`, `.first`, `dict[key]`, `URL(string:)`, `as?`) handled with `if let`, `guard let`, `?.` or `??`; `reduce`, `map`, `filter`, `prefix` or `ForEach` over an empty collection; `items[i]` inside `ForEach(items.indices)`. A default counts unless it is an extreme sentinel (`Int.max`, `.infinity`) that reaches output unchanged. Judge the PRACTICE — is the obvious failure handled at all — not an exhaustive lint: a finite check on a decoded Double, or a zero check on a field the source never sends as zero, is not the obvious case.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every site in this file that consumes a boundary value. Trace its source and the guards on its path. A file with no boundary consuming site does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers and the visible in-diff context. It establishes every consuming site the change introduces — the ITEM change boundary from the added lines — and whether each meets a guard you can see. It never establishes that the guards are sufficient for every input or that callers beyond the diff are safe.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when the guard that would decide a site could sit outside the hunk — above a truncated hunk, or in the caller or view that builds the value. It establishes whether such a guard exists. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
Per-commit patches are not in your context. If the context a deciding site needs remains unavailable after reading the pinned source, report a collection gap and record no result, rather than asserting absence or inapplicability.

## Judge
Scan the selected lines for a boundary value that gets consumed and trace each to its guard; then assess the standard.
- NOT_MET: a boundary value is consumed with nothing on its path ruling out its obvious bad case, so a realistic input — an empty or short response array, an empty bundled list, a library the user has not filled yet — crashes the new path or shows a wrong value. For example `Array(items[0..<2])` on a decoded array behind only an `isEmpty` check, or a minimum seeded with `Int.max` and printed while the list is still empty. Quote the exact `[L<n>]` span of each unguarded site, name the realistic input that breaks it and the missing guard ("count >= 2 before [0..<2]").
- MET: the ordinary result when the change consumes boundary values: you walked every consuming site and each handles its obvious bad case. Looks like a lapse but is not: `a[3]` inside `if a.count >= 4`; `Int(text)` bound with `guard let`; `try decoder.decode` in a throwing function whose caller catches; `pages[index]` when the only way in is a button disabled while `pages` is empty; `offset / 250` in a gesture. The claim is about the coverage of your reading, nothing about correctness.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for a consuming site you can see whose guard the diff and the pinned source do not settle; name the site and what would settle it. Having walked every site and found each guarded is MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE. Missing required context is a collection gap, not a result.
One result per practice per review, covering every unguarded site found.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a practice to grow, not a merge gate. Calibrate to the demonstrated consequence at the boundary and explain the observable risk. MINOR, the usual band: an omission on a low-impact operation. MAJOR: a missing check on a consequential operation, which one site can warrant; several harmless omissions do not escalate on their own. Identical hunks yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Judge only the added and modified lines and their visible in-diff context, plus pinned source you actually read; a site in unchanged code is never charged, even when a changed line feeds it. For NOT_MET, cite the `[L<n>]` span of each unguarded site. For MET, record `evidence.search` over the selected pinned source and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish: that the guards are sufficient, that they cover every case, that callers beyond the diff are safe. Never assert a missing guard you cannot point to; never claim to run, compile or test anything; never invent a clean bill of health. Describe the observable code behaviour, never intent or character.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
A value interpolated raw into a URL, query, command or markup belongs to `validates-and-escapes-untrusted-input`. A crash operator the author wrote — `x!`, `try!`, `as!`, `fatalError`, `unwrap()` — belongs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`: it is neither a guard nor a consuming site here. An implicit trap stays here: an unchecked subscript or slice, an integer division, a conversion to an integer of a value that can be NaN or infinite. The quality of error handling once input is guarded belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a catch that merely prevents the crash satisfies the guard here regardless of its body. Do not repeat another practice's complaint, and do not let another kind of defect stand in for this one.

guidance.whyItMatters: Data from a user, a file, or another service will not always arrive in the shape you expected: it can be empty, null, negative, or huge. Checking it where it enters means a clear rejection instead of a confusing crash three layers deep.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Code that reads an external value first asks what happens if it is missing or out of range and handles that on purpose, so an empty list or a malformed payload meets a clean guard instead of a null-pointer surprise.
guidance.goingWell: External values meet a guard before they are used
