guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Find each value in your change that comes from outside your code. Examples are request data, typed text, a decoded file, a configuration value, and a service response.
- Find the lines that index it, slice it, divide by it or add it up. Also find the lines that make it a whole number or pass it to code that expects a shape.
- For each line, ask what its obvious bad case is, such as empty, missing, zero, or out of range.
- Rule out that case before the line runs. Return early, reject the input with a clear error, use a safe default, or catch the failure. For example, instead of dividing by the item count from a response, return early when the count is zero.

## When it does not apply

- Your change is empty.
- Your change only passes outside values on, saves them, or shows them as they are.
- Your change holds only generated or vendored files.
- Your change adds no source code, such as a change to docs, images, or configuration only.
- Your change uses only typed data from your own app, view state, or controls that already limit the value.

It still applies when the value comes from a data file that ships with your app, or from a list that the user fills.

## Common mistakes

- Trying to check every possible value. Instead, find the obvious input that breaks the line, such as an empty list, and rule out that one.
- Checking a smaller case than the line needs. A check for an empty list protects `items[0]`, but not `items[1]`. Instead, check for as many items as the line reads.
- Trusting a parsed number when you divide by it or use it as an index. Parsing only proves its type. Instead, also check that it is not zero or out of range before that line.
- Starting a minimum at the largest possible number and showing it while the list is empty. Instead, show an empty state or a sensible default.

## Sources

- [Input Validation Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP. Check each value before use, including the range of a parsed number. Reject bad input with a clear error.
- [CWE-20: Improper Input Validation](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/20.html), MITRE. Lists sizes, positions and types to check, with an example of a zero size that the code did not reject.
- [CWE-369: Divide By Zero](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/369.html), MITRE. A division by zero usually comes from a value that the code did not expect.
- [Collection Types](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/collectiontypes/), The Swift Programming Language, the Swift project. An index outside an array causes a runtime error, and an empty array has no valid index.

definition.name: Avoid crashing on recoverable problems
definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: selected crash-shaped operators are safe under their captured provenance or contract, rather than aborting on recoverable runtime failure.

## The standard
Code degrades gracefully on ordinary, recoverable runtime failure rather than deliberately aborting. A chosen crash is an ADDED crash operator the author wrote — force-unwrapping or force-casting a value that can legitimately be absent, `try!` on a call that can throw, or a deliberate abort, panic, exit or fatal error — when its value rides an ordinary runtime path: user input, network, database, disk, a decoded payload, a fallible API's result. Judge two things: can a real input reach the operator and make it fail, and did the change crash on it anyway. Bad, for example: `try! decoder.decode(T.self, from: data)` on a server response; `Int(ageText)!` on text a user typed; `results.first!` on a fetched array; `fatalError` in the catch of a network call. Not a chosen crash, though each looks like one: a genuine programmer invariant that cannot fail unless surrounding code is already broken (an unreachable enum default, a force unwrap of a value just proven non-nil); a fail-fast at a CLI or startup entry point where aborting IS the contract; data the author ships — a literal, a constant, an Info.plist key the change commits, a resource bundled with the app, `URL(string: "https://api.example.com")!`; an operation total by language or platform contract (`String.data(using: .utf8)!`). Code that runs only in an Xcode `#Preview`, a preview-only sample or in tests is not an ordinary runtime path: `try! ModelContainer(…)` or `fatalError` in a preview is scaffolding. A `!` alone is not the defect; whether the operation can ACTUALLY return nil or throw on some real input is. Reason about provenance across languages as an experienced reviewer would, not from the spelling of a construct or the kind of a lead from the practice script.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every explicit crash operator in this file. Preserve proved invariants, entry-point contracts, tests, and preview-only examples. A file with no such operator does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers. It establishes the closed set of crash operators the change adds and, where the hunk shows it, where each crashed-on value came from. It never establishes anything about removed lines, unchanged code or code outside the diff, and it never establishes that anything compiled or ran.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it only to trace the origin of a value the hunk crashes on but does not source, or where the operator runs. It never adds an operator to judge — only operators the diff adds are judged — and it never establishes that unchanged code cannot crash.
If the diff is truncated or unavailable for a change that adds a crash operator, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Scan first, then classify. Enumerate every crash operator in the selected lines and trace where each crashed-on value came from and where the code runs; look before you leap. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- NOT_MET: a quotable added operator on an ordinary runtime path that crashes on a value with a named runtime source, and a real input you can name — a missing field, a failed request, text a user typed — makes it return nil or throw. Quote the deciding added line, name the source and the input.
- MET: the selected code contains crash operators from the closed list, you read every one, and each is guarded on its path, sits on a genuine programmer invariant, a total operation, author-shipped data, preview or test code, or an entry-point contract rather than an ordinary runtime path. Looks like a lapse but is not: `try! ModelContainer(for: Note.self, configurations: inMemory)` inside `#Preview`; `URL(string: "https://api.example.com")!` on a literal. Record it with `evidence.search` over the selected pinned source and say in the boundary that you judged the operators the diff adds, not whether unchanged code can still crash.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: an operator on an ordinary runtime path whose value provenance the diff and pinned source do not settle — you see the diff, not the whole program. Name the operator and the fact that would settle it. It is earned by the trace running out of evidence, never by skipping the trace, and it is never filed under DOES_NOT_APPLY, which claims no operator was here. A crash you cannot tie to a runtime-sourced value and a real input is not groundable as a negative.
One result per practice and assigned item. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. When NOT_MET, name each distinct proved problem. do not rewrite the whole change.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a defensive-programming practice to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band, and the ceiling when the input that makes the operation fail is possible but unusual. MAJOR: a clearly recoverable failure on a clearly ordinary runtime source — decoded or fetched input crashed on outright. Genuine uncertainty about recoverability lowers the band. Identical hunks yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Cite the exact added-line span and the value's origin from observable diff evidence. Judge only added or modified lines with new-side `[L<n>]` markers; never reason about removed lines or code outside the diff, and never claim to compile or run it. Never invent a file, a line, a value source or a clean bill you did not verify. For MET, cite the operators you enumerated and state the boundary you did not cross. Describe the observable behaviour of the code; never impute intent or character.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Empty or swallowed catches and logged-and-continued errors belong to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; missing input validation and implicit traps — an unchecked subscript or slice, an integer division, a trapping conversion — belong to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`. Here only: does an added crash operator deliberately crash on a recoverable runtime condition?

guidance.whyItMatters: Reaching for a force-unwrap or a panic on a condition that can actually happen turns an ordinary hiccup into a hard crash for your users. A problem the code can recover from deserves a graceful path, not a deliberate stop.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Where a value might legitimately be absent, the code unwraps it safely and falls back to a default or a clear error, instead of force-unwrapping and bringing the whole thing down.
guidance.goingWell: Missing values fall back instead of crashing

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, find each crash operator that you added. Examples are `x!`, `try!`, `as!`, `fatalError`, `unwrap()`, `expect()`, `panic`, `!!` and `process.exit`.
- For each one, ask where its value comes from and where the code runs. A value from a user, the network, a database, or a file can be missing.
- On such a path, give the code a way out. Use `if let`, a default value, or an error that the caller can handle. For example, instead of `Int(ageText)!` on text a user typed, use `if let` and show an error when it fails.
- Keep a crash operator where a failure means the code is already broken. Examples are a value that you just checked or a fixed URL that you wrote. Keep one in a test, in a preview, or at a command-line or startup entry point.

## When it does not apply

- The lines that you added have no crash operator. Examples are a change to only docs, configuration or data, or to only generated or copied-in files.
- The only lines that can crash use no crash operator, such as an index into a list or a division. Another practice covers those.

It still applies when you guard the operator on the same path, such as behind `if let` or a nil check.

## Common mistakes

- Treating every `!` as a bug. What matters is whether a real input can make it fail. Instead, trace where the value comes from.
- Force-unwrapping the first item of a fetched list, such as `results.first!`. An empty result is normal. Instead, handle the empty case.
- Calling `fatalError` or `panic` when a network call fails. Requests fail in normal use. Instead, return the error so that the caller can react.
- Copying `try!` from a preview or a test into app code. Instead, catch the error and show the person a way to recover.

## Sources

- [To panic! or not to panic!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch09-03-to-panic-or-not-to-panic.html), Klabnik, Nichols and Krycho, The Rust Programming Language. The book says to return an error for expected failure, such as malformed data. It allows a panic in tests or where your code makes sure a value is valid.
- [The basics](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/thebasics/), The Swift Programming Language, Swift project. Force unwrap only when a missing value is a programmer error, and otherwise use optional binding or a fallback value.
- [Error handling](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/errorhandling/), The Swift Programming Language, Swift project. Use `try!` only when the call cannot throw, such as loading an image that ships with the app.
- [Go code review comments](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments#dont-panic), the Go project. Do not use panic for normal error handling, and return an error instead.

definition.name: Neutralize untrusted input before a dangerous sink
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: untrusted input is neutralized for the exact dangerous sink it reaches in added code.

## The standard
When code added in this diff carries a value from outside the trust boundary into an operation where that value can change the operation's meaning, the value must be neutralized first — parameterized, escaped for the exact sink context, or validated against an allow-list or strict type — rather than concatenated or interpolated raw. Reason as an experienced security reviewer. A source is any externally-controlled value: a request param, header or body, an uploaded filename, a CLI arg, a remote service's response. A dangerous sink is any place where raw text changes execution: a built query string, a shell command, an HTML or template render, a filesystem path, a redirect target, a deserializer or eval, or a constructed URL whose path or query interpolates the value — `"/auth/\(token)"` then `URL(string: base + path)`, where the fix is percent-encoding via the platform URL builder, not raw interpolation. These lists are illustrative; recognize the shape in any language or stack, including sinks not named here. Neutralized looks like: bound as a parameter, run through a context-correct encoder, passed as an args array to exec, confined under a canonicalized base path, rendered through auto-escaping left on. Not neutralized looks like: string-concatenated or interpolated straight into the sink with nothing in the quoted hunk neutralizing it. For the constructed URL, the most common sink in an app, the rules are these: a remote or typed String interpolated into a path or query segment is a flow, and it is neutralized only by an encoder correct for the segment — `.urlQueryAllowed` is not a safe encoder for an individual query value or path segment: reserved delimiters can remain and change structure. Use a component builder or an encoder appropriate to the exact component; a value whose type renders as digits (an integer, a coordinate) cannot change the URL's meaning and is no flow; a whole remote URL string handed to the platform parser (`URL(string: remoteUrl)`) and then to a loader is parsed, not interpolated, and is no sink here; an author constant is no source.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop only when no untrusted value reaches a dangerous sink in the added lines at all. A dangerous sink is a query, command, path, URL or markup built from the value as text. A source-to-sink flow remains applicable when a typed or parameterized API neutralizes it — a prepared statement, a component-built URL or an auto-escaped render can establish MET. A value only displayed by a text control that does not interpret markup reaches no dangerous sink and is DOES_NOT_APPLY. Scan the added lines for a source-to-sink flow before abstaining; do not skip the scan because the diff looks routine. When the diff contains a sink-shaped line — raw input concatenated into a query, command, path or markup — and you still abstain, name the single most suspicious line by file:line and state why it is safe.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified `[L<n>]` lines and their immediate in-diff context. It establishes the closed set of source-to-sink flows this change introduces and whether each is neutralized in those same lines. It never establishes that code outside the diff sanitizes — or fails to sanitize — the value; never assume either.
2. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`) and the checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): which paths are generated or vendored. They establish the hand-written remainder you assess. They never establish neutralization for a flow the added lines do not show.
Trace only what you can see. If the diff was not captured completely, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: a quotable added hunk where a source reaches a sink unneutralized. Name the source and the sink end-to-end.
- MET: the added lines do carry untrusted input toward a sink, and you traced every introduced flow and each is neutralized before its sink. The injection that could have arrived with this change did not. This is a covered reading of the diff, never a security clearance.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for a flow you can see whose neutralization the added lines do not settle; name the flow and what would settle it. COULD_NOT_DETERMINE comes after the scan, never instead of it. No flow visible at all is DOES_NOT_APPLY, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, covering every unneutralized flow found; show the shape of the fix for the single most consequential one.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a security practice to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a render, redirect or header-style flow; the lightest nudge when the value is partly constrained but the context-correct escape is still missing. MAJOR: raw input that changes code or data execution — injection, traversal, RCE shapes. Identical hunks land at the same level.

## Grounding
For NOT_MET quote the exact added `[L<n>]` hunk where the source reaches the sink and name both ends; if you cannot point to both on quoted added lines, it is not assertable. For MET record `evidence.search` over the diff and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish: that the escaping is correct for every input, that sinks reached from unchanged code are safe, that the application has no other exposure. Never claim the code runs, compiles, is exploitable, or that a payload starts; assert only the visible practice. Never invent a file, a line or a clean bill. Describe the observable behaviour — raw input flowing into a sink — never intent or character.

## Defer
A generic missing bounds, null or format check with no dangerous sink belongs to `validates-inputs-and-edge-cases-at-the-boundary`; a committed secret belongs to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`. Defer to the sibling rather than double-flag. Here only: a taint-to-sink injection flow.

guidance.whyItMatters: Gluing raw user input straight into a query, a shell command, or a page is how injection bugs are born, the kind that leak a database or run an attacker's code. Parameterizing or escaping it first is what blocks that access path.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: User-supplied values reach the database through bound parameters and the page through proper escaping, never concatenated into a SQL string or dropped into HTML as-is.
guidance.goingWell: Untrusted input is bound or escaped before a sink

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Treat each value from outside your code as untrusted. This means request data, uploaded file names, command-line arguments, and replies from other services.
- Put a value into a database query only as a bound parameter. For example, instead of `"… WHERE name = '" + name + "'"`, write `WHERE name = ?` and bind `name`.
- In a page, keep the template’s auto-escaping on. If you build markup yourself, encode the value for its exact place: text, an attribute, or a script.
- In a command, a file path, or a URL, keep the value in its own slot. Examples are one list item per argument, one part of a built URL, and a path under a base folder.
- Some values cannot be bound, such as a column name. Check each of them against a list of allowed values.

## When it does not apply

- In the lines you added, no outside value reaches a query, a command, a file path, a URL, or markup.
- The value is only shown in a text control that does not read markup.

It still applies when you use a safe API, such as a prepared statement, a URL builder, or an auto-escaped template. The safe API is how you meet the practice.

## Common mistakes

- Encoding a whole URL with one general encoder. Characters such as `&`, `=` and `/` can stay, and change the URL’s structure. Instead, encode each path segment and query value on its own.
- Escaping for the wrong place. HTML escaping does not protect a value inside a script or an event handler. Instead, use the encoder for the place where the value lands.
- Turning off auto-escaping for one value, such as with React’s `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Instead, keep escaping on, or first clean the HTML with a trusted sanitizer, a library that removes dangerous tags.
- Writing your own escaping for a query. It breaks easily. Instead, bind the value, and check the parts that cannot be bound against a list.

## Sources

- [SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP. Bound parameters keep code and data apart, and hand-made escaping is strongly discouraged.
- [Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP. Encoding must match the exact place in the page, and each URL query value needs its own encoding.
- [OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/OS_Command_Injection_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP. Prefer a library function to a shell command, and pass the program and each argument separately.
- [2025 CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses](https://cwe.mitre.org/top25/archive/2025/2025_cwe_top25.html), MITRE, 2025. Cross-site scripting and SQL injection rank first and second. Path traversal and OS command injection are also in the top 10.

definition.name: Avoid insecure defaults and over-broad permissions
definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: selected access and exposure settings stay appropriately constrained under the captured boundaries and safeguards.

## The standard
Code should start locked down and open only what it can justify. Hunt the selected lines for a change that ships an insecure default or widens an access or exposure boundary without an adequate, evidenced justification. Judge the SETTING the change adopts, not the data flowing through it, and never as a blanket vulnerability scan. A sink-hunt, not a posture rating: do not read the top-level intent, conclude "looks secure" and stop. Walk these sink classes over the selected lines; they are classes to think in, not a closed value list, so recognise the same shape on any stack:
1. transport, certificate or host verification toggled off;
2. cross-origin, CORS or permission scope widened — a credentialed response that reflects the request Origin back without an allowlist, or a bare wildcard on an authenticated route;
3. a file, resource or object mode made world-readable or world-writable, or otherwise over-broad;
4. an existing auth or authz guard removed or loosened;
5. secret or credential exposure — trace dataflow here, do not pattern-match names: inspect EVERY logging, string-interpolation, persistence and URL-building call in the selected lines and ask what the interpolated value can hold at runtime. A print or log of a value that can carry credential material is a leak even when the variable is not named "token": the body of an auth, login, token or credential exchange (a login response that carries the issued token, for example), an Authorization or session cookie header, or a private API credential. Credential material protects access or data through confidentiality. Establish its authority and audience from use and captured contract, not its name, literal form or URL position. Provider-published public identifiers, shared free/test keys and nonfunctional placeholders are not secret merely because committed or logged. Account-specific sandbox/test secrets and flows that can carry private runtime credentials remain in scope. An ordinary API response or error body, a status code or the name of a missing key carries none;
6. a debug, verbose-error or permissive default shipped to a non-test surface.
Spotting one tightened setting (an ATS flag removed, say) does not discharge the hunt; finish every class. A candidate sink class establishes what to inspect, not an automatic defect. Clean: a setting correctly scoped, least-privilege or tightened; a widening whose quoted purpose and captured constraints establish an appropriate exception. A reason, or a test, sample or local filename, does not by itself make exposure safe: verify the actual boundary, the permitted audience and the applicable safeguards from the captured evidence. The absence of an insecure setting is a clean baseline, not a hardening act.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every applicable setting and exposure call in this file against the six sink classes. Establish the boundary and permitted audience. A file with no applicable setting or exposure call does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added lines with their `[L<n>]` markers, and any removed or weakened guard line. It establishes every candidate sink the change introduces — a closed corpus you can walk — and any in-diff comment or profile guard that justifies a widening. It never establishes that the existing configuration is sound, that unchanged settings are safe, or that the system has no other exposure.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when the boundary, audience or safeguard that would decide a candidate line sits outside the hunk (a dev profile, a network policy, the route's auth wrapper). It establishes the constraints an exception rests on. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
3. The leads from the practice script below these criteria, when present: to inspect, never evidence. An absent or empty lead list is never grounds for DOES_NOT_APPLY while a candidate line is visible.
Never infer a setting from a filename or a count you cannot quote.

## Judge
Walk every sink class first; then assess the standard.
- NOT_MET: a concrete added setting whose exposure is inappropriate under the evidenced constraints. Quote the added `[L<n>]` line, or the removed or weakened guard line, and name the file.
- MET: the selected lines touch at least one setting of a sink class, you walked every class over them, and none was touched insecurely. A COVERED search over a closed corpus, not an impression: an unwalked class makes it a false claim rather than an incomplete one. Record it with `evidence.search` over the selected pinned source, name the sink classes you walked in `lookedFor`, and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish. A report on a search, never a security clearance.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: a candidate sink line is visible but the fact that would settle it is not; name the line and what would settle it. Never file an unreadable sink under DOES_NOT_APPLY.
Before either abstention, state in the rationale what you found for the credential-exposure class (5). One result per practice per review; with several issues, name each distinct proved problem.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a security-hygiene practice to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a lower-blast-radius misconfiguration. MAJOR: a meaningfully widened blast radius — disabled verification, credentialed origin-reflection or wildcard exposure, a removed or loosened auth guard, or exposed credential material — when the captured boundaries establish consequential exposure. A merely asserted internal or dev rationale does not reduce that consequence; an evidenced appropriate exception is not a negative to grade at all. Do not sum severities.

## Grounding
Every result quotes the exact added `[L<n>]` line, or the removed or weakened guard line, and names the file. A claim that a setting was added, removed, hardened or mitigated must quote the changed line that does it. An appropriate exception must quote both the justification and the constraints that support it, and it does not remove an otherwise present review applicability. Never claim to run, compile or test; never invent a file, a line or a clean bill of health. Point forward to the safer default: verification on; the exact origin named instead of `*`; the toggle behind a dev profile; the least-privilege mode; the guard restored or its reason recorded. Talk about the configuration, never the contributor.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Whether untrusted input is escaped or validated belongs to `validates-and-escapes-untrusted-input`. A missing or placeholder usage description in `Info.plist` belongs to `declares-permissions-truthfully-at-point-of-use`, not to this practice. An access scope wider than the feature needs remains in scope here. Credential exposure stays here, graded by Severity above. If captured evidence cannot settle confidentiality or authority, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE and name the deciding missing fact.

guidance.whyItMatters: A default or permission that ships wider than it needs sits quietly until someone exploits it, and this kind of misconfiguration is among the most common security gaps there is. Starting locked down means you only open what you can justify.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A new endpoint or credential grants exactly the access it needs and no more, with scoped permissions and a specific allowed origin from an allowlist, not an origin reflected back from the request or a blanket wildcard, instead of a permissive default dropped in to make things work.
guidance.goingWell: New access grants exactly what it needs and no more

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Start each new setting closed, with no access, and add access for one named need at a time.
- Name the exact websites that may read your endpoint’s responses in a browser. For example, instead of copying the request’s `Origin` header into the response, check it against a fixed list first.
- Turn on each debug setting only in local development. Examples are detailed error pages and a skipped certificate check.
- Before you log, print or save a value, check what it can hold at runtime. Leave out or mask any token, password, key, cookie or `Authorization` header.
- If you must widen access or loosen an access check, say why in a code comment next to the setting. Keep the real limit in the code too, such as an access check or a development-only setting.

## When it does not apply

- Your change only changes the user interface, layout, docs, data models or tests. It adds no transport, origin, permission, file mode, access check, credential, logging or debug setting.
- Your change is mostly generated or vendored files. None of the lines you wrote by hand touches such a setting.

It still applies when you add a log, print or save call that includes any runtime value, because that value can hold a credential.

## Common mistakes

- Trusting a reason to make a wide setting safe. A comment such as “internal only”, or a test or sample file name, does not limit who can reach it. Instead, check the real boundary and who is allowed through it.
- Fixing one setting and stopping. Instead, check every setting that your change adds.
- Trusting the variable name. A log of a login response or a request header can leak a token, even when nothing is named “token”. Instead, follow what the value can hold.
- Using a wildcard origin, or a file that anyone on the machine can change, to get past an error. Instead, name the origin, user or group that needs access, and grant only that.

## Sources

- [The protection of information in computer systems](https://web.mit.edu/Saltzer/www/publications/protection/Basic.html), Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975. Base access on permission, so the default is no access. Give each program only the privileges it needs.
- [A02:2025 Security Misconfiguration](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A02_2025-Security_Misconfiguration/), OWASP Top 10, 2025. Every application tested had some misconfiguration, such as unneeded features or error messages that say too much.
- [Testing cross origin resource sharing](https://wstg.owasp.org/v4.2/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/11-Client-side_Testing/07-Testing_Cross_Origin_Resource_Sharing/), OWASP Web Security Testing Guide. A `*` origin, or an origin sent back unchecked, is insecure unless the API is public.
- [Logging cheat sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Remove or mask access tokens, session IDs, passwords and keys before they reach a log.

definition.name: Change dependencies deliberately
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: an external dependency edit, as the applicability defines it, whose manifest and lockfile stay coherent under the ecosystem's resolution rules, with a recorded reason for a notable new declaration or version bump.

## The standard
Judge whether this pull request makes the external dependency edit defined by the applicability deliberately. Two things hold together: the manifest and any lockfile remain consistent with the ecosystem's resolution rules and the repository's documented policy, and a notable new external declaration or version bump carries a one-line reason a reviewer can read — in the manifest context, the title or body, or a commit subject. The reason states the package's purpose in this change or why its version changes. A package name or an edit label is not a reason, even when the name describes the package's function. This is a supply-chain workflow practice about how a dependency edit is justified and kept coherent. It is never a claim about the dependency's own correctness, its CVEs, or whether the chosen version is the "right" one. The principle — coherence plus a traceable reason for notable changes — decides, not a fixed file list: reason as an experienced reviewer about manifests, lockfiles and ecosystems not named here. A patch or minor bump and a transitive-only delta need no prose. A large generated lockfile delta is normal evidence of coherence, not a problem. A supported version range is not itself a defect: libraries may deliberately declare compatible ranges, and a manifest edit need not change an already compatible locked resolution.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the change edits no external dependency: no added, removed or changed declaration, version constraint, source, resolution or pin of a third-party package, library, framework, plugin, container image or workflow action, in a manifest or lockfile of any ecosystem. The changed lines decide, not the file's name. Internal wiring alone — an internal target or module, a test target that depends on the app, a scheme or test-plan entry, build settings, sources or resources — declares no external dependency and is DOES_NOT_APPLY, even inside a dependency manifest. A resolution change on its own, such as a lockfile refresh, is applicable. A deciding hunk that failed acquisition is a collection gap, not DOES_NOT_APPLY.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) and the file spread (`work/change/files.json`): the manifest hunks and the matching or missing lockfile spans. They establish what changed on the dependency surface and whether manifest and lockfile move together. They never establish the dependency's quality or the correctness of the chosen version.
2. The title (`context/metadata.json`) and the whole description (`context/description.md`): where an explaining sentence for a notable new declaration or bump may live. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
3. The commit subjects and bodies (`context/commits.json`): a subject can carry the reason. Per-commit patches are not in your context; judge from subjects, the file spread and the quoted hunks.
4. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the repository's documented policy — a stated reproducibility requirement, a lockfile rule, a pinning convention. It establishes the policy a constraint removal is measured against. It never establishes a defect on its own.
Before calling a notable change unexplained you must have read the diff, the title, the body and the commit subjects. If one of those surfaces was not materialized for you, your search is incomplete: report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the dependency edit is coherent and, where a notable new declaration or bump needs one, explained. A new direct external declaration arrives with a sentence on what it is for and any required resolution update is present; a routine transitive resolution refresh is internally consistent.
- NOT_MET: the captured manifest and lockfile contradict one another under the ecosystem's resolution rules, with the deciding entries quoted; or a resolution constraint is removed in conflict with an evidenced repository reproducibility requirement. Establish the ecosystem's semantics and the captured policy before reporting inconsistency.
- NOT_MET: a notable new declaration or version bump is coherent but lands as an unexplained pin — no quotable why in the manifest context, the title, the body or the commit subjects. Name the pin and the surfaces you read.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE when the deciding policy or resolution context remains ambiguous after reading the sources; name the question. An unchanged or absent lockfile alone proves neither coherence nor a defect. A required source that was not captured is a collection gap, not a result.
One result per practice per review. Identical hunks yield identical assessments.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on dependency deliberateness alone — a non-blocking practice to grow, not a merge gate. Scale to how much reproducibility is actually at risk. MINOR, the usual band: an unexplained but coherent notable pin — a formative nudge. MAJOR: manifest and lockfile out of step on something that ships — the most serious case here.

## Grounding
Quote the manifest line, the matching or missing lockfile span, and the explaining sentence or commit subject verbatim. For NOT_MET the citations show the pin and the boundary searched: the diff, the title, the body, the commit subjects. Never invent a file, a reason, a CVE, or a clean bill you did not verify. Never claim a build resolved or ran. Describe the observable edit; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Generated-file hygiene belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`; review size belongs to `scope-one-reviewable-change`. Rationale for a separate architectural decision belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. Here only: is the dependency edit coherent, and is a notable change explained?

guidance.whyItMatters: Every dependency you add is code you now trust and have to keep patched, and many malicious packages slip in disguised as a real name a letter or two off. A one-line note on why a package is there, plus a lockfile that moves with the manifest, lets a reviewer sanity-check the addition and keeps the build reproducible.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A new package arrives with a sentence on what it is for. The manifest and resolution stay consistent with the ecosystem and the repository policy, updating a lockfile when needed rather than requiring one for every edit.
guidance.goingWell: Dependency changes stay coherent and notable choices have a reason

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you add a package, check whether you need it.
- Before you add a package, check that its name is exactly the one you meant.
- When you add a direct dependency or make a notable version change, write one sentence on why. Say what the package does in this change, or why its version changes. For example, instead of “Add yaml-lite”, write “Add yaml-lite to keep comments in plugin config files”.
- Put that sentence where a reviewer reads it. Use the description, a commit subject, or a comment in the manifest, the file that lists packages.
- Keep the manifest and any lockfile (the file of chosen versions) consistent with your package manager and repository policy. A compatible lockfile can stay unchanged.

## When it does not apply

- Your change does not add, remove or change a third-party dependency, its version, its source or its fixed version. Dependencies include packages, libraries, frameworks, plugins, container images and workflow actions.
- Your change only wires up your own code. Examples are an internal module, a test target, build settings, sources or resources. This is true even when the edit is inside a dependency manifest.

It still applies when your change only refreshes a lockfile.

## Common mistakes

- Writing a reason for every version change. A patch or minor version change needs no sentence, and neither does a change to the dependencies of your dependencies. A large lockfile diff from your tool is normal. Instead, explain each new direct dependency and each notable version change.
- Giving the package name as the reason. “Add yaml-lite” or “Update yaml-lite to 2.0” only says what changed. This is true even when the name hints at what the package does. Instead, say what the package does in this change, or why its version changes.
- Removing a fixed version or a lockfile entry to get past a conflict when your repository asks for reproducible builds. Instead, let your package manager resolve the conflict, and keep the lockfile consistent with the manifest.

## Sources

- [Concise guide for evaluating open source software](https://best.openssf.org/Concise-Guide-for-Evaluating-Open-Source-Software), OpenSSF Best Practices Working Group, 2025. OpenSSF recommends checking whether you need a dependency and whether its name is authentic.
- [Dependency management](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch21.html), Titus Winters, in Software Engineering at Google, 2020. A new dependency is not free, so weigh its costs before you import it.
- [package-lock.json](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/package-lock-json), npm Docs. npm records exact dependency versions in a lockfile intended for version control.
- [Why have Cargo.lock in version control?](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/faq.html#why-have-cargolock-in-version-control), The Cargo Book. A lockfile gives the same dependency versions at different times and on different systems.

definition.name: Record significant decisions and the rationale
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a written rationale for the architecturally significant decision this change makes, recorded where a future maintainer can find it.

## The standard
Work in two stages, in order. First establish an architecturally significant decision from the hand-written diff. Only then judge whether its need, constraint or trade-off is recorded rather than left to be reverse-engineered from the code. A recorded WHY may be one clause, but it must say something the code does not already show: the need the decision serves ("so a customer can save a draft and return to it", "a stored type because attachments must survive a restart") or the constraint that forced it ("the provider only accepts signed requests") records it; the lapse is silence about the decision, not brevity, and a clause quoted for the description's WHY may be the same clause. A user benefit can record the need without a "because" formula: "edits survive restart; returning users skip setup" records why a profile is persisted. A sentence that only restates what the model or the mechanism itself does ("added the AuditLog interceptor; every request is now logged", "the profile is now saved to disk") says WHAT the diff shows and is not a rationale, and a commit subject that names the addition is a label, not a why. Never demand the alternatives considered or the reason this approach over another: the need served is the rationale a maintainer needs. A feature goal counts for a separate schema, security or public-contract decision only when it explains the need for that decision. Significance is a closed list, so two readers find the same subject: a change to a PERSISTED model or schema (a stored type, a migration, a field that is saved); a public-contract or wire-API change (an endpoint, a message format, an exported library API); a new cross-cutting mechanism the rest of the app plugs into (a shared aspect, interceptor or event bus, a base class many types extend); an auth or security mechanism; the removal of a feature with persisted state. Not on the list, and never significant on their own: a dependency addition or version change, which `changes-dependencies-deliberately` judges; a call to an external web service (an HTTP API consumed at runtime is a mechanism used, not a dependency added to a manifest); a view or view model and how screens navigate; an in-memory draft, cache or value type; using the stack the project already uses (its persistence framework, UI framework or map kit) without one of the listed changes — a new persisted field built with that stack is still a persisted-model change; a helper, extension or calculation; a rename. When the only candidate is one of these, stage 1 fails and the cell is DOES_NOT_APPLY. For a significant decision, look for its rationale in the title, the description, a commit subject or body, or an ADR or design document the change links, adds or edits. A reason given in a review comment or the conversation is not recorded where a maintainer finds it and does not count; the discussion is where a rationale was asked for, not where it lives. A rationale clause counts in prose or inside a bullet or checklist item — "chose X because Y", "an event queue so a slow consumer can't block checkout", "to avoid Z" — so scan the whole body. Restating WHAT changed, an empty or template body, or a bare "added mechanism X" does not record a why.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the change is routine and carries no architectural decision: tests, formatting, docs, a rename without a contract change, a version bump of an already-present dependency, a tuned constant or threshold on an internal symbol, or an empty diff. Significance comes from hand-written hunks only: a hand-authored migration changeset is a decision, while a dependency edit alone is not. When the diff is unreadable, the change still made whatever decisions it made and you could not read them: report a collection gap and record no result, never a routine or a significant verdict.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the changed lines, added or removed, that establish significance, and any ADR or design document the same change adds or edits. Code establishes what was decided, not why. An ADR or design document can record the rationale in the same change. Read its prose.
2. The title (`context/metadata.json`) and the WHOLE description (`context/description.md`): every paragraph, bullet and checklist item. They establish a recorded rationale you can quote. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
3. The commit subjects and bodies (`context/commits.json`): a rationale stated there counts. Per-commit patches are not in your context; never claim a per-commit file mapping.
4. A linked ADR or design document materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`: read it before concluding the why is absent. Cite its file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased rationale sentence; a bare URL is not evidence the why was recorded. When the change names a specific document that was not materialised, the rationale may be there: report a collection gap and record no result, never a claim against prose you were not shown.
5. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): what a changed symbol or mechanism means, and an in-repository ADR the change links, adds or edits. It never supplies a rationale the change did not write.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: a significant decision is present and its rationale is written down in one of the sources above, so the intent survives without re-reading the code.
- NOT_MET: a significant decision ships with no recorded why anywhere in the description, the commit subjects or bodies, or an ADR or design document the change links, adds or edits. Name the decision.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: no ordinary case. Having searched every source and found no why is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE; a document you were not shown is a collection gap.
One result per practice per review. When several significant decisions co-occur, judge them together in one result.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on rationale alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a single contained unexplained significant decision — one isolated persisted schema field. MAJOR: the genuinely consequential — an unexplained auth or security mechanism, a persistence, public-API or wire-contract change, a real cross-cutting mechanism others build on, or several significant decisions co-occurring unexplained. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding
Quote the exact changed `[L<n>]` line(s), added or removed, that establish significance in every cell. For MET, also quote the verbatim rationale sentence, commit subject or document reference and where it lives. For NOT_MET, the citations show the search: the description, the commit subjects, and the referenced rationale sources or their absence. Never invent a rationale, never infer the why from the code itself, and never assert that the schema or endpoint is wrong — judge only whether the why is recorded. Never claim a build or test ran. Describe the observable record; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
The overall adequacy of the description — a clear title and a why for the change as a whole — belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; here judge only whether THAT significant decision's rationale is recorded, so the two never double-flag. Whether a public-surface change is documented for its consumers belongs to `documents-public-api-and-behaviour-changes`; whether a linked wiki document now contradicts the code belongs to `change-keeps-linked-docs-consistent`. Dependency edits belong only to `changes-dependencies-deliberately`. A separate architectural decision in the same change remains in scope here.

guidance.whyItMatters: When you pick one design over another, the rationale is the first thing to fade. A maintainer who cannot find why you chose it will either undo a good decision or be too afraid to touch it, and both cost the team later.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A meaningful design choice arrives with its rationale written down, in the description or a short architecture decision record (ADR), such as 'chose an event queue over direct calls so a slow consumer cannot block checkout', not just the code that does it.
guidance.goingWell: Significant decisions land with their reasoning

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, check whether the change makes a significant decision. Only these kinds count. A change to stored data or a schema counts. So do a change to a public API or a message format, and an auth or security mechanism. A new mechanism that other code plugs into counts too, and so does removing a feature with stored data.
- If it does, say why in the title, the description, or a commit message. A decision record that the change adds or links works too.
- Name the need the decision serves or the constraint that forced it. One clause is enough. For example, instead of “Added an attachments table”, write “Store attachments in a table, because they must survive a restart”.
- If the change makes more than one significant decision, give a reason for each one.

## When it does not apply

- The change makes no architectural decision. A new screen, a cache, or a helper is not one by itself.
- The change only touches tests, formatting, or docs.
- The change renames something without changing a contract, such as stored data, a public API or a message format.
- The change only adds a dependency or changes its version.
- The change tunes a constant or a threshold inside the code.
- The change only touches generated code. Only lines that a person wrote count.
- The change is empty.

It still applies when you write a migration by hand.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking you need a long document that lists every option you turned down. You do not. Instead, write one clause that names the need or the constraint.
- Repeating what the code does as the reason. “Added an audit log step that runs on every request, so every request is now logged” says what changed. Instead, say what need the logging serves.
- Giving only the goal of the feature. “Users can attach files” does not say why attachments are stored. Instead, connect the goal to the decision.
- Explaining the decision only in a reply to a review comment. A future maintainer will not look there. Instead, put the reason in the change itself.

## Sources

- [Documenting architecture decisions](https://www.cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions), Michael Nygard, 2011. A short record of the reasons, kept with the code, stops a team from accepting or changing a decision blindly.
- [Maintain an architecture decision record](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/well-architected/architect-role/architecture-decision-record), Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework. A decision recorded without its reason loses value, because readers cannot judge if it still holds.
- [A survey of architecture design rationale](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2006.04.029), Tang, Babar, Gorton and Han, 2006. In 81 responses, practitioners said that design rationale matters, but they reported barriers to writing it down.

definition.name: Document public API and behaviour changes
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: consumer-facing documentation of the changed public surface — a downstream caller hears what moved from the change itself.

## The standard
Judge one practice: when the change alters a PUBLIC or SHARED surface — something a SEPARATE consumer depends on and compiles or integrates against — does the change carry, in the same diff or in the description, documentation that tells consumers what moved? Public surfaces: a library's or framework's exported symbols, a published package's API, a documented HTTP or RPC contract, a persisted or wire schema, an error or response shape callers branch on, a config default a consumer sets. Good: the renamed parameter, new endpoint, changed response field or breaking removal lands with its doc-comment, a changelog line, or a description sentence naming the consumer-facing effect. Bad: a real exported-surface change ships with nothing a consumer could read to adapt. A generated API specification or reference documents a contract when its authoritative source and meaning are captured: judge the contract and the information a consumer receives, not whether the text was handwritten. Irrelevant generated output is not documentation, and generated churn alone never establishes an authored contract decision.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Establish the separate consumer from the captured contract or usage, never from package type alone: an application can expose HTTP endpoints, configuration or wire formats to other consumers without publishing a library. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the changed symbols are internal types, private signatures, local refactors or app-only fields with no separate consumer, or when no public-surface change is observable in the diff and description at all. Decide whether a changed symbol is actually exported and consumer-facing as an experienced reviewer would, not by keyword; a plainly internal symbol is DOES_NOT_APPLY.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the surface change itself, and any documentation shipped beside it — a doc-comment on or above the surface, a changelog or docs addition, an updated reference. It establishes what changed and what documentation arrived with it. It never establishes a consumer by itself.
2. The description (`context/description.md`): a sentence naming the consumer-facing effect. It establishes documentation a consumer would read on the change; it never establishes a surface change the diff does not show.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the contract and its usage — who depends on the surface, and the existing reference docs the diff leaves untouched. It establishes whether a separate consumer exists and where the documentation would live. It never supplies the note the change failed to write.
4. A linked wiki document the change references, when it was materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`: its body may hold the documentation consumers need. Cite its file path together with the quoted or closely paraphrased sentence relied on; a bare URL is not evidence that the document says it. When the change points at a specific document that was not materialised for you, the documentation may live there: report a collection gap and record no result, never an undocumented surface.
An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the public-surface change carries documentation naming what moved — quote the surface change and the documenting text.
- NOT_MET: documentation exists for the change yet never names the specific changed parameter, field, route or default a consumer must adapt to. Quote both.
- NOT_MET: a real public-surface change and, after looking in every place a consumer would — the doc-comment on or above the surface, a changelog or docs addition, the description, and a materialised wiki document — nothing a consumer could read to adapt.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE only when the evidence genuinely cannot settle whether the one symbol this practice turns on crosses a module or service boundary; name the question. Do not resolve that doubt into a result or into a claim that no public surface was here. Having looked everywhere and found no documentation for an established public surface is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review. When several surfaces change, grade by the least-documented one.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on documentation alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a new additive surface with no documentation, since nothing breaks but consumers cannot discover it; lighter still, documentation that exists yet never names the specific changed parameter or field. MAJOR: a breaking change — a removed or renamed symbol, route or field, a narrowed type, a changed default — shipping with no documentation anywhere, so callers break without a migration note. Equivalent situations land at equivalent severity.

## Grounding
Cite the diff lines of the observable surface change in every cell. For MET, quote the documenting text and its file. For NOT_MET, quote the documentation and the changed element it omits. For NOT_MET, cite the surface change and name the boundary searched: the surface's doc-comment, the changelog and docs in the diff, the description, and any materialised wiki document. Never invent a symbol, an export marker, a changelog or a clean bill you did not see. Never assert the compile or runtime correctness of the surface, and never impute intent or care; describe the documentation practice on the captured work only.

## Defer
The pull request's general what-and-why narrative belongs to `describe-what-and-why`; whether a design decision's rationale is recorded belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. A thin description or an unjustified choice is not a result here. Here only: is the public-surface change documented for its consumers?

guidance.whyItMatters: People outside your code depend on what you export. Change a public function or endpoint without a note and they find out at runtime, in their own project, with no warning, and they trust your library a little less each time.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A renamed parameter or a changed response shape lands with its reference docs and a changelog line updated in the same change, so the people building on your API hear about it from you, not from a broken build.
guidance.goingWell: API and behaviour changes ship with their docs

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, list what your change alters that other software depends on. Look for exported functions, published packages and documented endpoints. Include the format of stored or sent data, the errors and responses that callers handle, and default settings.
- For each item, write a note in the same pull request or merge request. Update the doc comment, add a changelog line, update the reference docs, or say it in the description.
- Name the exact parameter, field, route or default that moved. For example, instead of “Updated the users endpoint”, write “The users endpoint returns `fullName` in place of `name`”.
- If you remove or rename something, or change a default, tell consumers how to adapt. Say what to use instead, so their code keeps working after they update.

## When it does not apply

- The changed code is internal and has no separate consumer. Examples are internal types, private signatures, local refactors and fields that only your app uses.
- The diff and the description show no change to a public surface at all.

It still applies when your project is an app and not a library, and other software uses its endpoints, config or data formats.

## Common mistakes

- Deciding by the kind of project or by a keyword such as `public` or `export`. Instead, ask whether a separate consumer depends on the code you changed. That can be another team’s service or a project that installs your package.
- Writing a note that never names what changed, such as “API improvements”. Instead, name the parameter, field, route or default that a consumer must adapt to.
- Leaving the note for a later change. Instead, ship it with the change, so consumers hear about it when the change lands.

## Sources

- [What to look for in a code review](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html), Google Engineering Practices. A change to how people use code needs matching docs, including generated references.
- [Semantic Versioning 2.0.0](https://semver.org/), Tom Preston-Werner. Software that follows it declares a public API and updates its docs when it deprecates part of that API.
- [Keep a Changelog 1.1.0](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), Olivier Lacan. A changelog lists notable changes for people, with changed, deprecated and removed features in their own groups.
- [How to break an API: cost negotiation and community values in three software ecosystems](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~ckaestne/pdf/fse16.pdf), Bogart and others, FSE 2016. In interviews with 28 developers, maintainers eased the cost of breaking changes by telling users and documenting how to upgrade.

definition.name: Keep linked wiki docs consistent with the change
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the captured linked document and changed behavior agree on the same contract, setting or operational step.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this pull request changes a documented behaviour — a config default, a public API or wire contract, a CLI flag, an error or return code, an operational step — AND a linked wiki document describes that same behaviour, does the document still agree with the code, or has the diff left it contradicting reality? Work in two stages, in order. (1) From the hand-written diff, identify a concrete behaviour, contract or config the change alters. (2) Only if a materialised document describes that same thing, check whether the document now asserts something the code contradicts: an old default, a removed flag, a renamed field, a changed status code, a superseded step. The deciding evidence is a genuine contradiction between a specific document passage and a specific diff hunk — never staleness in the abstract, and never "the code changed, so the document is probably old". The presence or absence of a wiki link is never itself the result; a change with no relevant document is not a weakness.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when: the complete pull request description and all captured linked issues reference no wiki document, with no unreadable or uncaptured adopted linked issue that could carry the reference; the diff is empty; or the diff does not touch anything the materialised document describes. Before concluding that no wiki document is referenced, inspect the complete description and every adopted linked issue. If an adopted linked issue was not captured or cannot be read, report a collection gap and record no result unless the missing issue cannot affect the proposed result. A captured contradiction may support NOT_MET; MET or a no-relevant-document DOES_NOT_APPLY result requires every adopted reference that could change that result. No linked issue and no document reference in the complete description needs no Outline capture. A document is available to you only when the pull request references it and its body was materialised as a `.md` file under `context/docs/`. When the pull request references a specific document that a reader would expect to describe the behaviour this diff changes, and that document was not materialised, you cannot tell whether it now contradicts the code: report a collection gap and record no result. An unreadable diff is the same collection gap.

## Sources
1. The description (`context/description.md`) and each linked issue (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`): which wiki documents the change references, and any sentence saying the document was updated. They establish that a document is in scope; they never establish what the document says. A bare URL is not evidence of a document's content. An image: its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing.
2. The materialised documents (`context/docs/<collection>/<document>.md`): the passages that describe the behaviour. They establish what the wiki asserts today. Read the file before concluding anything about it.
3. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`, with `work/change/files.json`): the hand-written hunks that alter a behaviour, contract or config, and any documentation the same change updates. It establishes what the code now does; it never establishes what the wiki says.
4. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): context for what a changed symbol, flag or step means. It never supplies a document passage.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: the diff changes a documented behaviour and the materialised document still asserts the old behaviour, so a reader who trusts the wiki is misled. Quote both sides.
- MET: the diff changes something the document describes AND the same pull request updates that document, or the document already reflects the new behaviour, so code and document do not contradict.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: no ordinary case. A referenced document you were not shown is a collection gap, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE. Having read the materialised document and found no passage the diff makes false is MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, over the whole change.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR — the aim is a trustworthy wiki, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a contradiction on a minor or internal-facing detail, a nudge to update the document. MAJOR: a contradiction a consumer would act on wrongly — a wrong documented default or limit, a removed API or flag the document still offers, a changed auth, security or data-handling step. When unsure, prefer the lower severity.

## Grounding
Ground every NOT_MET in both sides: the exact added or removed `[L<n>]` diff line that changes the behaviour, and the verbatim sentence from the materialised `.md` document that still asserts the old behaviour, cited with its `context/docs/...` file path. If you cannot point to a specific document passage the diff makes false, do not raise the result: never infer a contradiction you cannot cite, and never fabricate a document quote. For MET, cite the diff line of the changed behaviour and the document line (in the diff or in the materialised file) that now agrees with it. Never claim a build or test ran, and never impute intent or care; describe what the document says and what the code does.

## Defer
Whether a change was documented at all, in any surface, belongs to `documents-public-api-and-behaviour-changes`. Whether the WHY of a decision is recorded belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. Here only: does a specific linked wiki document now contradict the code?

guidance.whyItMatters: A wiki that contradicts the code is worse than no wiki: teammates act on documented behaviour that no longer holds, and the drift compounds silently until someone is burned by it.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: When a change alters something the team's design or reference doc describes, the same PR brings the doc along, so the wiki keeps telling the truth about the system.
guidance.goingWell: The wiki moves with the change it describes
