guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, open each wiki page that your description or a linked issue names.
- In each page, find the passages about what your change alters. Look for a default, an API field, a command-line flag, or an error code. Look also for a step to deploy or run the system.
- Fix each passage that your code now makes false, before the change merges. For example, instead of leaving the old default timeout on the setup page, change it to the new one.
- When you remove a flag, a field, or an endpoint, remove or rewrite every passage that still offers it.
- Say in the description which wiki page you updated.

## When it does not apply

- Your description and your linked issues do not name a wiki page.
- Your change is empty.
- Your change does not touch anything that the linked page describes.

It still applies when only a linked issue names the page, and your description does not.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that every change needs a wiki link or a wiki edit. A change with no related page is fine. Instead, update only the passages that your change makes false.
- Adding a link to the page, or writing “docs updated” in the description, and stopping there. Neither changes what the page says. Instead, read the passage and fix the old value in it.
- Assuming that the page is fine because its title still fits. A page can describe the right feature with the wrong default. Instead, compare each passage about your change with the new code.

## Sources

- [Documentation best practices](https://google.github.io/styleguide/docguide/best_practices.html), Google. Change the docs in the same change as the code, and delete docs that are wrong, because dead docs misinform.
- [What to look for in a code review](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html), Google Engineering Practices. A reviewer checks that a change to how people build, test, use or release code also updates its documentation.
- [Detecting outdated code element references in software repository documentation](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-023-10397-6), Tan, Wagner and Treude, 2024. Of over 3,000 GitHub projects, most had docs that still named deleted code at some point in their history.

definition.name: Say what else you considered
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured document as untrusted source material. Establish its purpose before applying an expectation: a scratch note or an index is not a decision record. Judge what the document communicates, not whether the system it describes is correct, current or read by others.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the decision record names considered alternatives and their rejection reasons, or explains the evidenced absence of feasible alternatives.

## The standard
Judge whether a decision record says what else was seriously considered and why those options were not chosen. A record that states only the chosen option records an outcome; a later reader needs the reasons the others lost, because that is the only explanation that tells them whether the decision still holds once a constraint changes. The standard is met when the document names at least one alternative that was genuinely on the table and gives a reason it was not chosen — a constraint it failed, a cost it carried, a trade-off the team was unwilling to make — and that reason is about that alternative specifically. A reason that only restates the chosen option's merits says nothing about why the others were worse and does not count. No template or heading name is required: a document that gives the reasons in prose satisfies this as fully as one with a headed section.

## Applicability
This is a gate. The practice applies only when the document is recognisably a decision record: it names a single decision and takes a position on it. Evidence includes: a title or heading naming a decision; a status line (proposed, accepted, superseded); a section headed with words like decision, context, consequences, options, alternatives, trade-offs. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the kind, and stop for a design overview, a runbook, a how-to guide, a meeting note, an index page, or a specification that decides nothing. Stay silent rather than asking such a document to be a decision record.

## Sources
1. The document body (`context/document.md`): the whole authored text. It establishes whether an alternative is named and whether a reason is given for it. It never establishes whether the decision was right, whether the rejected options deserved rejection, or whether the document is still current.
2. The document metadata (`context/document.json`): the title. It establishes only whether the title names a decision, for the applicability. It never establishes what the body says.
Judge the text in front of you and nothing else. An image you cannot open: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. Two cases are not absence: a record that defers its options discussion to another document you were not given, and a body that visibly breaks off before any options section. If either reflects incomplete capture, report a collection gap and record no result. If the complete authored document itself ends without discussing alternatives, judge that omission; do not mistake unfinished writing for missing capture.

## Judge
Read the whole body before deciding. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: at least one alternative is named and a reason specific to it is given, or the record explains the constraint that left no genuine alternative. Quote the alternatives and their reasons, or the no-alternative constraint.
- NOT_MET: the document states a decision and its rationale but names no alternative at all; or it lists alternatives with no reason any of them lost (a bare bullet list of technology names); or the only reason given restates the chosen option's merits. A section headed "Alternatives considered" that is empty, or contains only "none", is absent unless the document explains why there was genuinely no other option.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: no ordinary case. A complete document either accounts for alternatives or does not; what Sources names as incomplete capture is a collection gap, not an open question, while a fully captured document that is itself unfinished is judged under the applicability and the standard. Having read the whole body and found no alternative with a reason is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, on the document as a whole.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; MINOR is the usual band: a bounded addition fixes it — one alternative and the sentence that ruled it out. Do not raise the band on this practice alone; the weight of the decision is not something the text lets you judge.

## Grounding
For MET, cite the exact lines naming the alternative and its reason, or establishing why no genuine alternative existed. For NOT_MET, cite the decision statement and the boundary you searched: the whole body, including any options or alternatives section quoted or stated to be empty. Never claim the decision was correct or incorrect, never claim a rejected alternative deserved its fate, and never claim the document is or is not up to date. Describe what the record says; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Whether a pull request records the decisions it makes belongs to `records-significant-decisions-with-rationale`. Whether the decision was right, whether the alternatives deserved rejection, and whether the document is current are not judged by any practice here. Here only: does the record name what else was considered and why it lost?

guidance.whyItMatters: A decision record that names only the winner tells the next person what was done, not what it cost. When a constraint later changes — a library is deprecated, the traffic grows, the team shrinks — the first question is always "what else did we look at, and does that reason still hold?". If the alternatives were never written down, that question can only be answered by redoing the whole investigation, and usually it is not answered at all: the decision quietly becomes something nobody feels able to revisit.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A record that names the two or three options that were genuinely in play and gives each one a sentence saying what ruled it out — the constraint it failed, the cost it carried, the thing the team was not willing to trade. Written for someone who arrives a year later with a changed constraint, so they can tell in a minute whether the decision still stands.
guidance.goingWell: Decisions say what else was considered and why not

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Name each option that was really on the table, not only the one you chose.
- For each option you did not choose, explain why it lost. Say what limit it broke, what it would have cost, or what you would have had to give up. For example, instead of “We chose PostgreSQL”, write “We chose PostgreSQL. We ruled out SQLite because our imports need several writers at once.”
- Make the reason about that option. A sentence about what the chosen option does well does not say why the others were worse.
- If there was no real alternative, say so, and name the limit that left you with one option.
- Use the form that suits your team. A section with a heading, a table, and plain prose all work. No heading name is needed.

## When it does not apply

- The document does not name one decision and take a position on it.
- The document is a design overview, a runbook, a how-to guide, or a meeting note.
- The document is an index page, or a specification that decides nothing.

It still applies when the record is only a proposal, or when it follows no template.

## Common mistakes

- Treating the heading as the point. An “Alternatives considered” section that is empty, or that says only “none”, names nothing. Instead, name the options and why they lost. If there were none, explain why.
- Listing option names with no reasons. A list such as “Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS” shows what you looked at, not why each one lost. Instead, explain why each option lost.
- Praising the winner instead of judging the others. “PostgreSQL is fast and well known” is a reason to pick it. Instead, say what was wrong with each option you did not pick.

## Sources

- [Maintain an architecture decision record (ADR)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/well-architected/architect-role/architecture-decision-record), Microsoft Azure Well-Architected Framework. A decision record includes the alternatives you ruled out, and a record without justification loses value over time.
- [Architecture decision records overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/architecture-decision-records), Google Cloud Architecture Center. A decision record gives an overview of the key options and the reasons behind the accepted choice.
- [Markdown Architectural Decision Records (MADR)](https://adr.github.io/madr/), Oliver Kopp, Anita Armbruster and Olaf Zimmermann. The template lists the considered options and gives each one its arguments for and against.

definition.name: Keep each commit to one logical change
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: how the pull request's commits are partitioned — each commit one cohesive logical change, as its authored subject and body describe it and its own files show.

## The standard
Judge one thing: whether the commits are SPLIT so each one captures a single logical change, rather than one commit tangling separable work into a bundle a reviewer cannot follow, revert, or cherry-pick on its own. One logical change is one piece of work with everything it needs: a feature with its model, view, view model, test, asset, the manifest entry for the package it uses and the navigation that reaches it; a fix with its test; a diagram with the README line that embeds it; one document's sections revised for one reason. That is one concern however many clauses or files name it ("parse the header and validate it"). Two concerns are two pieces of work that each make sense alone: two features or user stories, two unrelated fixes, behavioural work beside a chore (a reformat or lint sweep, a rename or move sweep, a dependency bump, tooling or editor settings), or code beside an unrelated document or course deliverable. Several cohesive commits in one pull request is fine here, and a chore or a revert in its own commit is the partition working, not a tangle. Decide what is separable as an experienced reviewer would; there is no fixed word list. This is a workflow practice about how the history is partitioned, never a code-defect claim.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name which case, and stop when there was no split to judge: no authored non-merge commit remains: every entry is an automatic merge commit (two or more `parents`, or a "Merge ..." subject).

## Sources
1. The commits (`context/commits.json`): each subject, full body, `parents` and the `files` it touched against its first parent, with status and line counts. They establish the author's partition — what each commit says it holds and what it actually touched. A commit whose files carry a second piece of work its subject does not name — a whole source-tree rename or a new view under a README subject, a user-story rewrite under a diagram subject — is a tangle the subject hides; the supporting files of the work it does name never are. `git show <sha>` in the checkout gives its patch when the file list is not enough.
2. The per-file changed-line spread of the whole change (`work/change/files.json`, `work/change/diff.patch`): the overall breadth the commits together cover.
Read subjects, bodies and each commit's files together and judge conservatively. The leads from the practice script below these criteria list every authored commit as one row — its subject's shape (bare, a repeat, joined clauses, cut off), how many files it only moved, and the files it edited with their line counts — as places to look, never verdicts: joined clauses are punctuation, not a count of concerns. If `context/commits.json` is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no result; uncollected subjects are never authored silence and never COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every commit holds one logical change, as its subject, body and files show. Looks like a lapse but is not: "Add order history, and adjust the order fetch" where the adjustment returns what the new history reads; "Rewrite the README goal for the new scope, update its user stories" revising one README for one reason; "Update class diagram: add Invoice, drop method signatures" revising one diagram; a feature commit that also edits `project.yml` for its package; README commits later reverted, each on its own. Each is one concern.
- NOT_MET: at least one commit holds two concerns — its subject or body names both ("Extract the card views, replace deprecated colour calls everywhere": a refactor and an API sweep; "add formatter settings + start the settings screen"), or its files carry one its subject does not name. Quote the deciding subject with its short SHA, name the two pieces of work, and name the path that shows an unnamed one.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE when a bare or vague subject ("fixes", "ccc", "Improve MR") leaves a commit's content open and neither its files nor its patch settle whether it holds one piece of work or two; name the commit and the missing distinction. A broad commit under a vague subject is not a tangle by breadth alone; a narrow one whose files show a single piece of work is cohesive.
One result per practice per review, over the whole series, including a single authored commit that can be cohesive or bundled.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on commit atomicity alone — a formative practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a single commit bundles separable work, and splitting it would isolate each concern. MAJOR: the history broadly tangles, so a reviewer cannot reason about or revert one concern at a time.

## Grounding
Every claim cites the commit record that supports it: quote the deciding subject(s) verbatim, each with its short SHA, for NOT_MET, and name any path from that commit's `files` that shows the unnamed concern; cite the subjects whose partition you accepted for MET. Never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot observe. Cite the corresponding subject, SHA and file entries in the captured `context/commits.json` files. Never cite a diff line for this result, and never record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE because the subjects have no line of their own to cite. Describe the observable split; never impute intent or character, and never frame a tangle as a defect in the code.

## Defer
Overall pull request size, and a pull request carrying several features in separate commits, belong to `scope-one-reviewable-change`; a large but cohesive partition can be a strength here. Subject wording belongs to `commit-subjects-explain-each-change`; a vague subject alone establishes neither cohesion nor a tangle. A generated or editor file swept into a commit (`.idea/`, `.DS_Store`, a regenerated `Info.plist`) belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`. Here only: does each commit hold one logical change?

guidance.whyItMatters: Mixing unrelated changes in a commit makes selective review, reverts and backports harder. Keeping changes separable makes the history more useful; clear commit subjects help a reader understand that intended separation.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Separate commits for separate ideas, such as 'Fix off-by-one in pagination' in one and 'Rename helper for clarity' in another, so each can be reviewed, reverted, or backported on its own.
guidance.goingWell: Each commit holds one logical change and no more

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Commit each piece of work when it’s done, before you start the next one. It’s easier to join small commits later than to split a big one.
- Keep everything one change needs in its commit. A fix goes with its test. A feature goes with its view, its model and its package entry.
- Give unrelated chores their own commits. For example, instead of one commit that fixes a paging bug and reformats the file, commit the fix first. Then commit the reformat.
- Before you ask for a review, read the subject, the body and the files of each commit. If a commit holds two pieces of work that each make sense alone, split it with `git rebase --interactive`.
- If one commit needs another, keep them in order. Each commit should still build and pass the tests.

## When it does not apply

- Every commit in the pull request or merge request is an automatic merge commit, such as “Merge branch …”. There is no split of your own to check.

It still applies when the pull request or merge request has only one commit that you wrote.

## Common mistakes

- Counting files or the word “and” in a subject. One change can touch many files and need two verbs, such as “Parse the header and validate it”. Instead, ask whether each part makes sense alone.
- Cutting one change into pieces that cannot stand alone, such as a fix and its test in two commits. Instead, keep the parts of one change together.
- Mixing an unrelated rename, lint fix or dependency update into a feature commit. Instead, put the unrelated work in its own commit. Keep the changes that the feature needs with the feature.
- Squashing separate ideas into one commit to keep the history short. Instead, keep each idea in its own commit. Several commits are fine, and so is a revert in its own commit.

## Sources

- [Separate your changes](https://docs.kernel.org/process/submitting-patches.html#separate-your-changes), Linux kernel documentation. Each logical change gets its own patch, even across many files, and each patch must keep the build working.
- [Separate changes](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitworkflows#_separate_changes), Git documentation. Split work into small logical steps, and edit the commits before you publish them.
- [Partitioning composite code changes](https://hunkim.cse.ust.hk/papers/tao-msr2015.pdf), Tao and Kim, 2015. In a study with 18 students, partitioned changes led to better review answers in a similar time.
- [The impact of tangled code changes](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-impact-of-tangled-code-changes/), Herzig and Zeller, 2013. Unrelated changes within bug fixes made associations between files and bug reports less accurate. One author worked at Microsoft, which sells version control tools.

definition.name: Track generated files only when justified
definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: tracked generated or build files are justified by captured repository policy or the source-to-output workflow.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does the change include generated or build files only where the repository's captured policy or its source-to-output workflow justifies tracking them? This is a repository-hygiene practice about what gets committed — never a code-defect claim about a file's contents, and generated output is not itself the defect. Judge from the file paths in the diff. Machine noise being reviewed as if it were source has a recognisable shape across any stack or language — a location or a banner that says "a tool wrote this": a build-output directory, an editor or OS cruft file, a coverage dump, a vendored or cached blob, a minified single-line bundle, or a tracked generated file someone hand-edited instead of regenerating. These are open examples, not a closed list. A repository may deliberately version-control some generated sources — a committed OpenAPI spec, a generated client, an ERD, a route tree. When such a tracked file moves in step with the hand-written change that drives its regeneration, that is intended, regeneration-consistent movement: do not flag it. An intentional regeneration may be appropriate without a simultaneous hand-written edit. Flag only output that is not meant to be tracked, or a tracked generated file left hand-edited or stale relative to its source.

## On a change
Judge the files this change adds or changes against the repository's captured tracking and regeneration policy. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge whether this tracked file belongs in the repository under its captured policy. A generated file can belong there. Present state alone cannot prove that somebody hand-edited generated output. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The file spread (`work/change/files.json`) and the per-file headers of the diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the paths. They establish which paths changed and where they sit — the primary evidence. A path never establishes compile, build or runtime behaviour.
2. The patch body (`work/change/diff.patch`): open it only to confirm a flagged path is machine-emitted when the path alone is ambiguous — a "DO NOT EDIT", "@generated" or "auto-generated" banner, a minified single line. The evidence is the path plus that confirming line, never a line-by-line review of the file's contents.
3. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the ignore rules, the documented generation workflow, and whether a file is tracked and which source drives it. It establishes whether tracking a generated file is intended. It never establishes manual editing or stale generation from an unchanged source file alone.
If the policy or source evidence a flag needs was not acquired, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: a quoted repository policy or an observable workflow establishes that a selected file should not be tracked, or a tracked generated file was hand-edited or left stale relative to the source that drives it. Quote each offending path.
- MET: a complete bounded search over every changed path establishes that the changed files are appropriately tracked — every path is something a person authored or intended: source, tests, docs, hand-written config, a lockfile moving in step with its manifest, or a tracked generated file whose regeneration is justified by the captured workflow, with or without a simultaneous source edit.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE when the one path this practice turns on is genuinely ambiguous — the path, any banner and the patch together cannot tell you whether it is machine-emitted, or whether tracking and regenerating that file is justified by the captured policy or workflow. Say so rather than let the doubt pass as a clean bill; name what would settle it. Having walked every path and found each justified is MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, covering every flagged path.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a practice to grow, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a lone stray file. MAJOR: a committed build-output directory, several leaked files, or a hand-edited generated file that should have been regenerated. Identical situations land identically.

## Grounding
Every NOT_MET names each offending path verbatim and, for a generated-file flag, quotes the confirming banner or names the tracked file and its driving source. If you cannot name an offending path there is nothing to flag; do not invent one. Cite a line of the flagged file from `work/change/diff.patch` (`scm.pull-request.diff`, the pinned `context/change.json`): `work/change/files.json` is derived here and is not citable; a flagged file the diff shows without numbered lines (binary, or renamed without edits) is cited through the `path` line of its entry in `context/commits.json`. For MET evidence.search records the boundary and the citations quote it: `changed_files` in `context/metadata.json` (`scm.pull-request.core`) and the paths you walked, listed in the rationale. Describe the observable fact ("this path is machine-emitted") and the next step (ignore it and drop it, or regenerate from source). Never assert compile, build or runtime behaviour from a path; never impute intent or character.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Whether a dependency change was deliberate or justified belongs to `changes-dependencies-deliberately`; a lockfile moving in step with its manifest is its concern. Do not infer that a lockfile was hand-edited merely because its manifest did not change — an intentional resolution refresh may update a lockfile alone. Here only: does the diff carry machine output that should not be tracked?

guidance.whyItMatters: A reviewer catches the most problems in the hand-written lines they can read closely, and a committed build output or editor config buries that source under machine noise nobody reviews. Leaving generated files out keeps the diff to the change a person can actually check, and spares everyone the odd conflict in a file no human wrote.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Build outputs, logs and editor files stay out of the repository. Deliberately tracked generated files follow the documented generation workflow; intentional regeneration can be appropriate even without a simultaneous source edit.
guidance.goingWell: Tracked files follow the repository generation policy

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, compare each changed path with the project’s ignore rules and documented generation steps. Tool output includes build folders, coverage reports, logs, minified bundles and editor files.
- For output that the project does not track, add its path to the project’s ignore file.
- Remove that output from Git tracking. For example, instead of leaving `dist/app.min.js` in the change, run `git rm --cached -- dist/app.min.js`.
- Put the files that your own editor and operating system make in your personal ignore file. Then they never reach any repository.
- For a generated file that the project tracks, follow its documented generation steps. Regeneration can be valid even when its source does not change.

## When it does not apply

- The change is empty.

It still applies when every file in the change is generated.

## Common mistakes

- Removing every generated file. Generated output is not wrong in itself. Some projects track it on purpose, such as a route tree or a diagram. Instead, check the project’s ignore rules and docs before you remove one.
- Fixing a generated file by hand. The next run of the generator undoes your fix. Instead, change the source and regenerate. A banner such as `DO NOT EDIT` or `@generated` at the top tells you that a tool wrote the file.
- Changing the source of a tracked generated file without regenerating it. The file then no longer matches its source. Instead, regenerate it in the same change.
- Adding a path to the ignore file and expecting the tracked copy to go away. An ignore rule does not affect a file that is already tracked. Instead, also remove the file from tracking with `git rm --cached`.

## Sources

- [gitignore](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore), Git documentation. Ignore rules name intentionally untracked files, such as temporary editor files, and do not affect files that Git already tracks.
- [What to look for in a code review](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html), Google Engineering Practices. Reviewers can scan over generated code, but they read every line that a person wrote.
- [Generate Go files by processing source](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Generate_Go_files_by_processing_source), Go documentation. A generated file carries a `DO NOT EDIT` line, and the build never runs the generator for you.

definition.name: Break large work into trackable subtasks
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no applicability for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.

For a practice about requested work, establish the current request from the complete issue body and the discussion the practice names. Brief, vague or title-only requests still pass this premise.

When genuinely conflicting current statements leave that request unresolved, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for the request-dependent judgment, cite the conflict, and judge neither statement under the standard. Position or date alone does not resolve it. If an explicit authored withdrawal leaves no work requested, record DOES_NOT_APPLY for that judgment and treat earlier requirements as history. Judge a remaining request under the practice's standard. Historical and closure practices retain their own subjects, including accounting for dropped or deferred work.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a trackable breakdown of work that is large enough to need one — checkable sub-items a maintainer can watch reach done, rather than one monolithic ask.

## The standard
Judge ONE thing: when the issue describes genuinely LARGE or work with several deliverables, is that work broken into explicit, trackable sub-items, rather than left as a single undivided block? Trackable means the deliverables are individually checkable or addressable: a task list of checkboxes that name work to do, a tracked sub-issue tree, or enumerated child or tracking issues the body frames as deliverables. Reason like a senior reviewer scanning a backlog: a big ask written as one block is either 0% or 100% done with no visible progress; a decomposed one lets pieces be picked up in parallel and tracked to done. What counts as LARGE is a judgment, not a word count: the deciding evidence is two or more SEPARABLE deliverables that could ship or be assigned independently, or an explicit epic, initiative, meta or tracking framing the issue itself chose. Largeness comes from what the deliverables are, never from how many items, clauses or characters there are: independent deliverables listed in one short sentence — a rename, a new tab, a theme, a changed default — are large work, while the sections, topics or checks of one page, screen or feature belong to one deliverable, not separate work. Sequential steps of ONE cohesive flow described as a journey are a single deliverable, not several deliverables. A checklist of verification items is not a work breakdown unless it also names concrete implementation sub-steps.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the case, and stop when: the issue is a pure question, a support request or an open discussion with no concrete deliverable; the body is empty, title-only or an unmodified template, so nothing is quotable; or the work is a focused single-concern deliverable (one feature, one bug), which neither needs a breakdown nor is penalised for lacking one. Never manufacture a strength from the mere absence of largeness, and never make the single-concern scope judgment here — that belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`.

## Sources
Your context is the issue only; there is no diff or code.
1. The title and the WHOLE body (`context/description.md`): every section, checklist and enumerated list. It establishes whether the work is large (separable deliverables, epic framing) and whether a checklist or a set of framed child issues breaks it down. It never establishes largeness from title length or tone alone.
2. The labels and the sub-issue rollup (`context/metadata.json`): a label such as epic or tracking, and the `sub_issues_total` / `sub_issues_completed` figures. A non-zero rollup is a tracked sub-issue tree; a null or missing figure is unknown, never zero. The labels establish the framing the issue chose; they never by themselves establish that a breakdown exists.
3. The comments (`context/comments.json`): a later comment can supply the breakdown or the child issues. They establish a breakdown on that surface; they never establish one the text does not show.
An image in the body: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. Before concluding that no breakdown exists, scan ALL three surfaces. If the body or the comments were not captured, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
These conformance cases apply after the shared issue premise establishes a current request.
- MET: the work is genuinely large AND a trackable breakdown is quotable — named sub-steps as a checklist ("design the schema", "add the endpoint", "wire up the UI"), a non-zero sub-issue rollup, or child issues the body frames as deliverables. Sibling issues in the project inventory that this body never names are not its breakdown, however well they match its sentences.
- NOT_MET: the work is clearly large AND the captured body and comments contain no trackable breakdown, with a reported zero sub-issue rollup. This establishes absence across the three surfaces; an unreported or null rollup does not.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE when no trackable breakdown is quotable and either the text cannot settle whether its spans are one journey or several separable deliverables, or the work is large and its sub-issue rollup is unknown. Cite the ambiguity or unknown source fact and say what would settle it.
One result per practice per review, over the whole issue. Identical evidence yields the same call.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on decomposition alone — a non-blocking workflow practice, not a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: only a couple of deliverables go untracked, and a short checklist would fix it. MAJOR: an issue the text itself frames as an epic, initiative, meta or tracking issue has nothing tracked under it at all.

## Grounding
Every "large" claim and every "no breakdown" claim quotes the exact span: a label name, a body sentence naming each separable deliverable, the rollup figure, or a comment. For MET, quote the checklist lines, the rollup figure or the framed child references. For NOT_MET, cite the spans that establish largeness and name the boundary searched: the body, the rollup, and the comments. Never invent largeness, never fabricate a breakdown you did not see. Never assert technical feasibility, hour estimates or design correctness, and never grade the reporter as a person; describe the recorded issue state only.

## Defer
Whether the work SHOULD have been one concern belongs to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`; treat a request with several deliverables as legitimately large work needing a breakdown, and do not re-judge its scope. Whether acceptance criteria or a Definition of Done are present belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`; do not re-flag a verification checklist here. Here only: is large work DECOMPOSED into trackable deliverables?

guidance.whyItMatters: A big ask written as one wall of text is either 0% or 100% done, with no way to see progress or split the load. Breaking it into checkable steps turns a daunting job into pieces people can pick up and finish one at a time.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A genuinely large issue split into a task list or linked sub-issues, such as 'design the schema', 'add the endpoint', and 'wire up the UI', so progress is visible and pieces can be worked in parallel.
guidance.goingWell: Large work arrives split into trackable pieces

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you file a big issue, list the parts that someone could ship or pick up on their own.
- Give each part its own check box, or open it as a child issue. For example, instead of one line that asks for “export, settings and alerts”, write three check boxes. Name them “Add the export”, “Add the settings page” and “Send the alerts”.
- Name the work to do in each item, so that anyone can tell when it’s done.
- If the issue is an epic or a tracking issue, give its work a task list or child issues.
- If you find the parts later, add a task list or child-issue links to the issue body or a comment.

## When it does not apply

- The issue asks a question, asks for support or opens a discussion, and asks for no concrete work.
- The issue body is empty, has only a title or is an unchanged template.
- The issue asks for one focused piece of work, such as one feature or one bug fix.

It still applies when one short sentence asks for several separate things, such as a rename, a new tab and a new default.

## Common mistakes

- Judging size by the length of the issue. Instead, look at the parts. Two or more parts that could ship or go to different people are large work, even in one line.
- Writing the parts as one paragraph. Instead, give each part its own check box or child issue, so each one can reach done on its own.
- Labeling an issue as an epic with nothing under it. Instead, add the task list or link the child issues when you open it.
- Treating a list of checks as the plan. A list of things to verify does not say what to build. Instead, add the steps of the work, such as “add the endpoint”.

## Sources

- [Adding sub-issues](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/adding-sub-issues), GitHub Docs. Sub-issues break larger work into tasks, and the parent issue shows their progress.
- [Tasks](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/tasks/), GitLab Docs. Tasks break an issue into smaller items that you can track and assign, and the issue shows their progress.
- [INVEST in good stories, and SMART tasks](https://xp123.com/invest-in-good-stories-and-smart-tasks/), Bill Wake, 2003. A good task makes clear what work it involves and what the team means by done.

definition.name: Classify the issue the way the project classifies issues

humanReason.description: Hephaestus captures the issue metadata, but not the project classification requirements that establish which labels, owners or milestones this issue should carry. Labels used elsewhere do not establish a required convention. A person with the project policy can assess this practice.

definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no applicability for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.

For a practice about requested work, establish the current request from the complete issue body and the discussion the practice names. Brief, vague or title-only requests still pass this premise.

When genuinely conflicting current statements leave that request unresolved, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for the request-dependent judgment, cite the conflict, and judge neither statement under the standard. Position or date alone does not resolve it. If an explicit authored withdrawal leaves no work requested, record DOES_NOT_APPLY for that judgment and treat earlier requirements as history. Judge a remaining request under the practice's standard. Historical and closure practices retain their own subjects, including accounting for dropped or deferred work.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the issue satisfies the classification requirements of the documented project policy applicable to it.

## The standard
Judge whether this issue follows the labelling convention the project actually keeps, not whether every metadata field is filled. A convention must be established by an explicit documented project policy applicable to this kind of issue. Label frequency, a list of labels in use or another issue's assignment does not establish a requirement. Compare the captured issue with that policy: require only the label kinds, native type, ownership or milestone it actually mandates. A native issue type can satisfy a corresponding label kind. Never demand a classification the project does not use.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY when a captured project policy establishes that no classification requirement applies to this kind of issue. Missing policy is not evidence of no convention. Current automated capture does not supply project classification requirements, so this practice is unavailable for automated review. In a manual review, use the documented policy; failed acquisition of required policy or metadata is a collection gap.

## Sources
1. The documented project classification policy supplied to the manual review: applicable label kinds, native issue types, ownership and milestone requirements. It establishes what this issue is required to carry, not how often metadata happens to occur elsewhere.
2. The issue metadata (`context/metadata.json`): native type, labels, assignees and milestone. It establishes what this issue carries.
3. The title and body (`context/description.md`): the issue kind and any explicit routing request. A request alone does not establish a project-wide rule.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every classification requirement applicable under the captured policy is satisfied. Quote the policy and corresponding metadata.
- NOT_MET: an applicable policy requirement is not satisfied. Quote the requirement and the complete metadata that lacks it.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: complete supplied policy or metadata leaves the applicability of a deciding requirement genuinely ambiguous; name what would settle it. Missing required acquisition produces no result.
One result per practice per review, over the whole issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MINOR — non-blocking feedback about routing, not a merge gate. MINOR: no label at all in a labelled project, or the body asks to be routed and no label answers it. TRIVIAL: one kind of several missing.

## Grounding
Quote the applicable documented requirement and this issue's metadata. Never infer a normative convention from label frequency, labels in use, ownership on other issues or the number of people in a project. Never assess whether the work is worth doing.

## Defer
Problem framing belongs to `issue-states-an-actionable-problem`, scope to `issue-scoped-to-single-concern`, and the definition of done to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: is the issue classified the way this project classifies its issues?

guidance.whyItMatters: A label kind the project filters and groups by — type, priority, size — routes the issue to the board column, the person and the sprint it belongs to. An issue outside that scheme is the one nobody's filter shows, so it waits.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: The issue carries the labels, native type, owner or milestone required by the documented project policy for its kind; fields that the policy does not require may remain unset.

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Find the project’s written policy for classifying issues. It often lives in a contributing guide or a triage page.
- For your kind of issue, set each label kind that the policy requires, such as type, priority or size.
- If the policy requires an issue type, set the built-in type or the type label that the policy accepts.
- If the policy requires an owner or a milestone for your kind of issue, set it.
- If the policy requires a team label for the issue, add it. For example, instead of only asking “Can the network team look at this?”, add the required network label.

## When it does not apply

- The project’s written policy says that this kind of issue needs no labels, type, owner or milestone.

A missing policy does not tell you whether classification requirements apply.

## Common mistakes

- Filling in every field you can see. The practice does not ask for that. Instead, set only what the policy asks for on this kind of issue. Fields that it does not ask for can stay empty.
- Copying the labels that other issues carry. A label that many issues use is not a rule. Instead, check what the written policy asks for.
- Picking a kind that does not match the issue, such as labelling a support question as a bug. Instead, pick the kind that the policy defines for this work. If you are not sure, ask a maintainer.

## Sources

- [Issue triage](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/product-development/how-we-work/issue-triage/), GitLab Handbook. GitLab’s written policy asks for type and group labels, plus a severity label for bugs.
- [Issue triage guidelines](https://www.kubernetes.dev/docs/guide/issue-triage/), Kubernetes contributor guide. Kubernetes uses kind, priority and owning-group labels, and an issue with no priority label has not been prioritized.
- [Best practices for Projects](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/planning-and-tracking-with-projects/learning-about-projects/best-practices-for-projects), GitHub Docs. GitHub suggests issue types to classify work and assignees to show who is responsible.

definition.name: Confirm the outcome before closing the issue

humanReason.description: Hephaestus reads an issue as it stands when the review runs, after the close. Its checklist, sub-issue progress and comments can all change after the close, and the issue can be reopened and closed again, so what Hephaestus reads cannot show what was still open when it was closed. Whether the outcome was confirmed at that close needs a person who saw it.

definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no applicability for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.

For a practice about requested work, establish the current request from the complete issue body and the discussion the practice names. Brief, vague or title-only requests still pass this premise.

When genuinely conflicting current statements leave that request unresolved, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for the request-dependent judgment, cite the conflict, and judge neither statement under the standard. Position or date alone does not resolve it. If an explicit authored withdrawal leaves no work requested, record DOES_NOT_APPLY for that judgment and treat earlier requirements as history. Judge a remaining request under the practice's standard. Historical and closure practices retain their own subjects, including accounting for dropped or deferred work.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: evidence dated to the close accounts for the issue's stated outcome, through confirmed completion or an explained remainder.

## The standard
When an issue is CLOSED as done, judge whether its own stated definition of done was confirmed at that close — every checkable acceptance item ticked and every tracked sub-issue finished — or whether a remainder was named at the close. Assess this single closure decision only, never the work: an empty checkbox may simply never have been ticked while the work was genuinely done. A closing comment that says plainly what is being dropped or deferred and why accounts for the remainder. The question is about the record as it stood at the close, and only evidence dated to that close can answer it. Never assert compile, runtime or correctness behaviour; there is no diff or code here.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when evidence dated to this close shows the issue was not closed as done: closed as not-planned, wontfix, duplicate, superseded or deferred. The current `state_reason`, body and rollup describe the latest state, not this close, so they cannot settle whether this close was done or stated a checkable outcome; when nothing dated to the close does, the gate is unresolved and the Judge records COULD_NOT_DETERMINE. DOES_NOT_APPLY belongs to scope facts dated to the close, never to evidence you could not read or could not date.

## Sources
1. The issue record (`context/metadata.json`): state, `state_reason`, `closed_at`, labels and the sub-issue rollup. `closed_at` dates the close and nothing else. The body, labels and rollup are their values when the review read them, which is after the close; they never show their values at the close.
2. The title and body (`context/description.md`): the current text. A checkbox can be ticked, unticked or added after the close, and the issue can be reopened and closed again, so a current checkbox is not a checkbox at the close.
3. Comments (`context/comments.json`): `created_at` dates when a comment was written, not its present text, which may since have been edited; a comment written after the close is never a disposition at the close.
4. The workspace inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): state the overlapping or closing issues you found, quoted as `#number "title" (state)`, or that you scanned it and found none.
When the comments or the issue record were not captured, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
The undesirable behaviour is closing as done with a stated outcome unmet and unaccounted for. Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: evidence dated to this close shows a done-item still open at it — an unchecked acceptance or Definition-of-Done line, or a rollup short of complete — and nothing at the close names where that remainder went.
- MET: evidence dated to this close shows every checkable item ticked and every tracked sub-issue completed, or a remainder named at the close.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the issue was closed as done or with an unrecorded disposition, and the only record of its checklist, rollup or closing comments is the one read after the close. Name the undated fact. Never decide either cell from the current body, the current rollup or current comment text, whichever way they point.
One result per practice per review, on the single at-close question. Do not infer a longitudinal or developer-wide pattern from this one issue.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on outcome confirmation alone — non-blocking. MINOR: an open sub-issue rollup alone. MAJOR: an unconfirmed acceptance or Definition-of-Done condition with nothing at the close accounting for it. A remainder named at the close is not a negative. Identical inputs yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Every claim cites an exact quoted span and says what dates it: the state or `state_reason` value, the `closed_at` timestamp, and for either assessed cell the at-close evidence of each item it relies on. A Could not determine result cites what was read, states that it is dated after the close, and records the unresolved question in its open questions. State the inventory result in every result. Describe only observable state — "closed as done with '<quoted line>' still unchecked at the close" — never a charge against the closer. Never fabricate a checklist, a clean bill or a disposition.

## Defer
Whether a NEW or OPEN issue defines a checkable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: was the stated outcome confirmed at the close?

guidance.whyItMatters: Closing an issue tells the whole team it is handled. Closing it with a checklist item still unticked or sub-issues still open drops that work quietly, and someone hits the gap later expecting it to be done.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Before closing, every acceptance item is checked and every tracked sub-issue is finished, or a comment says plainly what is being dropped and why, so 'closed' honestly means done.

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you close an issue as done, read its checklist and its sub-issues.
- Tick each checklist item that the work finished.
- Close each sub-issue that is finished.
- If an item is still open, name it in a closing comment that you post when you close. Say why it is dropped or deferred. For example, instead of closing with “Done”, write “Done except PDF export. We deferred it until the export library is ready.”
- If you drop the whole issue, close it as not planned instead of as done.

## When it does not apply

- You close the issue as not planned.
- You close it as wontfix, because you will not fix it.
- You close it as a duplicate of another issue.
- You close it as superseded, because other work replaced it.
- You close it as deferred, to come back to it later.

## Common mistakes

- Closing finished work with its boxes still empty. The work may be done, but the issue still says that it is open. Instead, tick each finished item before you close.
- Closing with “Done” or with no comment while an item is still open. The open item then looks finished. Instead, name the item and say why it is dropped or deferred.
- Adding the note or ticking the boxes days after the close. Until then, the team reads the issue as done. Instead, do it before you close, or in the same step.
- Leaving sub-issues open under a parent that you close as done. Instead, finish them first. Or name them in the closing comment.

## Sources

- [Closing an issue](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/administering-issues/closing-an-issue), GitHub Docs. You can choose a close reason to show that work is finished or not planned.
- [Manage issues](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/issues/managing_issues/), GitLab Docs. The `/close` quick action can close an issue from a comment.
- [The Scrum Guide](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html), Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, 2020. In Scrum, work that fails the team’s agreed quality checks returns to their list of future work.

definition.name: Record the outcome of a closed issue
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured issue: its title, description, labels and the discussion the practice names. Labels and templates are context, not proof; a placeholder issue may have no applicability for an actionable-work practice. Do not infer that a bug reproduces or that an outcome was implemented.

For a practice about requested work, establish the current request from the complete issue body and the discussion the practice names. Brief, vague or title-only requests still pass this premise.

When genuinely conflicting current statements leave that request unresolved, record COULD_NOT_DETERMINE for the request-dependent judgment, cite the conflict, and judge neither statement under the standard. Position or date alone does not resolve it. If an explicit authored withdrawal leaves no work requested, record DOES_NOT_APPLY for that judgment and treat earlier requirements as history. Judge a remaining request under the practice's standard. Historical and closure practices retain their own subjects, including accounting for dropped or deferred work.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the authored record of a closed issue — its body and discussion as captured now — accounts for the outcome the issue states.

## The standard
Judge one bookkeeping act on an issue that is CLOSED as this review reads it: do its body and discussion, as they stand now, account for the outcome the issue itself states? An outcome is stated when the issue gives an observable completion condition you can quote: an acceptance item, a Definition of Done, a Given-When-Then scenario, or an explicit outcome statement in its title or prose. A concrete title alone can state that condition; no checklist or separate body is required. A topic or activity name without a discernible completion condition does not state a checkable outcome, so there is no closure accounting to assess here. A stated item is accounted for when it is ticked, or when the body or a comment clearly confirms it done — a short confirmation is enough when it unambiguously covers the item — or, if it was not done, explicitly says which work was dropped or deferred. A remainder needs accounting only when there is one. Judge what the record says, never whether the work was done or done correctly: a tick or a confirmation records a claim, and an unticked item may describe finished work. The closed state or a closing pull or merge request accounts for nothing by itself, and a statement that names the feature counts only for the items it plainly covers. The person who closed the issue may not be its author; describe the record, never who failed to write it.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when: the captured issue is not closed; its current disposition is not planned, duplicate or superseded; or it states no checkable outcome you can quote. The current disposition is the current `state_reason`, or a comment that clearly speaks to the present close; a comment from before an earlier reopen does not decide it, and `completed` alone does not disprove an explicit current disposition statement: some providers synthesize it for every non-duplicate closure. If current statements genuinely conflict, use COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.

## Sources
1. The issue record (`context/metadata.json`): `state`, `state_reason` and `closed_at` as captured when this review ran. They establish the current state and disposition, never what any field said at the close.
2. The title and body (`context/description.md`): the stated outcome and its ticks as they stand now.
3. The discussion (`context/comments.json`): the mirrored comments with their author, `created_at` and `updated_at`, as they stand now; Hephaestus's own comments are left out. A comment can account for an item as fully as a tick. Its dates say when it was written and last edited, never that it existed at the close.
Sub-issue counts and other progress figures are not authored statements and decide nothing here; a sub-issue the body or a comment refers to counts only through what that text says. All of it is the record now; never claim what was true when the issue was closed. If the issue record or the discussion was not captured, or the discussion was captured incompletely, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: every stated item is ticked or accounted for in the body or discussion. Quote the ticks or the text that accounts for them.
- NOT_MET: the issue is closed, states a checkable outcome, and a portion of it is neither ticked nor accounted for in the body or discussion. Quote the unaccounted items.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: complete captured text leaves it genuinely ambiguous whether a statement covers an item, or what the current disposition is; name the deciding question.
One result per practice per review, on the issue's current authored record.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking bookkeeping. MINOR, the usual band: a few stated items neither ticked nor accounted for. MAJOR: most of the stated outcome neither ticked nor accounted for. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the stated items as written, their tick state, the `state` value, and any text you rely on with its author and dates, and say that this is the record as captured now. Never claim an item was or was not delivered, never claim the record looked this way at the close, and never read the closed state as a tick.

## Defer
Whether the issue stated a checkable outcome in the first place belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`; whether a merged change brought its linked issue's outcome into line belongs to `merge-confirms-the-linked-issue-outcome`; what the record showed at the moment of the close is a question for a person (`issue-closed-with-unmet-outcome`). Here only: does the closed issue's current authored record account for its stated outcome?

guidance.whyItMatters: A closed issue is where the team looks to learn what was delivered. When its record says which items were done and what happened to the rest, the next person neither guesses nor repeats the digging.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Once an issue is closed, its list is ticked as far as the work went or a comment confirms what was done, and anything not done is named as dropped or deferred.
guidance.goingWell: Each closed issue records what became of its outcome

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Go through each item that the issue states.
- For each finished item, tick its box or clearly confirm it in the body or a comment.
- For each item that is not done, name it in a comment and say if it was dropped or deferred. For example, instead of closing with “Done”, write “Export and import are done. Bulk delete is deferred to a new issue.”
- If the issue is already closed and its record is incomplete, add the comment now. The record that a reader sees today is the one that counts.

## When it does not apply

- The issue is still open.
- The issue was closed as not planned, as a duplicate, or because other work replaced it. Its close reason or a comment about this close says so.
- The issue states no outcome that someone can check, such as a topic name with no clear finish.

It still applies when the issue has no checklist and only its title says what must be true when the work is done.

## Common mistakes

- Letting the closed state speak for the issue. Closing it, or merging the pull request or merge request that closes it, does not say which items were done. Instead, tick the items or confirm them in a comment.
- Leaving unfinished items unticked with no word about them. A reader cannot tell if they were done, dropped, or forgotten. Instead, name each one and say what became of it.
- Writing a confirmation, such as “Search is done”, that covers only part of the list. Instead, make clear which finished work the confirmation covers.
- Ticking an item that you did not finish, so that the list looks complete. Instead, leave it open and say that it was deferred.

## Sources

- [Communication, collaboration, and bugs: the social nature of issue tracking in small, collocated teams](https://grouplab.cpsc.ucalgary.ca/grouplab/uploads/Publications/Publications/2010-IssueTracking.CSCW.pdf), Bertram, Voida, Greenberg and Walker, 2010. Teams went back to an issue’s history later to learn what was decided and why.
- [The Scrum Guide](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html), Schwaber and Sutherland, 2020. In Scrum, work that fails the team’s agreed quality checks returns to their list of future work.
- [What are work item statuses, priorities, and resolutions?](https://support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/what-are-issue-statuses-priorities-and-resolutions/), Atlassian. A resolution records how the work ended: it was done, it will not be done, or it is a duplicate.

definition.name: Link the change to the issue it implements
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the pull request names the issue it implements, so the work can be read against what was asked.

## The standard
Judge one thing: does this pull request say which issue it implements, in a way the platform links? A link is the issue's number in the title (`#12: …`), a reference in the body the author wrote — a plain mention such as `Related to #12` or a closing reference such as `Closes #12`, `Fixes #12`, `Resolves #12` or the provider's equivalent —, a branch created from the issue (`12-add-login`), or a captured linked work item. A number inside the form's template or an example is not the author's reference. A link makes the issue readable from the review. Closing the issue when the change merges is a separate, provider-recognized relationship and not what this practice asks for: a plain reference settles traceability, including for work that delivers only a portion of the issue, and never needs to become a closing keyword. A change with none of these stands alone. Judge the presence of the link, never the quality of the issue it points to or whether the change fulfils it.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the work has no issue to link: the repository tracks no issues (`context/project_inventory.json` lists none), or the change is of a kind that answers no issue by convention — a release or version bump, a dependency update from a bot, a revert, a merge of one long-lived branch into another. A change a person made to the product is expected to answer an issue; a missing issue is then the lapse, not a reason the practice does not apply.

## Sources
1. The title, source branch and body (`context/metadata.json`, `context/description.md`): the number references and closing keywords as written. They establish the link the author made. They never establish that the issue exists or that the change fulfils it.
2. The linked work items (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`, and `context/linked_work_items.json` with `how` per item) when captured: the items the platform resolved from those references, and for each whether the provider records it as a closing candidate for this change (`how: closesOnMerge`) or the text merely mentions it (`how: mentions`). Either kind is a link: a closing candidate links the issue whatever the text says, and a mention links it without closing it. Their absence establishes nothing when no reference was written.
3. The inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): whether the project tracks issues at all, and, for a change with no reference, whether an open issue plainly describes this work — quote its `#number "title"` if you find one, or say you scanned it and found none.
4. The commits (`context/commits.json`): a further place an issue number may appear. They establish a reference the author left in history, nothing more. The leads from the practice script below these criteria list every number referenced, where it was written, and whether the inventory or the linked items hold an issue of that number with its title and state.
A reference in the title, body, branch or linked work can settle traceability without commit history. If no captured source shows a reference, an unavailable commit inventory cannot establish that history contains none. Report that collection gap and record no result; do the same when the record or project inventory is unavailable for a change with no reference.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the title, body, branch or a captured linked item names a verified issue target, including a deliberate cross-project link. Quote the reference.
- NOT_MET: a reference is written but cannot be what it claims — it resolves to no issue, or claims to implement an issue whose captured contents clearly concern different work. A deliberate cross-project issue link can satisfy traceability; its closing behavior depends on the provider. Quote the reference and name the fact that breaks it.
- NOT_MET: the change is product work by a person and no title, body, branch, commit or linked item names an issue, after scanning all of them. Say what you scanned.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: a reference whose target you cannot resolve because the inventory was not captured and the number could be a pull request as well as an issue; name what would settle it.
One result per practice per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: product work with no reference where an open issue for it plainly exists in the inventory, or a reference that resolves to no issue or to different work. MAJOR: product work with no issue at all in a project that tracks its work in issues. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the reference as written in the title, body, branch name or commit subject, or the linked item's `#number "title"`. NOT_MET names every source scanned. Never invent an issue number, and never claim an issue's content from its number alone.

## Defer
Whether the change fulfils the issue's acceptance criteria belongs to `honours-linked-issue-acceptance-criteria`; the description's what and why belong to `describe-what-and-why`. Here only: is the change linked to the issue it implements?

guidance.whyItMatters: A change that names the issue it answers can be read against what was asked and leaves a trail anyone can follow later. When the platform recognizes the reference as closing, the issue also closes when the change merges; a plain mention links the two but does not establish automatic closure. One without a reference makes the reviewer guess what the work was for.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: The title, the description or the branch names the issue by number, with a closing keyword in the body when the change completes it, so the platform can close the issue with the merge and the two stay linked.
guidance.goingWell: Every change names the issue it implements
