guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you open the pull or merge request, search the open issues for the one that this work answers.
- Name the issue by its number in the title, the description or the branch name. For example, instead of the title “Add login timeout” and nothing else, write “Related to #12” in the description.
- If you start the work from the issue, create the branch from it. On GitLab, start the branch name with the issue number, such as `12-add-login`, in the issue’s project.
- Use a closing keyword such as “Closes #12” only when the change completes the issue. A plain mention links the change to the issue but leaves the issue open.
- If the issue lives in another project, use its full reference, such as `group/project#12`.

## When it does not apply

- Your project does not track its work in issues.
- The change is a release or a version bump.
- The change is a dependency update that a bot opened.
- The change reverts an earlier change.
- The change merges one long-lived branch into another.

It still applies when a person changes the product and no issue exists for the work. Then the missing issue is the gap.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that only a closing keyword counts. A plain mention such as “Related to #12” links the change too, even for part of an issue. Instead, keep the closing keyword for a change that finishes the issue.
- Leaving the number from the description template or an example in place. Instead, replace it with the number of your issue.
- Writing a number that is not the issue, such as a typo or a pull request number. Instead, open the link and check that it is the right issue.
- Opening product work with no reference while an open issue already describes it. Instead, name that issue.

## Sources

- [Linking a pull request to an issue](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue), GitHub Docs. A closing keyword in a pull request to the default branch links the issue and closes it when merged.
- [Crosslinking issues](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/issues/crosslinking_issues/), GitLab Docs. Mentioning an issue in a merge request description or commit message links the work to that issue.
- [Writing good CL descriptions](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/cl-descriptions.html), Google Engineering Practices. Google suggests that a description include background such as bug numbers, for future readers.
- [Traceability in the wild: automatically augmenting incomplete trace links](https://doi.org/10.1145/3180155.3180207), Rath and others, 2018. Across six open-source projects, about 60% of commits named an issue, leaving gaps between issues and code.

definition.name: Confirm the linked issue's outcome
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: for merged work, the captured record confirms the linked issue's stated outcome — its adopted outcome items reported as delivered or named as deferred — so the tracker accounts for what was delivered.

## The standard
Judge one thing about this merged pull request: does the captured record bring the linked issue's own definition of done into line with what landed? The merge establishes the applicability; this review assesses confirmation in the capture, not the issue body at merge time. An issue that stated a checkable outcome (an acceptance checklist, a Definition of Done, a Given-When-Then block, tracked sub-issues) is confirmed when the captured record accounts for each outcome item the change adopts — reported as delivered or named as deferred — in the issue, in the pull request body, or in a closing comment. Content decides, not form: a tick, a checked item, an authored delivery bullet or a sentence counts when its wording substantively names a specific adopted outcome item, even under a template heading and while the issue's own boxes stay unticked; no checkbox, heading, closing word or formula is required. A check that names none of the items (builds, reviewed, lint clean), a bare closing reference, a line that names only the feature ("added the search screen"), or an inventory of changes whose link to the items must be inferred from the code confirms nothing about them. Work that delivers a portion of what it adopts is confirmed only when the delivered portion is named and the rest is named as deferred; an adopted item left unmentioned is unaccounted for. It need not close the issue or tick an item twice. Assess only this bookkeeping act, never whether the work is correct: a tick or a delivery line is the author's report, not proof that an item works, was checked or is fulfilled, nor of when it was made; an unticked item may describe delivered work, and a ticked one may not.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when: the pull request is not merged; a complete linked-work inventory establishes no relevant item, or the linked item states no checkable outcome you can quote (a task list, an acceptance or Definition-of-Done block, a Given-When-Then, or a non-zero sub-issue rollup); or the linked item was closed as not planned, duplicate or superseded, since its outcome was deliberately abandoned. A linked item with an outcome and a merge are the applicability — every captured item this change explicitly implements, closing candidates and adopted partial work alike; a mention alone does not establish that this change must account for the item; the leads from the practice script list each with its items and ticks. A user story without a task list, an outcome heading or sub-issues is no applicability, however plainly the diff delivers it.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): `state` and `merged_at`. It establishes that and when the change merged. It never establishes the issue's state.
2. Each linked item (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`: number, title, state, body; `how` in `linked_work_items.json` says whether the provider records it as a closing candidate): the checkable outcome as written, with its ticks as captured. It establishes what was stated and which items are ticked. Confirmation captured after the merge counts. A missing confirmation describes this capture; it does not establish that confirmation never happened or that it was missing at merge time. Its body is the text as mirrored at capture, and its opening and closing dates are not when any line of it was written. A closed state alone confirms nothing; the ticks or the words do.
3. The body (`context/description.md`) and the discussion (`context/general_comments.json`): a done/deferred account as the standard describes it. They establish what the author said was delivered. They never establish that it was.
4. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): read only to ground a heavier severity when a named item is plainly not touched. It never establishes that an item is met.
If the linked item's body or the record's merge time is unavailable, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the capture accounts for every adopted outcome item as the standard says, as delivered or deferred. Quote the ticks, lines or sentence that name each item. Judge the recorded done/deferred mapping, not whether the code actually delivers the item.
- NOT_MET: the change merged, the linked item states a checkable outcome, and the capture leaves at least one adopted item unaccounted for as the standard says — unticked and unnamed, whether the issue is closed or open. Quote the unaccounted items and the merge time.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: complete captured text leaves the done/deferred mapping genuinely ambiguous; name the deciding question. A truncated capture of a required checklist is a collection gap and produces no result.
One result per practice per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one or two items left unaccounted for in the capture with the work plainly delivered, or an authored account that names the outcome loosely. MAJOR: most of the stated outcome is unaccounted for in the captured closed issue, or the captured issue is open with nothing said. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the outcome items from the linked item as written, the tick state, the merge time from the record, and any authored line that accounts for them. Never claim an item is met, unmet or accounted for from the code; never infer a tick that is not in the capture; never read a closed state as a tick. Credit a tick or an authored line in the item's body or the description as captured; say it was there before, at or after the merge only when independently dated evidence establishes that, since the creation date of a body, a description or a comment alone does not date text edited later. A later capture that confirms the outcome does not undo an earlier result that read it unconfirmed; each stands for the capture it read.

## Defer
Whether a closing pull request's own handoff says which acceptance criteria it covers belongs to `honours-linked-issue-acceptance-criteria`; the issue's own closing decision, when someone closes it by hand, belongs to `issue-closed-with-unmet-outcome`. Here only: does the captured record confirm the linked issue's outcome for the merged work?

guidance.whyItMatters: A linked issue with its outcome unconfirmed tells the next person little about what was delivered. After a change merges, recording what landed and naming what moves elsewhere keeps the tracker true.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: After a change merges, its linked issue accounts for what landed: delivered outcomes are marked or reported, any remainder is named, and the issue's state matches.
guidance.goingWell: The linked issue accounts for merged work

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- After the merge, find the checkable items in each issue that your change implements.
- Record each delivered item with a tick or a sentence that names it.
- If only part of an item is done, tick or name that part.
- Name what remains and say that it is deferred. For example, instead of “Added the search screen”, write “Search box and filters are done. Saved searches move to #318.”
- Put this record in the issue, in your description, or in a comment.

## When it does not apply

- The pull request or merge request is not merged.
- Your change does not implement any linked issue. A plain mention of an issue does not count.
- The linked issue states no outcome you can check. It has no task list and no sub-issues. It has no section that says what counts as done or lists steps with expected results. A user story alone does not count.
- The linked issue was closed as not planned, as a duplicate, or as replaced by other work.

It still applies when the issue is already closed, and when your change delivers only part of an item.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that you must tick every box. A plain sentence that says what is done and what is deferred works just as well.
- Letting the closed issue speak for you. On GitHub, a closing keyword closes the linked issue when you merge into the default branch. Its boxes stay as they were. Instead, tick the delivered items or add a closing sentence.
- Ticking template boxes such as “builds”, “reviewed” or “lint clean”. They name no item of the issue. Instead, tick boxes whose words match the issue’s items.
- Naming only the feature, such as “added the search screen”. Instead, name the items that are done and the ones that move on.

## Sources

- [The Scrum Guide](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html), Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, 2020. In Scrum, work that fails the team’s agreed quality checks returns to their list of future work.
- [Task lists](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/markdown/#task-lists), GitLab Docs. You can mark tasks complete, incomplete or inapplicable in issues, merge requests and comments.
- [Linking a pull request to an issue](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/linking-a-pull-request-to-an-issue), GitHub Docs. A closing keyword closes the linked issue when the pull request merges into the default branch.

definition.name: Track the review asks you defer
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a review ask the author defers rather than addresses is turned into tracked work or explicitly waived by the reviewer, never resolved on a bare promise.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when a reviewer asked for something in a thread and the author did not do it in this change, what happened to the ask at the merge? A deferral is tracked when the thread, the body or a comment names an issue for it (`#number`, a link, "tracked in …") or the reviewer explicitly agrees to drop it ("fine to skip", "not needed", a reviewer statement accepting the author's stated reason). An approval given on the condition that the ask be done later ("Approved, as long as you add the tests in a follow-up") keeps the ask alive: it is a deferral that needs a tracked item, never a waiver. A deferral is bare when the ask is resolved or the change merged with only "later", "next PR", "will do" or silence. Judge only asks the author deferred; an ask the author addressed in the diff, or answered with a reason the reviewer accepted, is not a deferral.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when: the pull request is not merged; the complete captured inline and general review record contains no ask the author left unaddressed in the change — every ask was addressed in the diff or answered with a reason the reviewer accepted. A question that requests no change ("what is this for?") is not an ask, whether or not it was answered, and neither is a remark aimed at later work ("something to keep in mind next time") or a suggestion the reviewer plainly leaves to the author's choice: it asks nothing of this change. Polite wording ("could you", "consider", "if possible") does not make a request optional; judge what the reviewer asked of this change. The author is the `author` login of `context/metadata.json`; a comment by any other login is a reviewer's, and a reviewer's own "ignore" or "fine" on an ask — theirs or a bot's — is a waiver. A merged change with at least one deferred ask is the applicability.

## Sources
1. The inline review comments (`context/comments.json`: `path`, `line`, `body`, `author`, `created_at`) and the conversation (`context/general_comments.json`): every ask and every reply, with authors and dates. They establish which asks were made, which were answered, and with what words. The threads (`context/review_threads.json`) carry each thread's path, line and resolution and no words; a resolution by the author establishes nothing about the substance, and a resolution by the reviewer after the author's stated reason is the reviewer accepting it. The leads from the practice script below these criteria list every comment by someone other than the author, one row each, with whether the change touches its file, whether the author replied, whether the reviewer had a later word on the thread or approved after it: decide every row that asks something.
2. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): whether an ask was addressed in the change — the file and line the thread anchors to, read as changed or not. It establishes addressed versus not; it never establishes a waiver.
3. The body and the discussion (`context/description.md`, `context/general_comments.json`): a follow-up list, an issue reference for the deferral, or the reviewer's agreement. They establish tracking or a waiver when quotable.
4. The linked work items (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`) when captured: an issue that names the deferred ask. It establishes the tracking; its absence establishes nothing when a comment names an issue by number.
If the change merged but the threads are absent or truncated, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Enumerate every ask by someone other than the author first and decide each against the diff — a request with two deliverables that is half-addressed leaves one deliverable deferred, and a thread marked RESOLVED decides nothing. An ask about the pull request itself rather than its code — mark it ready, retitle it, link an issue, fill in the description — is addressed when the captured record shows it done: the draft flag, the title, the description or the link. A draft cannot be merged, so a merged pull request settles a request to mark it ready; no transition time is needed. An ask about the code is addressed only by a changed line that does what was asked; an unchanged anchor alone does not establish that the ask was unaddressed: a guard or other relevant change elsewhere can satisfy it. Inspect the request's substance and the complete changed code before deciding. An ask the author answered with a reason is deferred bare unless the reviewer explicitly accepts the reason; a later approval without such evidence is not a waiver. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: at least one ask is deferred, and every deferred ask is tracked by a named issue or explicitly waived by the reviewer. Quote the ask and the tracking reference or the waiver.
- NOT_MET: at least one ask was deferred on a bare promise or in silence — resolved or merged past with no issue and no reviewer waiver. Quote the ask and the author's last word on it, or note the silence.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the thread's last word could be a waiver or a deferral and the reviewer's approval carries no comment; name the fact that would settle it.
One result per practice per review, on the single most consequential bare deferral when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a small ask (a rename, a comment, a nit) deferred bare. MAJOR: a correctness, safety or test ask deferred on a bare promise and the change merged. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the reviewer's ask and the author's reply verbatim with their authors and dates, and the issue reference or waiver when there is one. Never infer a waiver from an approval alone, and never claim an ask was addressed without the changed line that addresses it.

## Defer
Whether the author replied to comments at all belongs to `engaging-with-inline-review-comments`; a thread left unresolved at the merge belongs to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: where did the deferred asks go?

guidance.whyItMatters: A reviewer's ask answered with 'later' and nothing else is a promise that evaporates at the merge. Turning a deferred ask into a tracked issue, or getting the reviewer's explicit agreement to drop it, keeps the review's value after the thread is resolved.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Every review ask the author does not address in the change is either turned into an issue the thread links, or explicitly waived by the reviewer; nothing is resolved with a bare 'will do later'.
guidance.goingWell: Deferred review asks become tracked issues

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you merge, check which review asks your change leaves undone.
- When an ask waits, link an issue that tracks it in the thread. For example, instead of replying “Will do in the next change”, reply “Tracked in #482”.
- If no issue tracks the ask, open one from the review comment. The issue then shows where the ask came from.
- When you think an ask is not needed, ask the reviewer in the thread to accept your reason.
- When you do only part of an ask, track the part that is left.

## When it does not apply

- The pull request or merge request did not merge.
- Your change does every ask, or you gave a reason for each ask left undone and the reviewer accepted it.
- The comment asks nothing of this change. Examples are a question such as “what is this for?” and a remark for next time.
- The reviewer leaves the suggestion to your choice.

It still applies when an ask sounds polite, such as “could you” or “consider”, or when a review bot made it. It also applies when the reviewer approved on the condition that you do the ask later.

## Common mistakes

- Taking an approval as permission to drop the ask. “Approved, as long as you add the tests later” keeps the ask open. Open an issue for the tests and link it.
- Giving your reason and then merging. An approval with no word on your reason is not agreement. Ask the reviewer to confirm.
- Resolving the thread with “later”. A resolved thread does not say where the ask went. Link the issue first, then resolve the thread.
- Trusting yourself to remember. A promise in a thread is easy to lose after the merge. Put it in the tracker, where the team can see it.

## Sources

- [Handling pushback in code reviews](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/pushback.html#later), Google Engineering Practices. File a bug for cleanup that must wait, so that it does not get lost.
- [Creating an issue from a comment](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/creating-an-issue#creating-an-issue-from-a-comment), GitHub Docs. You can open an issue from a pull request comment.
- [Move open threads to an issue](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/merge_requests/#move-open-threads-to-an-issue), GitLab Docs. An open thread can become a new issue that the merge request links.
- [Potential technical debt and its resolution in code reviews](https://doi.org/10.1145/3544902.3546253), Fu and others, 2022. In OpenStack and Qt, some potential technical debt that reviewers found was still unresolved when the code merged.

definition.name: Merge only after someone else approved
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the merge happens after a current approval from someone other than the author, and never over an outstanding request for changes.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the moment this pull request merged: was there, at that moment, an approval from another person — an account other than the author's whose decision is not marked `bot` — that still stood? An approval stands when it was submitted before the merge and nothing later withdrew it — no dismissal, no revocation (`UNAPPROVED`) and no request for changes by the same reviewer after it. A request for changes stands when it was submitted before the merge and no later approval by the same reviewer replaced it. A decision marked `bot` is an automated account's recorded act, never another person's review: its approval is not an approval here, and its request for changes does not stand against another person's approval. A complete bounded event record with no dismissal, revocation or later request for changes establishes no recorded withdrawal within that boundary. A latest-state snapshot alone does not establish complete historical event coverage. Merging with a standing approval and no standing request for changes is the practice; merging with none, or over a standing request for changes, is the lapse. Judge the decisions as recorded, never whether the review was thorough — that belongs to the review practices. That the author presses the merge button on their own pull request is the ordinary course in most teams and is never the lapse here; the only lapse is merging without another person's standing approval. The subject is the person who merged, whether or not that person authored the change.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when: the pull request is not merged; or the repository plainly works without review — no reviewer was requested, no review decision or review thread exists on this pull request, and the inventory shows a single-person project. A pull request with a reviewer requested, a review decision or a review comment is the applicability; a decision marked `bot` is still a review decision for this gate.

## Sources
1. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): `merged_at`, `merged_by`, `author`. It establishes who merged and when. When `merged_by` is absent, record no result: the review cannot name the merger. A different recorded merger is still the subject.
2. The review decisions (`context/review_threads.json`, `reviewDecisions` oldest first: `state`, `author`, `submittedAt`, `body` when one was written, `dismissed`) and the threads: each captured decision with its author and time. `decisionHistoryComplete` is `false`, since a decision withdrawn or replaced earlier may be missing. `submittedAt` is the decision event time, absent when unknown. On GitLab, a native approval date is recovered from a standing approval after merge; a native date before `merged_at` is therefore a positive witness that the approval stood at merge. Last-known rows alone do not establish current review readiness when `metadata.json` omits `review_decision`. Do not erase a sufficient historical witness merely because current readiness later became unknown. The record's silence about a withdrawal never proves that none happened. A current `DISMISSED` state or `dismissed` flag with no withdrawal time establishes only the state at capture, not whether dismissal preceded merge. A dismissal withdraws only the decision of the reviewer it belongs to. On GitHub, a dismissed review keeps its original state beside `dismissed`; a `DISMISSED` state alone leaves that original state unknown. On GitLab, the sync records `DISMISSED` only on an approval row, never on a request for changes. A `truncated` record is a collection gap for this practice. The leads from the practice script below these criteria list the merge and one row per decision with `beforeMerge`, `isAuthor`, `dismissed` and `bot` computed, and each reviewer's last captured decision apart: decide from the rows, and quote the decision and the merge from the record.
3. The inventory (`context/project_inventory.json`): whether other people work in this project, for the applicability only.
If `merged_at` or the decisions are unavailable, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context, reviewer by reviewer: first whether another person's approval stood at merge, then whether another person's request for changes stood or may have stood at merge. Each reviewer's own rows decide that reviewer's standing: one reviewer's dismissal, withdrawal or unknown time never unsettles another reviewer's confirmed approval, and `decisionHistoryComplete: false` alone neither withdraws a confirmed approval nor stands for a request for changes.
- MET: at least one confirmed standing APPROVED decision by another person — a login other than the author's, not marked `bot` — submitted before `merged_at`, with no later dismissal, revocation or request for changes by that reviewer, and no captured request for changes by another person that stood or may have stood at merge. An approval marked `bot` never makes this cell. Who pressed merge does not enter into it. Quote the approval and the merge time.
- NOT_MET: evidence that covers the merge moment establishes no qualifying approval, or establishes another person's request for changes that still stood at merge. Absence of a human approval in a current snapshot, including a snapshot with only bot approvals, does not establish absence at merge when historical coverage is incomplete. Quote the merge time and the evidence that settles the state at that moment. History the record does not hold never decides this cell.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the captured record cannot settle a deciding event's order or standing membership at merge. When no approval by another person is confirmed as standing, this includes an approval by another person that is undated, dated after `merged_at` or dismissed with no dated withdrawal — an earlier approval may have stood at the merge and been replaced since — and absent human approvals with incomplete historical coverage: a previously standing human approval may have been withdrawn after merge. Even beside a confirmed approval, it includes another person's captured request for changes, or a dismissed decision whose original state is unknown, that may have stood at merge because the record cannot settle its time or its replacement. Current review readiness and historical approval-at-merge are separate facts. An original review submission timestamp does not date a later withdrawal. A truncated required record is a collection gap, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: merged with no approval where a reviewer was requested and had not answered. MAJOR: merged over a standing request for changes, or after an approval was dismissed and not renewed. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote `merged_at`, `merged_by` and each decision as recorded with its `author`, `state` and `submittedAt`. Identity is the login as recorded, compared as text: the same login is the same account. Whether an account is automated is the captured `bot` marker, never the login's shape or a display name; a decision without the marker counts as its reviewer's own. Never infer that a reviewer is the author from a display name, a repository path or a namespace; never infer an approval from a comment or a thumbs-up; never treat the author's own approval as one.

## Defer
Whether review threads were resolved belongs to `merged-past-unresolved-review-threads`. Here only: did another person approve before the merge?

guidance.whyItMatters: A change merged before anyone approved it skips the one check the team agreed on: a second pair of eyes before the code is everyone's. It is also how a reviewer's outstanding request for changes gets buried. Waiting for the approval, and re-requesting it after a rework, is what keeps the review real.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: The person who merges does so after an approval from someone other than the author that is still current — no later request for changes, no dismissal — and after a rework asks for the approval again before merging.
guidance.goingWell: Nothing merges without a current approval from someone else

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you merge, check that a person other than the author approved the pull request or merge request. Approvals from the author or a bot do not count.
- If you see only a thumbs-up or a “looks good” comment, ask for an approval in the review.
- If an approval was dismissed, or the same reviewer later requested changes, ask for a new approval.
- After you fix a person’s request for changes, ask that reviewer to approve again. For example, instead of merging when your fix passes the tests, wait for their approval.
- Then merge. You can press merge on your own work.

## When it does not apply

- The pull request or merge request did not merge.
- You work alone on the project. Nobody was asked to review this work, and it has no review or review comment.

It still applies when a reviewer was asked, or when someone left a review or a review comment, even a bot.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that the author must not press merge. Authors often merge their own work. Instead, make sure that someone else approved it first.
- Merging on an old approval. An approval that the same reviewer later withdrew by requesting changes, or that someone dismissed, no longer stands. Instead, ask for a new approval after your rework.
- Merging while a person’s request for changes still stands. Another person’s approval does not cancel it. Instead, wait until the reviewer who asked for changes approves. A bot’s request does not block a person’s approval.
- Counting a bot’s approval as a review. A bot is not a second person. Instead, ask a person to approve.

## Sources

- [About protected branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches), GitHub Docs. A protected branch can require approval before merge and dismiss old approvals after changes.
- [Merge request approval settings](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/merge_requests/approvals/settings/), GitLab Docs. A project can stop authors from approving their own merge requests, and remove approvals when you add changes.
- [Code-Review check](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard/blob/main/docs/checks.md#code-review), OpenSSF Scorecard. The check looks for human review before merge and excludes bot reviews.
- [An empirical study of the impact of modern code review practices on software quality](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-015-9381-9), McIntosh, Kamei, Adams and Hassan, 2016. In Qt, VTK and ITK, the share of changes that were reviewed had a significant link with defects after release.

definition.name: Record the plan before the first commit
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned version: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the tracked issue this change implements exists no later than the earliest captured authored commit, without inferring actual work-start or motive.

## The standard
Judge one thing: did the issue this pull request implements exist no later than the first recorded commit? The earliest captured commit author date (`context/commits.json`, `authoredAt`) is the recorded timing proxy. It does not establish when actual work began, and the pull request creation time is a handoff time, not a substitute for it. The issue's opening is its `createdAt` in the linked work item. An issue opened before the first captured commit precedes that recorded step; an issue opened after it follows that step. Neither timing establishes the author's intent or the order of unrecorded work. Judge only the recorded order of the two dates, never the quality of the issue or of the change.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when: no named issue is one this pull request implements — a captured item or one among the `unresolvedReferences` — because the description names none, or rules each out (`Not related to #N`, an aside about other work); or the change is of a kind that answers no issue by convention — a release, a bot dependency update, a revert. Only a candidate issue the leads from the practice script list can be that issue: one captured as this repository's closing candidate (`how: closesOnMerge`, including a link made in the provider's UI), or named by a closing keyword, the title, the branch or the author's own `Related to #N`. One named only by `Related to` counts when the description or the issue shows this change delivers a portion of that issue's work, not when the sentence is about other work. A number the leads do not list is no applicability — a bare `#N`, a `Related to` in a quotation, code or HTML comment, another project's issue. A related issue is captured as a mention, not a closing candidate: never say it closed or will close with this merge. Whether an issue is linked at all belongs to `links-the-change-to-its-issue`; here the linked issue is the applicability.

## Sources
1. The linked work item (`context/linked_work_items/<n>.md`, its opening line `Opened <time>`, and `linked_work_items.json`, `createdAt`): when the issue was opened. It establishes the plan's date.
2. The commits (`context/commits.json`, `authoredAt`): author dates of recorded commits. Require a usable author date for every captured commit and compare the earliest; neither a commit date nor a handoff timestamp substitutes for missing author dates. These dates do not establish actual work-start.
3. The pull request record (`context/metadata.json`): the identity of the reviewed work, never a substitute start time.
4. The leads from the practice script below these criteria: each candidate issue, how it was named, its opening time, the earliest commit's author date and the hours between them, computed; read the two dates from it and check them against the sources above.
Failed or missing required linked-work-item or commit capture is a collection gap and produces no result. Successfully captured records with missing native dates leave the timing COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the issue's `createdAt` is no later than the earliest captured commit's usable `authoredAt`, and every captured commit has a usable author date. Quote both times.
- NOT_MET: the issue's `createdAt` is later than the earliest captured commit's usable `authoredAt`, and every captured commit has a usable author date. Quote both times.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the complete captured commit record is empty or any captured commit has no usable author date, so the timing proxy cannot be established; or the issue this change implements has no opening time here — its number is among the `unresolvedReferences`, so this repository holds no synchronized issue under it, or its linked item carries no `createdAt`. Record as the open question which issue that is and when it was opened, and as what would settle it that issue's opening time in this repository; never claim it exists, predates the work or closes. Or several named issues remain plausible as the one this change implements, their dates fall in different outcomes, and the description and issues do not settle which. Name them; never choose the favourable one.
One result per practice per review, on the issue the change implements; when several plausible issues fall in the same cell, on the one a closing candidate names, else the title, else the branch, else the `Related to`.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MINOR on this alone — non-blocking. Calibrate the nudge to the recorded planning gap and its coordination cost; elapsed time alone does not establish an intention or raise severity.

## Grounding
Cite the linked item's `Opened <time>` line and the reviewed pull request record; cite the earliest usable author date and SHA from the captured `context/commits.json` files. Never infer an order from issue and pull request numbers; never read a commit date where an author date exists.

## Defer
Whether the change names its issue belongs to `links-the-change-to-its-issue`; whether the issue states a checkable outcome belongs to `issue-has-checkable-outcome`. Here only: did the issue exist before the first recorded commit?

guidance.whyItMatters: A tracked issue written before the first recorded commit gives reviewers a prior statement of the work. Commit timestamps provide a recorded ordering, not proof of when someone actually started thinking or coding.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: The tracked issue this change implements has an opening timestamp no later than the earliest captured commit author timestamp. The record names both times without inferring intent or unrecorded work.
guidance.goingWell: The issue exists before the first recorded commit

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before your first commit, open an issue that says what you plan to change. For example, instead of committing a first draft and then filing the issue, file the issue first.
- You can start your branch from the issue page. GitHub and GitLab can both create a branch there.
- Compare the issue’s opening time with the author date of your earliest commit in the change.

![Open the issue and say what you plan. You can then start a branch from the issue page. Your first commit comes after the issue opens.](figures/issue-to-commit.svg)

## When it does not apply

- Your pull request or merge request carries out no issue. You name none, or you say that each named issue is other work, such as “Not related to #12”.
- The change is a release, a dependency update from a bot, or a revert.
- You mention the issue only as a plain number, or only inside a quote, code or a hidden comment.
- The issue belongs to another project.

It still applies when you name the issue only with “Related to” and the change does part of that issue’s work.

## Common mistakes

- Opening the issue just before you open the pull request or merge request. Your first commit counts, not the moment you ask for review. Instead, open the issue before you commit.
- Waiting to open the issue until the plan is complete. Only the order counts here, not the length of the issue. Instead, open a short issue first and add details as you learn.
- Comparing the issue with only the commit that adds its work. Earlier commits in the same change still count. Instead, compare with your earliest commit.

## Sources

- [How to contribute to open source](https://opensource.guide/how-to-contribute/), GitHub Open Source Guides. Before you work on a large contribution, open an issue to ask about it.
- [Merge requests workflow](https://docs.gitlab.com/development/contributing/merge_request_workflow/), GitLab Docs. For a new feature idea, GitLab asks contributors to create an issue first, if there is not one already.
- [Creating a branch to work on an issue](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/creating-a-branch-for-an-issue), GitHub Docs. You can create a branch from the issue page, and a pull request from that branch links to the issue.
- [Create a merge request](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/merge_requests/creating_merge_requests/), GitLab Docs. From an issue, you can create a branch and a merge request together, both marked as related to that issue.

definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: selected SwiftUI view code delegates I/O appropriately or uses the framework's supported view-side persistence idiom.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the SwiftUI code the selected code adds: does a `View` type perform I/O itself? I/O in a view is a `URLSession` or `URLRequest` call, `JSONDecoder`/`JSONEncoder` use, `UserDefaults` or `FileManager` access, `Data(contentsOf:)`, a Core Data fetch request, or a `fetch`/`load`/`save` implemented inside a `struct … : View` — in `body`, a modifier closure (`.task`, `.onAppear`, a button action) or a method of the view. A view that calls a model's method (`store.load()`, `viewModel.save(item)`) or passes a `Binding` is not performing I/O, and the framework's own view-side storage — SwiftData's `@Query` and `modelContext.insert`/`delete` through `@Environment(\.modelContext)`, Core Data's `@FetchRequest`, and SwiftUI's `@AppStorage` and `@SceneStorage` — is the framework's designed use of a view, not I/O the view took on. The judgement is about where the work lives, never about the architecture's name.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge all code inside SwiftUI view types in this file. Preserve model calls and framework-designed view storage. A file with no code inside a view type does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added lines and the type each hunk lies in, read from the hunk header and the surrounding declaration. It establishes which added lines are inside a view type and which call I/O. It never establishes what unchanged code does.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the enclosing type of a hunk when the diff context does not show it, and whether a called method belongs to a model or store. Read it only to place a line; it never adds an I/O call the diff does not show.
3. The leads from the practice script below these criteria: the I/O calls it found inside view types, as leads to inspect, never as conclusions.
If the diff of a Swift file is truncated where a view type is edited, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Scan the selected lines inside view types first, then assess the standard.
The undesirable behaviour is I/O inside a view. Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- NOT_MET: an added line inside a view type performs I/O itself — a `URLSession`/`URLRequest` call, `JSONDecoder`, `UserDefaults`, `FileManager`, `Data(contentsOf:)`, a direct Core Data fetch or an inline fetch-and-parse. Framework view-side storage named above is not direct I/O. Quote the line and name the view type.
- MET: a complete bounded review of the added view code shows no direct I/O outside the supported framework view-side storage named above. The view may need no I/O at all, or it delegates required I/O to a model, store or service. Cite the added view code and its enclosing declaration; quote a delegating call only when one exists.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the hunk shows the call but neither the context nor the checkout shows whether the enclosing type is a view; name the declaration that would settle it.
One result per practice per review, on each distinct proved problem.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one read (`UserDefaults`, a decode) inside a view, or I/O in a small preview-only or prototype view. MAJOR: a network request or a persistence write implemented inside a shipped view, or the same I/O repeated in several views. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` added line that performs the I/O and the `struct … : View` declaration it lies in, For MET, cite the added view code and its enclosing declaration, and record the diff as the source searched: every added line inside a view type was read. Include a delegating call when relevant. Never claim I/O from a method name alone (`load()` may be a model call); never claim a type is a view without its declaration; never count the supported framework view-side storage named above as direct I/O.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Duplicated logic across views belongs to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; oversized view bodies to `keeps-functions-small-and-single-purpose`. Here only: does the view do I/O itself?

guidance.whyItMatters: A SwiftUI view that fetches, decodes or saves is a view nobody can preview, test or reuse, and its logic is invisible to the next screen that needs the same data. Keeping that work in a model or store is what lets the view stay a description of the screen.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Views describe the screen from state they are handed; requests, decoding and file or preference access live in a model, store or service the view talks to through a method or a binding, and SwiftData is used through its own view-side idiom.
guidance.goingWell: Views render the state they are handed and never fetch or persist

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Put I/O in a model, a store or a service. I/O means reading or writing data, such as network requests, decoding, and file or `UserDefaults` access. The view calls a method or passes a binding. A binding lets the view read and change data that another type owns.
- Start the work from a modifier by calling the model. For example, instead of calling `URLSession` in a view’s `.task`, write `.task { await store.load() }` and keep the request in the store.
- In a button action, call a method of the model, such as `viewModel.save(item)`. The action does not encode the item or write the file.
- Hand the view the state it shows, such as the loaded items. Then a preview or a test can pass in sample state, with no network and no disk.
- Use the framework’s own view-side storage in the view. It is `@Query`, `@FetchRequest`, `modelContext.insert` and `delete` through `@Environment(\.modelContext)`, `@AppStorage` and `@SceneStorage`.

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds no line inside a SwiftUI view type: a `struct` that conforms to `View`, or a computed property that returns `some View`.
- Your change touches only models, services, tests or files that are not Swift.

It still applies when the lines you add to a view do no I/O.

## Common mistakes

- Looking for one architecture, such as a view model for each screen. The practice asks only where the work runs. Instead, check that any request or write runs outside the view, in whatever model, store or service you already have.
- Moving `@Query`, `@FetchRequest`, `@AppStorage` or `@SceneStorage` out of a view to follow this practice. They are the framework’s own way for a view to read and store data. Instead, keep them in the view.
- Moving the request into a private method of the view, such as `fetchItems()`. The method is still part of the view. Instead, move it to the model and call it from the view.
- Reading `UserDefaults` or calling `FileManager` in a view for one value. Instead, use `@AppStorage` for a setting, or let the model read the value.

## Sources

- [Managing model data in your app](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/managing-model-data-in-your-app), Apple. A data model keeps the data apart from the views that show it, which makes the app easier to test.
- [Data Essentials in SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2020/10040/), Apple, 2020. A separate model handles storage, syncing and side effects, while a view’s `body` only describes the screen.
- [SwiftData](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftdata), Apple. SwiftData provides `Query` for stored models, and a view reaches the model context through its environment.

definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: each piece of SwiftUI state declared where it is owned — view-local values as `@State`, shared models observed and injected, edits through `Binding`, derived values computed rather than stored.

## The standard
Judge the state declarations the selected code adds to SwiftUI views against four rules. (1) A value one view owns and mutates is `@State` (or `@AppStorage` for a persisted setting); a `let` or plain `var` that the view mutates is a lapse. (2) A model shared by more than one view is one object: `@Observable` (or `ObservableObject`) created once by its owner and reached through `@Environment`, `@Bindable` or a passed reference — a child view that creates its own instance of a shared model (`@State private var store = Store()` in a child, `StateObject` for a model the parent already holds) is a lapse. (3) A child that edits a parent's value takes a `Binding` (`@Binding`, `$value`), not a copy it mutates. (4) A value derivable from other state (a count, a filtered list, a formatted string) is a computed property, not a second stored variable kept in sync by hand. Judge declarations and how they are wired, never naming or file layout.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every SwiftUI state declaration and state connection in this file against the same four standards. Read parent and model definitions when needed. A file with no applicable declaration or connection does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added declarations and the wiring that hands state between views (`init` arguments, `.environment(…)`, `$` bindings). It establishes what was declared where. It never establishes what unchanged views hold.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether a model type is `@Observable`, whether a parent already owns an instance a child recreates, and whether a stored value is derivable from other declared state. Read it to place a declaration; it never adds a declaration the diff does not show.
3. The leads from the practice script below these criteria: the declarations it found inside view types, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view's declarations are edited, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Enumerate the added state declarations first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added declaration follows the four rules — local values `@State`, shared models observed once and injected, edits through bindings, derived values computed. Quote the declaration you accepted as the representative.
- NOT_MET: a declaration breaks a rule — a mutable stored property in a view without `@State`; a child creating a second instance of a model the parent owns; a copied value the child mutates where a `Binding` was needed; a stored value kept in sync by hand with the state it derives from. Quote the declaration and name the rule.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: whether a model is shared or owned by this view alone cannot be told from the diff and the checkout; name the type and the fact that would settle it.
One result per practice per review, on each distinct proved problem.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a derived value stored, or a mutable `var` that should be `@State` in a leaf view. MAJOR: a shared model recreated in a child (state that silently resets or diverges), or a copied value edited where the parent's value was meant to change. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` declaration and, for a shared-model lapse, the parent's declaration of the same model. Never claim a model is shared without a second view that holds it; never claim a value is derivable without naming the state it derives from.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
I/O inside views belongs to `keeps-views-free-of-networking-and-persistence`; concurrency belongs to `uses-structured-concurrency-safely`. Here only: is the state declared where it is owned?

guidance.whyItMatters: State declared in the wrong place is the root of the bugs that make SwiftUI feel unpredictable: a model recreated on every render, a value copied into two views that drift apart, a derived value stored and forgotten. Declaring each piece of state where it is owned keeps the screen a function of its data.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Value state a single view owns is `@State`; a shared model is `@Observable` and injected through the environment or passed down, never recreated in a child; a child that edits a parent's value takes a `Binding`; a derived value is computed, not stored.
guidance.goingWell: Each piece of state lives at the level that owns it

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Identify the view that owns each piece of state that your change adds.
- Use `@State private var` for a value that one view owns and changes, or `@AppStorage` for a setting that must persist.
- Create a shared model once, in its owner. Pass it to children as an argument or through the environment.
- When a child changes its parent’s value, give the child a binding. For example, instead of `@State var isOn` in a toggle row, use `@Binding var isOn` and pass `$isOn` from the parent.
- When a value comes from other state, such as a count or a filtered list, make it a computed property.

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds no state to a SwiftUI view, and no wiring that hands state from one view to another. It adds no `@State`, `@Binding`, `@Environment`, `@Bindable`, `@AppStorage`, `@Observable`, `ObservableObject`, `StateObject` or `ObservedObject`, and no `var` that a view changes.
- Your change only alters the layout of a view.

## Common mistakes

- Looking at names or at the file a view is in. Neither decides where state belongs. Instead, look at where each value is declared and how it reaches other views.
- Creating a shared model again in a child, such as `@State private var store = Store()` in a row. The row then has its own store, which can reset or differ from the parent’s. Instead, pass the parent’s store in, or read it with `@Environment`.
- Copying a parent’s value into the child’s own `@State` and editing the copy. The parent never sees the edit. Instead, take a `@Binding`.
- Keeping a count in its own `@State` and updating it by hand. One missed update leaves a wrong number on the screen. Instead, compute the count from the list.

## Sources

- [Managing user interface state](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/managing-user-interface-state), Apple. Store shared state in the closest common parent of the views that need it, as one source of truth.
- [State](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/state), Apple. Private state in the highest view that needs it reaches editable children through a `Binding`.
- [Managing model data in your app](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/managing-model-data-in-your-app), Apple. Create an observable model once with `@State`, then pass it down or add it to the environment.
- [Data flow through SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2019/226/), Apple, WWDC 2019. One source of truth avoids the bugs that come from copies that you keep in sync by hand.

definition.name: Make the UI accessible by default

appliesWhen.otherwise: the change touches no Swift source file

definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the selected SwiftUI interface is usable with a screen reader and at large text sizes — icon-only controls and meaningful images labelled, text sized semantically, layout free of size caps that clip.

## The standard
Judge the interface code the selected code adds against a closed list of accessibility facts. (1) An icon-only control — a `Button`, `Toggle`, `Link` or tappable `Image` whose visible content is an `Image(systemName:)` or an asset image with no text — carries an `accessibilityLabel` (or a `Label` with a text title). (2) An image that carries information carries a label. Judge its role in the accessibility element it belongs to: an image whose information that element's text already gives — artwork beside the title it shows, in a container read as one element by `.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)` — adds nothing for a screen-reader user and is correctly hidden with `.accessibilityHidden(true)`; a label would repeat the text. An image used only for decoration, with no relevant information to convey, may also be hidden. An image that conveys relevant information absent from its accessible text is informative, whatever its source. (3) Text, and an SF Symbol shown with it, use a semantic font (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, `.title2`, …) or a scaled custom font, not `.font(.system(size: 14))` or a fixed-size custom font — a symbol sized in points stays small when the text around it grows. (4) No text container is capped in height (`.frame(height:)`, `.lineLimit(1)` on body copy) in a way that clips at larger text. (5) A state shown by colour alone (red for error, green for done) is also shown by text, an icon or a trait. Judge selected lines only; an existing lapse the change did not touch is not the selected code's.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every applicable control, image, font, layout cap, and color-only state in this file. Read complete modifier chains. A file with no applicable interface code does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added interface lines and the modifiers attached to them in the same expression. It establishes what each control and text carries. A modifier on the same view chain counts; one on a distant ancestor does not establish a label for an inner icon.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the element an image belongs to and the text it holds, which settle whether the image is decorative or informative, and which font overload a custom font uses: `.custom(_:size:)` scales with the body style, `.custom(_:size:relativeTo:)` scales with the style it names, and only `.custom(_:fixedSize:)` stays fixed. Read it to classify; it never adds a control the diff does not show.
3. The leads from the practice script below these criteria: the icon-only controls, fixed-size fonts and height caps it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a view body is edited, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Enumerate the selected controls, images and text first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added icon-only control and informative image is labelled, added text uses a semantic or scaling font, no added cap clips text, and no added state relies on colour alone. Quote a representative labelled control or scaling font.
- NOT_MET: at least one added item breaks the list — an unlabelled icon-only control, an informative image left unlabelled or hidden, a fixed-size font, a clipping cap, a colour-only state. Quote the line and name the rule.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: an image whose informative or decorative role the checkout does not settle; name the asset.
One result per practice per review, on each distinct proved problem. count the rest in the summary.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one unlabelled icon or one fixed-size font. MAJOR: a primary action of the screen unreachable by screen reader, or a screen whose main text cannot scale. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` line of the control, image, font or cap. Never claim a label is missing without reading the whole view chain the control sits in; never call an image informative without naming what it shows that no text in its element gives; never claim clipping from a `.frame` on a non-text container.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Localisation of the strings belongs to no practice here; magic numbers in layout to none. Here only: can everyone use what was added?

guidance.whyItMatters: A control a screen reader cannot name, a label that cannot grow with the user's text size, an image that says nothing — each locks a group of people out of the screen, and each is a line the author could have written when the view was made. Accessibility added later is the expensive kind.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Every icon-only control and meaningful image has a label; text uses semantic fonts so Dynamic Type works; nothing is fixed to a size that clips at larger text; colour is never the only way to convey a distinction.
guidance.goingWell: Every control carries a label and text scales with the user

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Give each control that shows only an icon a label that says what it does. For example, instead of a button that holds only `Image(systemName: "trash")`, add `.accessibilityLabel("Delete")` to it, or use `Label("Delete", systemImage: "trash")`.
- Label an image that carries information that the nearby text does not give.
- Use `.accessibilityHidden(true)` for an image that only decorates, or whose meaning the text already gives.
- Use a text style, such as `.font(.body)` or `.font(.headline)`, for text and for any SF Symbol beside it. SF Symbols are Apple’s built-in icons. A text style grows with the text size that the person chooses.
- Leave room for text to grow. A `.frame(height:)` or `.lineLimit(1)` on body text is a problem only when it cuts the text off at larger sizes.
- When color shows a state, such as red for an error, also show the state with text or an icon.

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds no interface code to a SwiftUI view. It adds no `Image`, `Button`, `Toggle`, `Text` or `Label`. It adds no `.font(` or `.frame(` line, and no state shown by color.

It still applies when every interface line you add already follows this practice.

## Common mistakes

- Treating every `.frame(height:)` as a problem. A fixed height on an image or a shape is fine. Only a height cap on text can clip it at a larger text size.
- Putting `.accessibilityLabel` on a stack around a row of icon buttons. That label does not name the icons inside it. Instead, put a label on each control.
- Sizing an SF Symbol in points, such as `.font(.system(size: 14))`, next to text that scales. The symbol stays small when the text grows. Instead, give it the text style of the text.
- Choosing `.custom(_:fixedSize:)` for a custom font. It is the only custom font call that never grows. Instead, use `.custom(_:size:relativeTo:)` with the text style that the text replaces.

## Sources

- [VoiceOver](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover), Apple Human Interface Guidelines. Give every key control a label, describe meaningful images, and hide images that only decorate.
- [Typography: Supporting Dynamic Type](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography#Supporting-Dynamic-Type), Apple Human Interface Guidelines. Layouts adapt to every text size, icons grow with the text, and text truncation stays to a minimum.
- [Applying custom fonts to text](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/applying-custom-fonts-to-text), Apple SwiftUI documentation. A custom font from `custom(_:size:)` scales with the body style, and `relativeTo` picks the style to scale with.
- [Accessibility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility), Apple Human Interface Guidelines. Convey information with more than color alone, and let people enlarge the text.

definition.name: Use structured concurrency safely

appliesWhen.otherwise: the change touches no Swift source file

definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: async work tied to the lifetime that owns it, UI state mutated on the main actor, and no fire-and-forget task where structure was available.

## The standard
Judge the concurrency code the selected code adds against a closed list. (1) View-lifecycle work belongs in `.task { }` or an equivalent observed cancellation lifecycle. A `Task { }` in a synchronous button action is a native bridge to asynchronous work, not a defect by itself. Judge whether its lifetime and cancellation fit the operation: work that must stop with the view has an effective cancellation path, while a user-initiated operation can legitimately complete after the view disappears. A stored handle or a written reason can establish intent but is not mandatory when the captured code already establishes the lifecycle. (2) State the UI reads is mutated on the main actor: a type that holds view state is isolated to the main actor — by `@MainActor`, by the target's default actor isolation or by what it inherits, including SwiftUI `View` when the project's SDK declares it main-actor isolated — or the mutation is `await MainActor.run`; a mutation of `@Published`/`@Observable` UI state from a background context is a lapse. (3) Detached work and delivery queues have an evidenced need for their independent execution or scheduling; the captured code may establish that need without a redundant comment. (4) A result needed by the operation is consumed; a task can perform a side effect without its handle being stored. Judge selected lines; existing concurrency the change did not touch is not the selected code's.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every concurrency construct in this file. Read the effective isolation and cancellation contract. A file with no concurrency construct does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: the added concurrency constructs and where they sit (a view modifier, a model method, a service). It establishes what was written. It never establishes the actor a type is isolated to when that declaration is outside the diff.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the declaration of the type a mutation lands in and the target's default actor isolation, and whether a `Task` handle is stored. Read it to place a construct; it never adds one.
3. The leads from the practice script below these criteria: the `Task {` blocks, `.onAppear` with async work, detached tasks and delivery queues it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where async code is added, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Enumerate the selected constructs first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added construct follows the list — view-lifecycle work cancelled appropriately, user-triggered async work with an appropriate lifetime, UI state isolated correctly, and needed results consumed. Quote a representative construct.
- NOT_MET: an added construct breaks the list — view-lifecycle work that can outlive its owner without appropriate cancellation, UI state mutated off the main actor, detached work or a delivery queue with no evidenced need, an unconsumed result needed by the operation. Quote the line and name the rule.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: an added line mutates UI state from an async context and the isolation of its type is in neither the diff nor the checkout; name the type. An added call into an unchanged method is judged as a call, never by what that method does inside.
One result per practice per review, on each distinct proved problem.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a lifecycle mismatch on a short local operation. MAJOR: a network request in an uncancelled task that writes view state, or UI state mutated from a background context. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` construct and, for an actor lapse, the declaration of the type mutated. Never claim a mutation is off the main actor without the type's isolation; never claim a task is fire-and-forget when a handle is stored in the same hunk.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Swallowed errors in async code belong to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; crash-shaped constructs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`. Here only: is the concurrency structured?

guidance.whyItMatters: An unstructured task that outlives its view, UI state mutated off the main actor, a fire-and-forget request that cannot be cancelled — these are the crashes and stale screens that appear only on a slow network. Swift's structured concurrency prevents them when it is used the way it is designed.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: View-lifecycle work runs in `.task` or another effective cancellation lifecycle. A synchronous user action can start a Task whose lifetime fits the operation; UI state stays correctly isolated and needed results or failures are handled.
guidance.goingWell: Async work is scoped to its view and cancelled with it
