guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Start the work that a screen needs in `.task` on its view. SwiftUI cancels that task when the view goes away. For example, instead of `.onAppear { Task { await model.load() } }`, write `.task { await model.load() }`.
- Match the lifetime of a button-started task to its operation. A `Task { }` in the button action is a valid way to start it. Work that must stop with the screen needs a way to be canceled. A save that the user asked for can finish after the screen closes.
- Keep changes to view state on the main actor. The model can already have this protection by inheritance or through the target’s default isolation. Otherwise, mark the model `@MainActor` or use `await MainActor.run`.
- Use `Task.detached` or a `DispatchQueue` only when the work must run apart from its caller. Otherwise, use `async let` or a task group, so cancellation reaches the work.
- If your code needs the result of a task, await the task’s value and use it.

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds no concurrency code to Swift files. That means no new `async`, `await`, `Task`, `.task`, `@MainActor`, `MainActor.run`, `Task.detached`, `DispatchQueue` or actor declaration. Concurrency code that your change does not touch does not count.

## Common mistakes

- Treating every `Task { }` as a bug. A task in a button action is the usual way to start async work. Not every task needs a stored handle or a comment. Instead, check that the lifetime of each task fits its work.
- Setting a `@Published` property from a background queue or a detached task. SwiftUI can miss the change, and the screen shows old data. Instead, keep the model on the main actor and `await` the slow work.
- Moving work into `Task.detached` to keep it off the main thread. The detached task drops its actor and the cancellation of its caller. Instead, `await` the slow call. The main actor stays free while it waits.

## Sources

- [Concurrency](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/concurrency/), The Swift Programming Language, Swift project. Child tasks inherit cancellation from their parent, while you manage each unstructured task yourself.
- [`task(name:priority:file:line:_:)`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/view/task(name:priority:file:line:_:)), SwiftUI documentation, Apple. SwiftUI cancels a view’s task if the view goes away before the task finishes.
- [Discover concurrency in SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2021/10019/), Apple, WWDC 2021. Use `.task` to tie work to a view, and change an observable object only on the main actor.
- [`Task.detached`](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swift/task/detached(name:priority:operation:)-795w1), Swift standard library documentation, Apple. Use a detached task only when child tasks cannot do the work, and handle its cancellation yourself.

definition.name: Ship a preview with each new view

appliesWhen.otherwise: the change touches no Swift source file

definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the new SwiftUI presentation a change adds arriving with a `#Preview` (or `PreviewProvider`) that shows it with known representative sample data for whatever it shows from variable data, and its important states.

## The standard
Judge one thing: when this change adds new SwiftUI view types, can the presentation they add be seen in a preview from the same change? A preview is a `#Preview` block or a `PreviewProvider`. It covers a view it constructs, and a view that a host it constructs demonstrably renders: a new row, badge or section shown through a previewed host's body is covered by that preview. Where the presentation shows variable data or state, the preview is representative when the source establishes known, meaningful values of the shape the presentation shows (a filled model, a non-empty list with varied entries) and you trace them into that presentation. Where those values live does not decide it: the preview may pass them, a sample helper may build them, or the previewed view or its owner may hold them as in-memory literals; no preview needs an initializer or injection only to receive values the source already establishes. A default expression alone is not a sample: an empty list, a placeholder model, a value whose content you cannot read, or an `@AppStorage` or other persisted default, which leaves what is stored unknown, establishes nothing representative, and neither does a fresh or live view model; a live fetch inside a preview is not sample data. Such a preview exists but is not representative. Fixed presentation — a view whose body shows only constant content — needs no sample: a preview that constructs it covers it. It is complete when presentation that has an empty, loading or error state is also supplied that state by a preview. A preview supplies a state it demonstrably reaches; trace it as you trace a host. A default-constructed view or model reaches the state its initial value and the work it starts lead to — an idle prompt before any input, for example — so default construction neither proves nor disproves a state until you trace it, and it supplies no sample for variable data. A state a preview only passes through, such as loading on the way to results, is not supplied; a preview supplies it by holding it, for example by giving the content view that state. A view that only owns lifecycle or effects — starting and cancelling work, holding the model — and passes everything it shows to a content view adds no presentation of its own: representative previews of that content view cover it, and it needs no new initializer, injection or architecture just so a preview can construct it. What such a wrapper renders itself — a navigation title, a toolbar, an overlay, other chrome, or a state the content view never receives — is its own presentation, and a preview must show it. A preview for an existing view the change edits is welcome but not required. Judge coverage and representativeness, never layout, naming, or which type a `#Preview` names.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no new view type: no added `struct … : View` declaration in a non-test file. An edit to an existing view, a model-only change or a preview-only change carries no surface.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): the added `struct … : View` declarations and the `#Preview`/`PreviewProvider` blocks in the same change. It establishes which new views a preview constructs and which sample values and states it supplies.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): a preview that lives in another file of the same change, sample-data helpers it uses, the body of a host it constructs, and the body of a new owner view. Read it to find the preview, to establish that a host renders a new view with the data the preview supplies, and to establish that an owner passes everything it shows to a previewed content view; it never supplies a preview the change did not add.
3. The leads from the practice script below these criteria: the new view types and the previews it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where a new view is declared, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Enumerate the new view types first — every added `struct … : View`, `private` and file-scoped ones included — and for each name the presentation it adds and the preview that covers it. A view is covered by a preview that constructs it; a nested view, by a preview that constructs a host whose body you read renders it with that preview's data; an effect-only owner, by tracing its body to the content view it passes everything to and naming that content's previews, while any chrome or state the owner renders itself still needs a preview that shows it. Never assume a host renders a view you did not trace; a helper's smallness goes to the severity, not to the outcome. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: every new view's presentation is covered by a preview in the same change that supplies representative sample data for any variable data it shows, and its important states. Quote the declaration and its covering preview; for a nested view also the host line that renders it, for an effect-only owner the line in its body that delegates to the content view, and for values the view or its owner holds, the lines that hold them.
- NOT_MET: every new view is covered, but a preview supplies presentation that shows variable data nothing representative — only an empty list for a list screen, a placeholder model, or defaults that establish no representative values — or, after you trace the state each preview in the change reaches, supplies no preview with a state the view plainly has. Quote the preview and name what it lacks.
- NOT_MET: at least one new view's presentation is covered by no preview in the change — presentation no preview covers, or a wrapper's own chrome or state that no preview shows — after scanning every Swift file in the diff. Quote the declaration and say what you scanned.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: a preview exists in the checkout but the diff does not show whether this change added it, or whether a host renders the new view, or an owner only delegates, cannot be read; name the file.
One result per practice per review, on the single most consequential view when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MINOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR: a new view with no preview or with an unrepresentative one. TRIVIAL: a small portion of covered presentation left out — a row's alternate state, a wrapper's toolbar button — while the main presentation is previewed. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` `struct … : View` declaration and the covering `#Preview` line — with the host line that renders a nested view, or the owner's line that delegates to its previewed content view — or for absent the declaration and the scan. The source is static: tracing what a host's body renders reads its declaration, never shows that a preview was run, rendered or compiles, and a declared `@AppStorage` or other persisted default leaves what is actually stored or shown unknown. Never claim a host covers a view, or an owner only delegates, without quoting the line in its body that shows it.

## Defer
How to verify the change as a whole belongs to `states-how-to-verify-the-change`; tests for logic to `ships-tests-with-the-change`. Here only: can the new screen be seen?

guidance.whyItMatters: A SwiftUI view without a preview is a screen nobody can see without running the whole app to it, and the first thing the next person deletes when it breaks. A preview with representative data is the cheapest verification a view can have, and the way a reviewer sees what changed.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: The new screens and presentation a change adds can be seen in a `#Preview` with representative sample data — including an empty, loading or error state when they have one — so they can be checked without launching the app.
guidance.goingWell: New views ship with previews that show what they present

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Cover the presentation of each new SwiftUI view with a `#Preview` or a `PreviewProvider` in the same change. A preview of a host view counts when it shows that presentation.
- When the view shows variable data, supply known values that match what it shows. For example, instead of `TaskList(tasks: [])`, pass tasks with varied titles.
- Take the sample values from the preview, a sample helper, or fixed values that the view or its owner holds. A live fetch does not give sample data.
- Preview each empty, loading or error state that the new presentation supports.
- Some new views only start work and hold the model, and pass all that they show to a content view. Preview what the outer view draws itself, such as a navigation title, a toolbar or an overlay. Previews of the content view cover the rest.

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds no new SwiftUI view. It declares no new `struct … : View` outside test files.
- Your change only edits a view that already exists.
- Your change only touches models or other code that is not a view.
- Your change only adds or edits previews.

It still applies when the new view is `private` or used only inside one file.

## Common mistakes

- Using only an empty list or a placeholder to preview a view that shows variable data. The preview exists, but it shows nothing that you can check. Instead, give it varied values that look like real data.
- Relying on a fresh or live view model, or on a stored value such as `@AppStorage`, for the data. Nobody knows what the preview then shows. Instead, give the preview known sample values.
- Adding a new row or section to a screen and counting on the screen’s preview. That preview covers the new view only when the screen really draws it with the preview’s data. Instead, check that it does, or preview the new view on its own.

## Sources

- [Adding previews to your interface files](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/xcode/adding-previews-to-your-interface-files), Apple Developer Documentation. A preview shows a view without running the app, and it can use sample data kept apart from the app.
- [Build programmatic UI with Xcode Previews](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2023/10252/), Kevin Cathey, Apple, WWDC 2023. A preview sets up data and passes it into the view, and it runs the real code of your project.
- [What to look for in a code review](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html), Google Engineering Practices. A user interface change is hard to judge from its code alone, so a reviewer can ask to see it.

definition.name: Declare permissions truthfully and ask at the point of use

appliesWhen.otherwise: the change touches no Swift source file

definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Leads from a practice script are starting points to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a capability that needs the user's permission arriving with a truthful usage description and a request made where the feature needs it.

## The standard
Judge the permission-bearing capabilities this change adds against three facts. (1) Declaration: when the platform requires usage-description keys for the access actually requested, the matching keys are present in `Info.plist`, `project.yml` or the target's build settings. Determine the keys from the actual authorization API and deployment target, not an import or one fixed key per framework. For example, modern EventKit full or write-only calendar access uses the corresponding `NSCalendarsFullAccessUsageDescription` or `NSCalendarsWriteOnlyAccessUsageDescription`; legacy calendar APIs differ. Notification authorization needs no usage-description key, and the system photo picker needs no full-library authorization. (2) Truth: the description names what the app does with the access, not a placeholder ("needed", "for the app", an empty string). (3) Point of use: the authorization request (`requestWhenInUseAuthorization`, `requestAuthorization`, `PHPhotoLibrary.requestAuthorization`, …) is made from the feature that needs it, not from launch before the feature is reached. A root view can be that feature. Its `onAppear` is not early access when the view presents the feature that needs authorization. Judge added capabilities; an existing one the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no permission-bearing capability: no added permission-requiring access through `CoreLocation`, direct photo-library APIs, `AVFoundation` capture, `UserNotifications`, `EventKit`, `Contacts`, `HealthKit`, `AppTrackingTransparency` or an authorization request. `SwiftUI`'s `PhotosPicker` or `PHPickerViewController` alone needs no full-library permission and is not the applicability; an import alone does not establish restricted access.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with the file list (`work/change/files.json`): the added capability code, authorization requests, and usage-description keys in `Info.plist`, `project.yml` or `*.pbxproj`. It establishes what was added where. It never establishes what the app already declared.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the existing `Info.plist`/`project.yml` for a key the change relies on but did not add, and the call site of the request. Read it to complete the picture; a key present there satisfies the declaration.
3. The leads from the practice script below these criteria: the permission-related references, requests and usage keys it found, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where the capability is added, or the project's plist is unreadable, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Enumerate the added capabilities first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added permission-requiring capability has a truthful usage key when required (in the change or checkout), and authorization is requested at the point of use. Quote the required key and request, or name the platform exemption.
- NOT_MET: the key is present but the description is a placeholder, or the request runs before the feature that needs it is reached. Quote the description or the request site.
- NOT_MET: an added capability requires a usage key but has none anywhere in the change or the checkout. Quote the capability line and say where you looked.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: the usage keys live in a build setting or generated file the checkout does not carry; name it.
One result per practice per review, on the single most consequential capability when there are several.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a placeholder description, or a request made one screen early. MAJOR: a capability whose required usage key is missing everywhere, so its access cannot be authorized, or a request made at launch for a feature the user has not reached. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` capability or request line and the plist/project key as written. Never claim a key is missing without stating the files scanned; never claim a request site is launch without the call chain that reaches it.

## Defer
Over-broad permissions and insecure defaults belong to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`. Here only: is the permission declared truthfully and asked for at the point of use?

guidance.whyItMatters: Access that requires a usage description cannot be authorized without one. A specific explanation and a request made when the feature needs access help users make an informed choice. The declaration and the request belong to the feature.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: When a change adds a capability that needs the user's permission, the `Info.plist` usage description arrives in the same change, says truthfully what the app does with the access, and the permission is requested where the feature needs it, not at launch.
guidance.goingWell: Permissions say truthfully why and are asked for in use

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- For each access that your change adds, add any missing usage key. The authorization API and the iOS version decide which key.
- Put the key where the project keeps them: in `Info.plist`, in `project.yml`, or in the target’s build settings.
- Write a plain usage description that says what the app does with the access. Instead of “Camera access is needed”, write “Scan receipts to add expenses.”
- Ask for access from the feature that needs it, not at launch.
- Before you add a key, check that the system needs one. Notifications need no usage description.

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds no access that needs the user’s permission. It adds no use of location, the photo library, camera or microphone capture, notifications, calendars, contacts, health data or tracking. It adds no authorization request.
- Your change only adds the system photo picker, such as `PhotosPicker` or `PHPickerViewController`. It needs no access to the whole library.
- Your change only imports a framework. An import alone asks for no access.

It still applies when the first screen is the feature that needs the permission.

## Common mistakes

- Adding one fixed key for each framework that you import. Instead, read which authorization call the code makes and which iOS version the app targets.
- Asking for every permission when the app starts. The user has not reached the feature, so they cannot see why you ask. Instead, move each request to its feature.
- Moving a request away from a first screen that needs the access. If the app opens on a map, asking for location when the map appears is the point of use. Instead, keep the request there.
- Writing a placeholder such as “Needed for the app”, or leaving the text empty. Instead, name the task that the access makes possible, in words the user knows.

## Sources

- [Privacy](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy), Apple Human Interface Guidelines. Ask for access when people use the feature that needs it. Avoid a launch request unless the app needs the access to function.
- [Requesting access to protected resources](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/requesting-access-to-protected-resources), Apple Developer Documentation. The system asks once, and a missing purpose string can crash the app or lead to App Review rejection.
- [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/), Apple, section 5.1.1 (ii). Purpose strings must clearly and completely describe how the app uses the data.
- [Explanation beats context: the effect of timing and rationales on users’ runtime permission decisions](https://group.cispa.io/bugiel/publication/elbitar-usenix-21/elbitar-usenix-21.pdf), Elbitar and others, 2021. In a study with Android mockup apps, requests in context and requests with a reason were each granted more often.

definition.name: Use adaptive colors so every appearance works

appliesWhen.otherwise: the change touches no Swift source file

definition.criteria:
Review the selected code at its pinned commit. On an ITEM review, use the captured change to prove which occurrences it introduces or materially changes. In a SCAN, read every relevant occurrence in the assigned file and use state basis. Context files support this judgment; they are not additional assigned files. Script leads are starting points, never conclusions. A sampled lead list does not narrow the standard. MET requires complete relevant reads and, in a scan, a complete read receipt for the assigned file. Do not claim to have compiled or executed code.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the selected interface takes its colors from colors that resolve per appearance — standard and dynamic system colors, semantic styles, materials, the accent color or asset colors with both appearances — not from literals that hold one value.

## The standard
Judge each color the selected code contains to SwiftUI views by what it resolves to, never by its spelling. A literal holds one value in every appearance: a color built from fixed components (`Color(red:green:blue:)`, `Color(white:)`, `Color(hex:)` or another hex-parsing initializer, `UIColor(red:green:blue:alpha:)`), white or black (`Color.white`, `.black`), a fixed UIKit constant such as `UIColor.green` or `UIColor.gray`, or a color converted from one of these (`Color(uiColor: .green)`), with or without opacity. An adaptive color resolves per appearance: SwiftUI's standard colors, which Apple documents as context-dependent (such as `Color.green` or `.gray` where a `Color` is expected); UIKit's dynamic colors (such as `UIColor.systemGreen`, `UIColor.label`, `UIColor.link`, or one built with `UIColor(dynamicProvider:)`); semantic styles (`.primary`, `.secondary`); materials (`.regularMaterial`); the accent (`.accentColor`, `.tint`); and an asset color whose colorset carries a dark appearance. These are examples of each kind, not complete lists. One spelling can name different types: `.green` passed to `foregroundStyle` is SwiftUI's standard color, while `Color(.green)` converts UIKit's fixed `UIColor.green` unless the app defines an asset of that name. A name the app defines — a `Color` or `UIColor` extension, an asset, a property named like a system color — is whatever its definition says. Read the expression's type and, for the app's own names, the definition or colorset; when neither the diff nor the checkout settles it, the color is unclassified. A literal is not a lapse where the color is the content: text or a symbol over a fill or image the same view sets, a brand color deliberately constant, a shadow or a translucent scrim over an image. Judge the selected lines only.

## On a change
Judge only the occurrences introduced or materially changed by this change. Prove introduced, worsened, or an event duty from captured evidence before returning a problem.

## In a scan
Judge every color expression in SwiftUI views in this file. Read named definitions and colorset appearances. A file with no applicable color expression does not apply. Use state basis and a witness in this assigned file at the pinned commit. Read the full file and relevant permitted context. If a required read fails, withhold the result.

## Sources
For an ITEM, the captured diff bounds the change. For a SCAN, the assigned file and pinned tree establish present state. Shared context is limited to the declared capture.

1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers: each added color expression and the modifier chain it sits in — what it colors (text, background, fill) and what fill the same view sets around it. It establishes the literal and its role. It never establishes an unchanged view's colors.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the asset catalog (`*.xcassets/<name>.colorset/Contents.json`) for a named color's appearances, and a color extension (`Color+App.swift`) a name may resolve to. Read it to classify a name; a `Color("x")` whose colorset has only one appearance is a literal in disguise.
3. The leads from the practice script below these criteria: the added color lines it found, each under the first shape its text shows, and, for each named asset color, whether its colorset has a dark appearance. A shape is spelling, not a type: leads, never conclusions, and a line holding several colors is listed once.
If the diff is truncated where a view body is edited, report a collection gap and record no result.

## Judge
Enumerate the added color expressions first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added color is adaptive, or a literal only where the color is the content. Quote a representative adaptive color or a permitted literal and its content role.
- NOT_MET: an added literal colors text on a system background, a screen or card background, or a fill the rest of the interface adapts around — one appearance baked in. Quote the line and name what it colors.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE: a color the outcome turns on stays unclassified — an asset whose colorset the checkout does not carry, or an app-defined name whose definition it does not show; name it.
One result per practice per review, on each distinct proved problem. count the rest in the summary.


A SCAN judges every applicable occurrence in the assigned file, including unchanged code. List every distinct proved problem within the contract bound. MET requires complete relevant coverage and the assigned file's complete pinned read receipt. Missing required capture withholds the result; it is never a semantic outcome.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one literal text or fill color on a secondary element. MAJOR: a screen or card background, or the primary text of a screen, hard-coded to one appearance. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` color line and, when the role matters, the fill or background line of the same view; for an asset color, the colorset's appearances. Never call a color a literal without its line, nor classify one from its spelling alone; never call an asset or app-defined color adaptive without its colorset or its definition.


For an ITEM problem, prove introduced, worsened, or the captured event duty. For a SCAN problem, use state basis and cite the affected extent in the assigned file at the pinned commit. Context supports that witness and never replaces it.

## Defer
Labels, fonts and colour-only state belong to `makes-ui-accessible-by-default`. Whether a text color reads well against the fill behind it is a contrast question, not this one: an adaptive color adapts even where a pairing reads poorly. Here only: does the color hold in both appearances?

guidance.whyItMatters: A screen built from literal colors is right in one appearance and wrong in the other: white text vanishes on a light background, a hard-coded card stays white in Dark Mode, and every screen has to be revisited when the palette changes. Semantic and asset colors adapt on their own, and the whole app follows one palette.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: Text, backgrounds and fills use colors that adapt — SwiftUI's standard colors such as `.green`, UIKit's dynamic colors such as `UIColor.systemTeal` — semantic colors (`.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`), materials, the accent color or named asset colors with light and dark variants; a literal is used only where the color belongs to the content, such as text over a fill the same view sets.
guidance.goingWell: Colors adapt to light and dark appearance alike

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Color text with a semantic style such as `.primary` or `.secondary`. For example, instead of `.foregroundStyle(.black)`, write `.foregroundStyle(.primary)`.
- Give a screen or a card a system background such as `Color(.systemBackground)`, or a material such as `.regularMaterial`.
- For a highlight, use the accent color with `.tint`, or a standard SwiftUI color such as `.green`. SwiftUI picks its value for the current appearance.
- Use a named asset color whose color set defines both light and dark values.
- Keep a fixed color only where the color is part of the content. One example is text on a fill that the same view sets. A brand color that you keep the same on purpose is another. So is a shadow or a see-through layer over an image.

## When it does not apply

- Your change sets no color in a SwiftUI view. It adds no `.foregroundStyle`, `.foregroundColor`, `.background`, `.fill`, `.tint` or `.shadow(color:)`, and no `Color` or `UIColor` inside a view.

It still applies when every color you add already adapts.

## Common mistakes

- Judging a color by its name. `.green` passed to `foregroundStyle` is SwiftUI’s standard green, and it adapts. `Color(.green)` converts UIKit’s fixed `UIColor.green`, and it does not. Instead, check the type and, for a name that your app defines, its definition or color set. `UIColor.systemGreen` is the adaptive UIKit green.
- Using a color set with only one appearance for an interface color that must adapt. `Color("brand")` then shows the same value in light and dark. Instead, add a dark value to the color set.
- Building an interface color from fixed parts, such as `Color(red:green:blue:)` or a hex value, in a shared extension. Every screen that uses it gets one value. Instead, point the extension at an asset color or a system color.
- Adding opacity to fixed white or black, such as `Color.black.opacity(0.7)`, for text on a system background. It still holds one value. Instead, use a semantic style or an adaptive system color.

## Sources

- [Dark Mode](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/dark-mode), Apple Human Interface Guidelines. Apple recommends system colors that adapt and custom color assets with values for both appearances.
- [Supporting Dark Mode in your interface](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/supporting-dark-mode-in-your-interface), Apple Developer Documentation. Semantic colors and asset variants adapt to appearance changes, while colors built from fixed components do not.
- [Color](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui/color), Apple Developer Documentation for SwiftUI. SwiftUI resolves system and asset colors when it draws, so their values can depend on the appearance.

definition.name: Ask questions a teammate can answer
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured conversation: the turns the practice names, read in their surrounding context. Social chat and acknowledgements create no applicability for an unrelated communication practice. Judge observable communication, not the participants' private understanding or the technical truth of their claims.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a question posed in the captured exchange carries enough context — the goal, what was tried, what happened — for a teammate to answer it in one reply.

## The standard
Judge whether a question raised in this conversation gives a teammate enough to answer it in a single reply, rather than forcing a round of clarifying questions first. A well-formed ask names the concrete goal, what was already tried, and what actually happened or is blocking. A bare "it doesn't work" or "how do I do this?" with no context makes the responder guess. Judge only the observable way the question is posed; never whether the underlying problem is real, hard or worth solving. Use judgment about how much context the question genuinely needs: a quick clarification among people who plainly share the context is not a defect. The review is about the frozen developer in `about.developerId`. Judge only turns whose `accountId` equals that decimal-string id. The other turns are context. Never assign another participant’s words to this developer.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the turn is not actually a question (a statement, an acknowledgement, social chat), or when there is no settled conversation to read. A real question whose needed context is supplied by the surrounding turns is not DOES_NOT_APPLY; it is MET.

## Sources
1. The turn that poses the question (`context/conversation_thread.json`): its stated objective, what was tried, the exact behaviour seen or the specific point of confusion. It establishes how the question is posed. It never establishes whether the problem is real or worth solving.
2. The surrounding turns of the same thread (`context/conversation_thread.json`): earlier turns may supply the context the question leans on; a later reply that has to ask what was meant shows what the responder had to extract first. They establish what context was shared inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether what the question leans on was supplied in a turn you never saw, report a collection gap and record no result; that is neither absent nor COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: a knowledgeable teammate could answer the question from the message alone, or from the message plus the surrounding turns, because it states the objective and the specific point of confusion or the exact behaviour seen. A quick clarification between people who share obvious context belongs here.
- NOT_MET: the question is so thin on context that answering it requires asking the author what they mean, what they tried, or what they expected — and no surrounding turn supplies it. Name the missing element.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE only when every declared turn was captured and the meaning still genuinely admits incompatible readings; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. Having read the whole thread and found the context missing is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE. A thread that begins mid-conversation is a collection gap, not a result.
One result per practice per review, on the question turn you assessed.

## Severity
NOT_MET only. Scale to how much a responder must extract before they can help. MINOR, the usual band: a little more detail would sharpen the ask. MAJOR: the question as written cannot be answered without a full exchange of clarifications first. Never above MAJOR on question phrasing alone; this is a formative practice, never a gate.

## Grounding
Quote the exact turn you assessed. For MET where the surrounding turns supply the context, quote those turns too. For NOT_MET, the citations show the question and the boundary you searched: the whole captured thread, with no turn supplying the goal, the attempt or the observed behaviour. Describe the observable gap — "the question names no goal and no attempt" — never laziness or intent. Never invent missing context, grade an exchange you cannot quote, or claim the problem is or is not real.

## Defer
Whether the reply moves the asker forward belongs to `gives-actionable-answers`. Here only: does the question, as posed, let a teammate answer it in one reply?

guidance.whyItMatters: A vague question forces the person helping you to stop and ask what you actually mean before they can even start, turning a one-message answer into a slow exchange. A question that carries its own context gets answered on the first reply.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A question that says what you are trying to do, what you already tried, and exactly where it broke, so a teammate can answer it in a single reply without asking you anything first.
guidance.goingWell: Questions carry the goal, the attempt and the error

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Start with your goal. Say what you are trying to do.
- Say what you already tried and what happened after each try.
- Say exactly what happened, and what you expected. For example, instead of “Why does the build fail?”, write “I’m trying to run the tests on my laptop. After a clean install, `npm test` stops with ‘Cannot find module config’. Reinstalling did not help.”
- Before you send, read your question as a teammate who does not know your work.
- Add what they would have to ask first, unless earlier messages already give it.

## When it does not apply

- Your message is not a question. For example, it is a statement, a thank-you or social chat.
- The conversation has not settled yet, so there is no finished thread to read.

It still applies when your question leans on earlier messages in the same thread. Those messages count, so you do not need to repeat them.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking that every question needs a long background. When you and your teammate clearly share the context, a quick question is fine. Add only what your teammate would otherwise have to ask for.
- Writing only “Help, it’s broken”. Your teammate can only guess what you did. Instead, say what you ran, what you saw and what you expected.
- Sharing an error with no explanation. An error alone does not say what you ran or what you expected. Instead, describe what you ran, what happened and what you expected.
- Pasting your whole program or the whole log. Instead, share just enough code and output for a teammate to see the problem.

## Sources

- [How do I ask a good question?](https://stackoverflow.com/help/how-to-ask), Stack Overflow Help Center. Explain the problem, copy errors as text, and check that someone without your context can understand the question.
- [How to report bugs effectively](https://www.chiark.greenend.org.uk/~sgtatham/bugs.html), Simon Tatham, 1999. Report what you did, what you saw and what you expected to see, so the programmer can help.
- [An empirical study of question discussions on Stack Overflow](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-022-10180-z), Zhu, Zhang, Hassan and Godfrey, 2022. Questions with more comments were answered more slowly, but the study shows a link, not a cause.

definition.name: Give answers people can act on
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured conversation: the turns the practice names, read in their surrounding context. Social chat and acknowledgements create no applicability for an unrelated communication practice. Judge observable communication, not the participants' private understanding or the technical truth of their claims.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: a reply to a question in the captured exchange gives the asker something to act on now — the answer, the exact place to look, or the next step.

## The standard
Judge whether a reply to someone's question actually moves them forward, rather than leaving them where they started. A useful answer either resolves the question directly or names a concrete next step the asker can take. A reply that only restates the problem, points vaguely at "the docs", or answers a different question does not. A short answer can be fully actionable; length does not establish helpfulness. Judge only the observable helpfulness of the reply as written, never whether its technical content is ultimately correct. Use judgment about what the asker needed. The review is about the frozen developer in `about.developerId`. Judge only turns whose `accountId` equals that decimal-string id. The other turns are context. Never assign another participant’s words to this developer.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the turn is not answering a question; when no question was actually asked; when the reply is a reasonable partial step in an ongoing exchange; or when there is no settled conversation to read.

## Sources
1. The question turn (`context/conversation_thread.json`): what was asked and what the asker needed. It establishes the question the reply is measured against. It never establishes whether the problem is real or hard.
2. The reply turn (`context/conversation_thread.json`): the answer given, the place named, the step proposed. It establishes what the asker can do next. It never establishes that the answer is technically right.
3. The surrounding turns (`context/conversation_thread.json`): whether the exchange is still in progress, and whether the answer had already been given elsewhere in the thread. They establish the state of the exchange inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing; judge the reply by its own words. When a real question and its reply are both in front of you but the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the answer had already been given elsewhere in it, report a collection gap and record no result; that is neither absent nor COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the asker could act on the reply immediately because it gives the answer, the specific place to look, or the exact next step.
- NOT_MET: a genuine question was met with a reply that leaves the asker still stuck — too vague to act on, or it sidesteps what was asked. Name what the asker still lacks.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE only when every declared turn was captured and the meaning still genuinely admits incompatible readings; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. Having read the reply and the surrounding turns and found no actionable content is NOT_MET, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE. A thread that begins mid-conversation is a collection gap, not a result.
One result per practice per review, on the question-and-reply pair you assessed.

## Severity
NOT_MET only. Scale to how stuck the asker remains after the reply. MINOR, the usual band: the answer is nearly there and one pointer would land it. MAJOR: a real question is met with a reply that cannot be acted on at all. Never above MAJOR on reply clarity alone; this is a formative practice, never a gate.

## Grounding
Quote the question and the reply you assessed. For NOT_MET, the citations show the question, the reply, and the boundary you searched: the surrounding captured turns, with no other turn supplying the answer. Describe the observable gap — "the reply names no place to look and no step" — never dismissiveness. Never fabricate an answer the reply did not give, and never claim the reply's content is correct or incorrect.

## Defer
Whether the question itself carried enough context to be answerable belongs to `asks-answerable-questions`. Here only: does the reply, as written, let the asker move forward?

guidance.whyItMatters: When someone asks for help, a reply that only gestures at the problem leaves them exactly as stuck as before and burns another round of messages. An answer with a concrete next step lets them get moving right away.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: A reply that either solves the question outright or points to the exact next step or place to look, so the person who asked can act on it immediately instead of asking again.
guidance.goingWell: Answers give the next step, not another question

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Read the question again before you reply.
- Answer what the person asked, not a nearby question that is easier.
- When you know the answer, give it in the reply. A short answer is enough if the person can act on it.
- When the answer is in a document, name the exact page or section and the part that answers the question. Instead of “See the docs”, write “Set `retries` in the deploy config. The Retries section of the deploy guide has an example.”
- When you do not know the answer, name the next step. Say who to ask, or where they can look next.

## When it does not apply

- Your message does not answer a question.
- No one asked a question.
- Your reply is a reasonable partial step in a conversation that is still going on.
- The conversation has not settled yet, so there is no finished exchange to read.

## Common mistakes

- Writing a long reply so that it looks helpful. Length is not what helps. A short reply that gives the answer or the exact step is enough.
- Pointing at “the docs” or a whole wiki. Instead, name the exact section and the part that answers the question.
- Saying the problem back to the person. “That build fails a lot” tells them nothing new. Instead, add one thing they can do about it now.
- Answering a different question from the one they asked. Instead, answer their question first. Then add the other point if it still helps.

## Sources

- [How do I write a good answer?](https://stackoverflow.com/help/how-to-answer), Stack Overflow Help Center. It asks for an answer to the question asked, a thing to try instead, and context around each link.
- [Why and how are some answers deleted?](https://stackoverflow.com/help/deleted-answers), Stack Overflow Help Center. It lists replies that do not answer the question, such as a different question or barely more than a link.
- [GitLab Handbook usage](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/about/handbook-usage/), GitLab. It asks team members to link to the relevant handbook information when they answer questions.

definition.name: Post clear status and blocker updates
definition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured conversation: the turns the practice names, read in their surrounding context. Social chat and acknowledgements create no applicability for an unrelated communication practice. Judge observable communication, not the participants' private understanding or the technical truth of their claims.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: an update about ongoing work says where things stand and, when stuck, names the blocker and what would clear it.

## The standard
Judge whether an update about ongoing work tells the team where things stand and, when the author is stuck, names the blocker plainly along with what is needed to clear it. A clear update lets teammates plan around the work or step in to unblock it; an update so vague no one can tell whether help is needed leaves the team guessing. Judge only the observable clarity of the update, never whether the work itself is on track. Use judgment about how much an update needs to say: a brief "still on it, no blockers" among teammates already in sync is fine, and a real update made clear by its surrounding context is a good update, not a missing one. The review is about the frozen developer in `about.developerId`. Judge only turns whose `accountId` equals that decimal-string id. The other turns are context. Never assign another participant’s words to this developer.

## Applicability
This is a gate. Record DOES_NOT_APPLY, name the fact, and stop when the turn is not a status update, when there is no in-flight work or blocker to report, or when there is no settled conversation to read. A real update whose standing or blocker is established by the surrounding turns is not DOES_NOT_APPLY; it is MET.

## Sources
1. The update turn (`context/conversation_thread.json`): what it says about the current standing, whether it reports being blocked, what it names as the blocker and what it asks for. It establishes the clarity of the update as posted. It never establishes whether the work is actually on track or whether the blocker is real.
2. The surrounding turns of the same thread (`context/conversation_thread.json`): earlier turns may already establish the standing an update omits, or show that the teammates are in sync; a later turn that has to ask what is needed shows what the update left unsaid. They establish what was shared inside the captured thread and nothing outside it.
An image or attachment in a turn: read its caption and the sentence around it. An external link: nothing. When an update IS posted but the thread begins mid-conversation, so you cannot tell whether the standing it omits was already established, report a collection gap and record no result; that is neither absent nor COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.

## Judge
Assess conformance to the standard in this context.
- MET: the update states the current standing and, if blocked, says what is blocking and what would unblock it — from the turn alone or from the turn plus the surrounding thread.
- NOT_MET: an update on stalled or in-flight work that hides a blocker behind a vague line, or reports being stuck without naming what is actually needed, so no one can plan or help. Quote the vague line and name what the team cannot tell from it.
- COULD_NOT_DETERMINE only when every declared turn was captured and the update's meaning still genuinely admits incompatible readings; quote the ambiguity and say what would settle it. A thread that begins mid-conversation is a collection gap, not COULD_NOT_DETERMINE.
One result per practice per review, on the update turn you assessed.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on update clarity alone — a formative practice, never a gate. Scale to how much the update leaves the team unable to plan or help. MINOR, the usual band: the standing is clear but the ask is fuzzy. MAJOR: a real blocker is present yet the update gives the team nothing to act on.

## Grounding
Quote the update you assessed. For MET where the surrounding turns supply the standing or the ask, quote those turns too. For NOT_MET, quote the vague line and the turns you read around it. Describe the observable gap — "the update says it is blocked and names no blocker" — never avoidance or intent. Never invent a blocker the author did not mention, and never claim the work is or is not on track.

## Defer
Whether a question posed in the thread carries enough context to answer belongs to `asks-answerable-questions`; whether a reply moves the asker forward belongs to `gives-actionable-answers`. Here only: does the update tell the team where things stand and what would unblock them?

guidance.whyItMatters: When work stalls quietly, the people depending on it keep waiting without knowing anything is wrong, and a blocker someone else could have cleared in minutes sits for days. A plain update on where things stand and what you need keeps the team moving.
guidance.whatGoodLooksLike: An update that says where the work stands and, when you are stuck, names the blocker and what would unblock it, so teammates can plan around it or step in to help.
guidance.goingWell: Updates say where the work stands and what blocks it

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Start with where the work stands, such as done, in progress or blocked.
- If you are stuck, name the blocker plainly. For example, instead of “Still stuck”, write “Blocked: the test server fails because its access key is missing”.
- Say what would clear the blocker, such as access, a decision or a review. Naming someone who can help can make the request clearer.
- If teammates need to plan around your work, say what comes next. Do not list everything you did since the last update.
- If teammates might wonder whether you need help, say whether anything blocks you. A short “No blockers” answers that.

## When it does not apply

- Your message is not a status update.
- You have no work in progress and no blocker to report.
- The conversation has not settled yet.

It still applies when earlier messages in the thread already say where the work stands or what blocks it. Then a short update that relies on them is a clear update.

## Common mistakes

- Hiding a blocker because it sounds like bad news. The practice looks at how clear your update is, not at whether the work is on track. Say plainly that you’re blocked.
- Padding a short update. Among teammates who already know the work, “Still on it, no blockers” is enough. Add detail when the team needs it to plan or to help.
- Saying you’re stuck with no ask, such as “Kind of stuck on this”. Then a teammate has to reply and ask what you need. Instead, say what you need in the same update.
- Listing everything you did since the last update. That rarely starts a discussion that solves a problem. Instead, name what comes next and what is in the way.

## Sources

- [The Scrum Guide](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html#daily-scrum), Schwaber and Sutherland, 2020. The Daily Scrum checks progress toward the goal and helps the team find what blocks its work.
- [Daily stand-up meetings: start breaking the rules](https://doi.org/10.1109/MS.2018.2875988), Stray, Moe and Sjøberg, 2020. In 102 observed stand-ups, a next task or an obstacle usually led to talk about solutions. Past work rarely did.
- [Engineering communication](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/workflow/engineering-comms/#sending-status-updates-to-engineering-fyi), GitLab Handbook. GitLab asks for updates on what was completed and what is blocked or at risk. It also asks you to tag relevant people as needed.
